notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [א] שֶׁמַּאֲרֶכֶת שְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל אָדָם
notes.body_html: Yoma 86b: R’ Shmuel bar Nachmani said: Great is teshuvah, for it lengthens a person’s years (per the Bach’s reading: “his days and his years”), as it says (Yechezkel 18), “and when a wicked man turns back from his wickedness — he shall live.”

notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 38:5: “הָלוֹךְ וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶל חִזְקִיָּהוּ, כֹּה אָמַר ה׳ אֱלֹקֵי דָּוִד אָבִיךָ: שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת תְּפִלָּתֶךָ, רָאִיתִי אֶת דִּמְעָתֶךָ, הִנְנִי יוֹסִף עַל יָמֶיךָ חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה” — “Go and say to Chizkiyahu: Thus says Hashem, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears; behold, I am adding onto your days fifteen years.” Context: Chizkiyahu HaMelech, mortally ill, “turned his face to the wall” and prayed; Yeshayahu — who had told him “you shall die and not live” (a sealed decree; cf. Berachos 10a) — is sent back with this reprieve. Rashi: the fifteen years granted after his prayer. R’ Tzadok’s use: Chizkiyahu’s teshuvah, awakened “with such force as to burst through all the fences, decrees, and boundaries set upon his life,” drew down the deathless vitality of Yaakov — the very model of how teshuvah “lengthens a person’s years.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: ״עַד פֹּה תָבוֹא״
notes.body_html: Iyov 38:11: “וָאֹמַר עַד פֹּה תָבוֹא וְלֹא תֹסִיף, וּפֹא יָשִׁית בִּגְאוֹן גַּלֶּיךָ” — “and I said: until here you shall come and no further; and here shall your proud waves be stayed.” From God’s answer to Iyov out of the whirlwind, of the sea whose bounds He fixed at creation. Meforshim (Rashi): God set a limit (gevul) upon the sea, that it not overflow the dry land. R’ Tzadok’s use: “ad po tavo ve-lo tosif” is the archetype of the fixed boundary — the limit the Creator set upon every created thing, including the span of a man’s life; and teshuvah of the rung of Yaakov reaches “the inheritance of Yaakov without straits [bli metzarim],” beyond all such bounds, so that “death has no relevance to him.”

notes.body_html: Shabbos 118a: “Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: Whoever delights in the Shabbos is given a boundless inheritance [nachalah bli metzarim], as it says (Yeshayahu 58:14), ‘Then you shall delight upon Hashem, [and I will cause you to ride upon the high places of the earth,] and I will feed you the inheritance of Yaakov your father’ — not the inheritance of Avraham, of whom it is written ‘arise, walk the land, to its length and to its breadth’ [a bounded measure], nor of Yitzchak, of whom it is written ‘for to you and to your seed I will give all these lands,’ but the inheritance of Yaakov, of whom it is written (Bereishis 28:14), ‘and you shall spread forth to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south’ [without limit].” (Yaakov’s inheritance alone is ‘without straits’ — the boundlessness the se’if identifies with his deathlessness.)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi §6): "“but Yisrael shall be your name” — and this name is called so because he defeated Samael, the minister of Esav, who is the Satan and the yetzer hara, as is known." Exactly the se’if: the name Yaakov bears is the one won over the very power whose whole instrument is death — which is why “death has no relevance to him.”

notes.body_html: Taanis 5b: R’ Yochanan said: Yaakov Avinu did not die. [Rav Nachman] objected, “was it for nothing that the eulogizers eulogized, the embalmers embalmed, and the buriers buried him?!” He replied, “I am expounding a verse — as it says (Yirmeyah 30), ‘and you, fear not, My servant Yaakov, says Hashem — for behold I save you from afar and your offspring from the land of their captivity’ — Scripture likens him to his offspring: just as his offspring are alive, so too is he alive.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל דּוֹר וָדוֹר בִּכְלָל הוּא נֶפֶשׁ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzadik, Lag BaOmer §3): “[Yaakov] did not die, but was only as one asleep — as it is written, ‘Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust’ (Yeshayah 26:19); and as expounded in the Gemara (Taanis 5b), ‘He likens him to his offspring — just as his offspring are alive, so is he alive.’ And since ‘there is no partial analogy,’ He likewise likens his offspring to him: that all the seed of Yaakov will [in the end] be clarified to stand in the level of ‘Yaakov did not die.’ And when [each one] is roused from his sleep, he will remember all the words of Torah; and concerning this we plead, ‘let us not be forgotten by You — neither in this world nor in the World to Come.’”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל דּוֹר וָדוֹר בִּכְלָל הוּא נֶפֶשׁ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §40): “and they said (Taanis) ‘Yaakov Avinu did not die — he is likened to his offspring’; and this is ‘Yaakov who redeemed Avraham’ (Yeshayah 29:22) — for from the levels of Avraham and Yitzchak alone, which are the seeking of the love of Hashem and His fear in the ultimate clarification, salvation [from death] would not have been compelled.” This is §6-1’s own verse (Taanis 5b, makish hu l’zaro): Yaakov “does not die” because his life is the life of his offspring — and his rung so surpasses even Avraham and Yitzchak that he “redeems” them, the deathless root of every generation.Chassidic parallel - Sefat Emet, Vayechi 22:3 and 4:3: Sefat Emet gives an especially close Chassidic formulation of the life of Yaakov that R. Tzadok is invoking here. On "Yaakov Avinu lo meis," he explains that Yaakov "left all of his power within Klal Yisrael," so that his force can be awakened in Israel in every generation; elsewhere in Vayechi he explains that Yaakov drew the hidden vitality of Torah even into Egypt, and that through the middah of emes one can find life within the concealment of galus itself. This complements R. Tzadok's use of Taanis 5b: the "lengthening of years" produced by teshuvah is not merely an extension of biological time. Teshuvah reconnects the individual to the undying root of Yaakov, whose life persists in his descendants and can be reawakened within them. In that sense, the penitent's renewed life is a participation in a life that was never severed by death in the first place. The Sefat Emet also helps explain why R. Tzadok immediately moves from Yaakov himself to his seed: Yaakov's immortality is revealed precisely through the continuity of the souls and avodah of Israel.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [ב] וְהִנֵּה תּוֹלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב יוֹסֵף, שֶׁהוּא עִיקַּר תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו
notes.body_html: Bereishis 37:2: “אֵלֶּה תֹּלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב: יוֹסֵף בֶּן שְׁבַע עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת אֶחָיו בַּצֹּאן” — “these are the offspring of Yaakov: Yosef…” The opening of the Yosef narrative (Vayeishev). Rashi: Scripture reckons the whole line of Yaakov’s toldos through Yosef — because Yaakov served Lavan only for [Rachel] Yosef’s mother, because Yosef’s features resembled his, and because all that befell Yaakov befell Yosef. R’ Tzadok takes “toldos Yaakov Yosef” to mean that Yosef is Yaakov’s essential offspring — the shomer ha-bris (guardian of the covenant) — so that Israel is called “the remnant of Yosef,” the holy root-soul of Yaakov borne onward through him.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 84:8: “‘And Yisrael loved Yosef’ (Bereishis 37:3) — R’ Yehuda and R’ Nechemya [expound it]: R’ Yehuda says, because the radiance of [Yosef’s] countenance [ziv ikonin] resembled his [Yaakov’s]; R’ Nechemya said, [because] all the halachos that Shem and Ever had transmitted to Yaakov, he transmitted to him [Yosef].” (Both readings underlie the se’if: Yosef is Yaakov’s ‘essential offspring’ — mirroring his father’s very form and his Torah.)

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל שְׁמוֹ ״שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף״
notes.body_html: Amos 5:15: “שִׂנְאוּ רָע וְאֶהֱבוּ טוֹב וְהַצִּיגוּ בַשַּׁעַר מִשְׁפָּט, אוּלַי יֶחֱנַן ה׳ אֱלֹקֵי צְבָאוֹת שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף” — “hate evil and love good, and establish justice in the gate; perhaps Hashem, God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Yosef.” From Amos’s call to repentance. Meforshim: “she’eris Yosef” is the remnant of Israel, called by Yosef’s name. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel is called “the remnant of Yosef” because Yosef, the guardian of the covenant, “comprises the souls of Israel in every generation” — and therefore even the transgressors of Israel are included in “the remnant of Yosef — all of them tzaddikim.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְנֶאֱמַר ״וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״
notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 60:21: “וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים, לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ, נֵצֶר מַטָּעַי מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי לְהִתְפָּאֵר” — “and your people are all tzaddikim; they shall inherit the land forever; the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which to glory.” From Yeshaya’s prophecy of Zion’s future glory. Meforshim: in the future all Israel will be found righteous (the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 90a, opens “all Israel have a share in the World to Come” from this verse). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the middah of all Israel — “kulam,” even the transgressors and the wholly wicked — for the essential meaning of “tzaddik” is a guardian of the covenant like Yosef; every Jew’s root is holy, whatever appears to the eye.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּעִיקַּר שֵׁם ״צַדִּיק״ — שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית כְּיוֹסֵף
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §4): “‘your people are all tzaddikim’ — guardians of the covenant; and therefore, from the revelation of the illumination of yesod abba, comes the rectification of the bris and the fulfillment of milah, the sign of the holy covenant in every Jew.” This is §6-2 precisely: the essential title tzaddik is the shomer habris like Yosef, and it is this guarded covenant that makes “all Israel tzaddikim” — the holy root that no outward “orlah” can reach.

notes.body_html: Nedarim 31a (Mishnah): “One who vows [not to benefit] ‘from the arelim [the uncircumcised]’ is permitted [to benefit] from the uncircumcised of Israel and forbidden from the circumcised of the nations — for ‘orlah’ [uncircumcision] is called only after the name of the nations, as it says (Yirmeyah 9:25), ‘for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the House of Israel are uncircumcised of heart.’” (Hence even an ‘uncircumcised’ Jew is essentially ‘circumcised’: orlah is, in its root, a name belonging to the nations alone.)

notes.body_html: Eruvin 19a: Reish Lakish taught that the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the transgressors of Israel, and that Avraham Avinu raises them up [by the sign of the covenant] — “except for a Jew who cohabited with a gentile woman, for his foreskin is drawn [moshech orlaso] and he is not recognized.” (As the se’if explains, this means only that the sign is not outwardly recognizable — not that he is truly ‘arel’; a mashuch is not really uncircumcised.)

notes.body_html: Pesachim 56a (and Vayikra Rabbah 36:5) — “mittaso shleimah”: the Gemara relates that as Yaakov lay dying he feared there might be a blemish in his “bed” (as Avraham had produced Yishmael, and Yitzchak, Esav); his sons declared, “Shema Yisrael, Hashem Elokeinu Hashem echad — just as in your heart there is [but] One, so in ours,” whereupon Yaakov responded “Baruch shem kevod malchuso le-olam va’ed.” The Sages conclude that Yaakov’s bed was whole [mittaso shleimah] — all his offspring were worthy, none cast off (so too Vayikra Rabbah 36:5). R’ Tzadok’s use: “mittaso shleimah” means all his offspring were [conceived] in holiness, for Yaakov completed the rectification of Adam’s sin (which was rooted in desire); hence no true “dross” issues from him — and the same holds of all Israel, his seed.

notes.body_html: Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 (on “behold, in iniquity was I fashioned,” Tehillim 51:7): R’ Acha said: even the most pious of the pious cannot be wholly free of some trace of iniquity. David said before the Holy One, “Master of the worlds — did my father Yishai intend to bring me into being? He intended only his own pleasure” And this is [the meaning of] what they said in Shabbos 55b: “Four died [solely] through the counsel of the serpent [i.e., without personal sin]: Binyamin son of Yaakov, Amram father of Moshe, Yishai father of David, and Kilav son of David.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: הַיְינוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הֲסָתַת הַנָּחָשׁ בְּחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §258): “‘More precious than wisdom and honor is a little folly’ (Koheles 10:1) — for there must be in every person at least a small measure of folly, and this [very thing] is [the mark of] wholeness; only that it is good for a man that this folly be as minimal as possible — and the two [evil] inclinations are desire, and the murderous [inclination of] anger, which stem from Adam and Chavah through the serpent’s incitement, and from Kayin. And this is [why] ‘the counsel of the serpent’ [etyo shel nachash] is in every person — as the Sages said (Yoma 69b), ‘the world has need of it’ [the inclination] and it cannot be nullified. This is the indispensable ‘little folly,’ [needed] in any case for the world’s continuance.” (Thus even a tzaddik like Yishai bears “the counsel of the serpent” not as a personal sin but as the residual, world-sustaining root of desire.)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §18): “as they said (Shabbos 55b) that [Yishai] died through the counsel of the serpent — and from yesod comes malchus… the beginning of the [royal] choice was in one of the sons of Yishai, for the father earns [merit] for his son.” This lights up §6-2’s “they said of Yishai that he died b’etyo shel nachash — the root of the serpent’s incitement in Adam’s sin”: even flawless Yishai tasted death only from that primordial counsel, yet from his guarded yesod issued the malchus of David — “dross” that is, in truth, no dross at all.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 2:25: “וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים, הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ, וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ” — “and the two of them were naked, the man and his wife, and they were not ashamed.” The state of Adam and Chavah before the sin. Rashi: they did not yet know the way of modesty, to distinguish good from evil — before the sin no yetzer hara stirred bodily desire, so there was no shame. R’ Tzadok’s use: shame entered only after the sin, when “they felt bodily pleasure”; Yaakov, by contrast, “felt no bodily pleasure whatever,” intending solely to establish offspring — hence “his bed was whole,” free of the shame that Adam’s sin drew into the world.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 74:18: “And Yaakov said to Lavan, ‘give me my wife’” (Bereishis 29:21). R’ Aivu said: even a licentious man does not speak in such [blunt] language! Rather Yaakov said: the Holy One told me I would raise up twelve tribes; now I am about eighty-four years old — if I do not raise them up now, when? — therefore, “give me my wife.” [His blunt words were not from desire but from an urgent, holy intent to establish the tribes.]

notes.body_html: Yechezkel 36:26: “וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ וְרוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם, וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת לֵב הָאֶבֶן מִבְּשַׂרְכֶם וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר” — “and I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” From Yechezkel’s prophecy of Israel’s future purification. Meforshim: the stubborn “heart of stone” will be replaced by a responsive heart. R’ Tzadok reads “lev basar” at its depth — a heart that removes [the pull of] flesh — so that in the Future the marital act will be, like Yaakov’s, “as the donning of tefillin,” a pure mitzvah to which no shame applies.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל כֵּן ״מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה״, דְּשׁוֹמֵר מִצְוָה לֹא יֵדַע דָּבָר רָע
notes.body_html: Koheles 8:5: “שׁוֹמֵר מִצְוָה לֹא יֵדַע דָּבָר רָע, וְעֵת וּמִשְׁפָּט יֵדַע לֵב חָכָם” — “one who guards a mitzvah will know no evil thing; and a wise heart knows time and judgment.” From Shlomo’s counsel (Koheles 8). Meforshim: one engaged in a mitzvah is shielded from harm (cf. “those on a mission of mitzvah are not harmed,” Pesachim 8b). R’ Tzadok’s use: “shomer mitzvah lo yeda davar ra” proves that “his bed was whole” — it is entirely impossible that a sin or evil thing should issue from a mitzvah; the “dross” that appears in one’s offspring comes only through the admixture of bodily pleasures drawn from “the counsel of the serpent,” never from the mitzvah itself.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּאָמְרִי עֲלֵיהּ ״אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם״
notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 29:22 (with Sanhedrin 19b): “לָכֵן כֹּה אָמַר ה׳ אֶל בֵּית יַעֲקֹב אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם: לֹא עַתָּה יֵבוֹשׁ יַעֲקֹב, וְלֹא עַתָּה פָּנָיו יֶחֱוָרוּ” — “therefore thus says Hashem to the House of Yaakov, who redeemed Avraham: not now shall Yaakov be ashamed, nor now shall his face pale.” The phrase “who redeemed Avraham” is difficult (where do we find that Yaakov redeemed Avraham?). The Gemara (Sanhedrin 19b) resolves: Yaakov redeemed Avraham from the anguish of raising children [tza’ar giddul banim] — Avraham was spared distress over his descendants once Yaakov came, all of whose children were worthy. R’ Tzadok’s use: the completion of the rectification of Adam’s sin was in Yaakov — so that Avraham and Yitzchak too were “clarified” and, retroactively, “called Yaakov”; only Yaakov is, in the fullest sense, “the seed” of the Avos, and their “beds” too are reckoned whole, the “dross” (Yishmael, Esav) being no true part of their seed.

notes.body_html: Shabbos 118a — “nachalah bli metzarim”: R’ Yochanan said in the name of R’ Yosi, whoever delights in the Shabbos is granted “a boundless inheritance [nachalah bli metzarim],” as it says (Yeshaya 58:14), “then you shall delight in Hashem… and I will feed you the inheritance of Yaakov your father” — not the bounded inheritance promised to Avraham (“arise, walk the length and breadth of the land”) or to Yitzchak, but the unbounded inheritance of Yaakov, of whom it says “u-faratzta — you shall spread out to the west and east, north and south” (Bereishis 28:14). R’ Tzadok’s use (recurring from §1): the whole “power of Yaakov” is this “inheritance without boundaries”; the “boundaries” of this world exist only “according to the revealed appearance to the eye,” but in the inward truth the seed of Yaakov is beyond all straits — so that any apparent “dross” among the poshei Yisrael is only external.Izhbitz-Radzin and Sefat Emet parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Anthology, Collectanea, Siddur 1; Sefat Emet, Vayera 30:3: The Izhbitz-Radzin tradition sharply supports the distinction in this se'if between the holy root of the Jewish soul and the external corruption produced by sin. Mei HaShiloach teaches on "Neshamah shenasata bi tehorah hi" that the neshamah itself is never reached by cheit or pegam; nefesh remains joined to the body, while ruach signifies the faculty of bechirah through which a person chooses good and rejects evil. Thus sin is terribly real at the level of choice and embodied life, but it does not rewrite the deepest origin of the neshamah. Sefat Emet, Vayera 30:3, develops the complementary side: Israel are "zera emes" because their souls extend from beginning to end, and the bris is meant to bring the body itself into correspondence with the holy neshamah. This illuminates R. Tzadok's insistence that even poshei Yisrael retain the name and root of tzaddikim. The dross can cover, distort, and damage the vessel, but it is not the essential identity of the soul. Teshuvah therefore does not manufacture a new Jewish essence; it uncovers and re-aligns the embodied person with the holy root that remained intact beneath the concealment.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: זֶה לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה עֲדַיִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַד שֶׁיְּבֻלַּע הַמָּוֶת
notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 25:8: “בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח, וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי ה׳ דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים” — “He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord God will wipe away tears from every face.” From Yeshaya’s prophecy of the end of days (ch. 25). Meforshim (Rashi; and the Sages, Kesuvos 111b) take “bila ha-maves la-netzach” to mean that death — decreed on mankind through Adam’s sin — is abolished in the World to Come. R’ Tzadok’s use here: the measure of Yaakov Avinu himself, “that he did not die at all,” cannot yet be revealed in this world until death is swallowed up — a world still ruled by death cannot contain an openly deathless man; therefore “him too the buriers buried and the embalmers embalmed,” the outward “death” that this world’s concealment requires. (The verse is treated also at Siman 3 §5.)
notes.body_plain: Yeshayahu 25:8: “בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח, וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי ה׳ דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים” — “He will swallow up death forever , and the Lord God will wipe away tears from every face.” From Yeshaya’s prophecy of the end of days (ch. 25). Meforshim (Rashi; and the Sages, Kesuvos 111b) take “ bila ha-maves la-netzach ” to mean that death — decreed on mankind through Adam’s sin — is abolished in the World to Come. R’ Tzadok’s use here: the measure of Yaakov Avinu himself, “that he did not die at all,” cannot yet be revealed in this world until death is swallowed up — a world still ruled by death cannot contain an openly deathless man; therefore “him too the buriers buried and the embalmers embalmed,” the outward “death” that this world’s concealment requires. (The verse is treated also at Siman 3 §5.)

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְזֶה נִקְרָא יוֹסֵף לְשׁוֹן הוֹסָפָה
notes.body_html: Bereishis 30:24 (the name Yosef): “וַתִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ יוֹסֵף לֵאמֹר, יֹסֵף ה׳ לִי בֵּן אַחֵר” — “and she called his name Yosef, saying, ‘May Hashem add [yosef] to me another son.’” Rachel, upon bearing Yosef (Vayeitzei). Rashi: the name is from the root y-s-f, “to add” — her prayer for an additional son. R’ Tzadok’s use: the name itself — “Yosef, a term of addition [hosafah]” — expresses the very mode by which Yaakov’s deathless vitality persists in this world: not as his own continued life, but as the adding of ever more souls of the seed of Israel in each generation.

notes.body_html: Berachos 10a: When Yeshayahu told Chizkiyahu “you shall die and not live” (Yeshayahu 38:1) — because “you did not engage in the mitzvah of procreation” — Chizkiyahu answered that he had seen by ru’ach ha-kodesh that unworthy children would issue from him. Yeshayahu replied: “What have you to do with the secrets of the Merciful One? What you are commanded, you are obligated to do.” Chizkiyahu said: “Then give me your daughter — perhaps my merit together with yours will cause worthy children to issue from me.” (Only after he accepted to marry and beget were his years lengthened.)

notes.body_html: Yevamos 50a: It was taught: “‘the number of your days I will fill’ (Shemos 23) — these are the years preordained to a person at birth. If he merits, they complete [the full span] for him; if he does not merit, they reduce it — the words of R’ Akiva. And the Sages say: if he merits, they add to him; if not, they reduce.” They said to R’ Akiva: does it not say (II Melachim 20), “I will add to your days fifteen years” [to Chizkiyahu]? He answered: they added to him “from his own” [preordained allotment]. [R’ Akiva holds that merit “completes” one’s years rather than truly “adds” to them.]

notes.body_html: Yechezkel 18:27 (and 33:19): the phrase “through his return from his wickedness — he shall live” draws on the teshuvah-prophecy of Yechezkel: “וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה, וַיַּעַשׂ מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה — הוּא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ יְחַיֶּה” (18:27), and “וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ… עֲלֵיהֶם הוּא יִחְיֶה” (33:19) — “when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, he keeps his soul alive.” Meforshim (Rashi, Radak): the penitent who turns from evil thereby lives. R’ Tzadok’s use: it is precisely by delving deeper in teshuvah and cleaving to the living God that one merits not merely the pushing-off of the decree (Chizkiyahu’s lower rung) but true life and length of days — “through this he shall live.”

notes.body_html: Devarim 9:4–5: “אַל תֹּאמַר בִּלְבָבְךָ… בְּצִדְקָתִי הֱבִיאַנִי ה׳ לָרֶשֶׁת אֶת הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת… לֹא בְצִדְקָתְךָ וּבְיֹשֶׁר לְבָבְךָ אַתָּה בָא לָרֶשֶׁת אֶת אַרְצָם, כִּי בְּרִשְׁעַת הַגּוֹיִם הָאֵלֶּה ה׳ אֱלֹקֶיךָ מוֹרִישָׁם מִפָּנֶיךָ” — “Do not say in your heart [when Hashem drives them out], ‘in my righteousness Hashem has brought me to possess this land’… not through your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart do you come to possess their land, but through the wickedness of these nations…” Moshe’s warning to Israel on the threshold of the Land. Rashi: they inherit it through the wickedness of the nations and the merit of the Avos — not their own righteousness. R’ Tzadok’s use: this admonition is addressed precisely to the perfect tzaddik — the “addition” / Yosef rung — who is liable to the illusion that he is “better than his Cause and his Root,” failing to recognize that “the essence of whatever good he has is only from Him.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §36): “‘I am a shield [Magen] to you’ — as they said, ‘were it not that the Holy One helps him, [a person could not withstand the yetzer]’ (Sukkah 52b); ‘and I will guard them, lest they stumble in the yetzer hara with no recovery.’” This is the ground of §6-3’s warning to the perfect tzaddik not to say “through my righteousness”: even the tzaddik stands only because “the Holy One helps him” — the good is never his own doing, so the “addition” that seems to exceed its Root is, in truth, wholly a gift.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Korach §6): “he was not aware of this at all, and held no credit to himself — he looked only to Hashem who chose him, and not to his own power at all, as it says, ‘and what is Aharon [that you murmur against him]?’” This is §6-3’s tzaddik who does not stumble into the pride the se’if warns of: the rung of “addition” tempts one to “think he is truly better,” but Aharon — the very embodiment of drawing-near — took no credit, seeing all his good as flowing from the One who chose him.Chassidic parallel - Chiddushei HaRim on Torah, Chayei Sara 1; Sefat Emet, Vayechi 4:3: Chiddushei HaRim makes the relation between teshuvah and "length of days" unusually explicit. Commenting on Sarah's years, he notes the Zoharic principle that through teshuvah "in one hour and in one moment" a person can repair days that have already passed as though those days had been filled with mitzvos and good deeds; this is the deeper meaning of willful sins becoming merits. The point closely complements R. Tzadok's distinction here between merely postponing a decree of death and true arichus yamim. A penitent does not only receive additional days at the end of life; teshuvah can restore content and holiness to days already spent. Sefat Emet, Vayechi 4:3, adds that Yaakov drew a hidden current of life even into Egypt and that "Yaakov Avinu did not die" can be found by seeking the concealed Torah-life within exile. Read together, these sources sharpen R. Tzadok's claim: genuine lengthening of life reaches backward as well as forward. It is the recovery of the life concealed in apparently lost time, rooted in Yaakov's deathless emes rather than simply an extension of the calendar.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §206): “All the imaginings and stray musings in a person are fixed in three roots — envy, desire, and honor [kinah, taavah, kavod] — which are the roots of the evil traits; and the root of [these] roots is haughtiness [gaavah], as is known, for the root of evil is from the World of Tohu and the ‘shattering of the vessels,’ which came about through the thought ‘I shall reign’ [ana emloch]. And from this the evil inclination [yetzer] is born — for ‘yetzer’ means a [stray] thought and musing in the heart, for there is the beginning of evil in the heart, as they said (Berachos 61a), ‘[the evil inclination] sits at the two entrances of the heart.’”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְגַאֲוָה הוּא נֶגֶד מִדַּת אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב שֶׁמִּדָּתוֹ עֲנָוָה
notes.body_html: Michah 7:20: “תִּתֵּן אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב, חֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם, אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּעְתָּ לַאֲבֹתֵינוּ מִימֵי קֶדֶם” — “You will grant truth to Yaakov, kindness to Avraham, which You swore to our fathers from days of old” — the sealing verse of Michah’s prophecy of pardon. Rashi: God will fulfill the oath of emes toward Yaakov and chesed toward Avraham. The Sages pair each Patriarch with a middah — Avraham = Chesed, Yitzchak = Gevurah/Pachad, Yaakov = Emes/Tiferes. R’ Tzadok’s use: “emes le-Yaakov” — truth is Yaakov’s middah, and its lived trait is anavah (humility), the opposite of gaavah (haughtiness, which is itself falsehood); therefore haughtiness stands “this-opposite-that” to Yaakov, the third of the three roots of impurity (envy, desire, honor) over against the three Avos.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 93:1: “ה׳ מָלָךְ גֵּאוּת לָבֵשׁ, לָבֵשׁ ה׳ עֹז הִתְאַזָּר, אַף תִּכּוֹן תֵּבֵל בַּל תִּמּוֹט” — “Hashem reigns, He has clothed Himself in majesty [ge’us]; Hashem has clothed Himself, girded Himself with strength…” (the Shir shel Yom of Erev Shabbos). Meforshim: “majesty/loftiness” is ascribed to God as a garment — outward adornment, not essence. R’ Tzadok’s use: gaavah is falsehood — for even of Hashem “majesty” is spoken only “as a garment”; “He shows Himself lofty over the lofty, but to the lowly He gives grace and honor” (cf. Mishlei 3:34, “to the humble He gives grace”), and “in the place of His greatness, there you find His humility” (Megillah 31a). True greatness is thus inseparable from humility — the middah of Yaakov.

notes.body_html: Iyov 31:2: “וּמֶה חֵלֶק אֱלוֹקַּ מִמָּעַל, וְנַחֲלַת שַׁדַּי מִמְּרֹמִים” — “and what is the portion of God from above, and the heritage of Shakai from on high?” From Iyov’s closing avowal (ch. 31). This half-verse became the classic proof-text (in the Zohar and the mussar tradition) that the neshamah is “a portion of God from above” — a Divine portion within man. R’ Tzadok’s use: man is composed of this exalted soul — “hewn from the world of the Throne, above the angels” — together with a body of dust, the utmost lowliness; and from the soul’s side comes the cleaving to Hashem, so that the very height of the soul is what makes man liable to the yetzer of pride.

Meforshim (Rashi, Metzudos): his heart was raised up — emboldened and exalted — in the service of God, a praiseworthy “loftiness of heart” (as opposed to sinful pride). R’ Tzadok’s use: there is a legitimate elevation of heart, from the side of the soul (the “portion of God from above”), which is the true cleaving to Hashem — yet “through this very loftiness the yetzer can insinuate coarseness of spirit,” turning genuine spiritual height into self-importance (as befell R. Elazar b’R. Shimon with his Torah).

notes.body_html: Taanis 20a: R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon, returning from his teacher’s house riding on a donkey by a riverbank, was in high spirits and conceited over how much Torah he had learned. A strikingly ugly man greeted him, “peace upon you, Rebbi,” but he did not return the greeting, saying, “Empty one! how ugly is that man — are all the people of your town as ugly as you?” The man replied, “I do not know; but go and tell the Craftsman who made me, ‘how ugly is this vessel You have made!’” Realizing he had sinned, he dismounted and prostrated himself before him [in apology].

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 1:5: “בְּטֶרֶם אֶצָּרְךָ בַבֶּטֶן יְדַעְתִּיךָ, וּבְטֶרֶם תֵּצֵא מֵרֶחֶם הִקְדַּשְׁתִּיךָ, נָבִיא לַגּוֹיִם נְתַתִּיךָ” — “Before I formed you in the belly I knew you, and before you emerged from the womb I sanctified you; a prophet to the nations I appointed you” — God’s word to Yirmeyahu at his calling. Rashi: he was designated for prophecy from before his birth. R’ Tzadok’s use: this seals the lesson of the “ugly man” and of Avos 2:8 — “if you have learned much Torah, do not hold the credit to yourself… for it is for this that you were fashioned [notzarta]”: whatever a person is and attains is “from the Craftsman who made him,” fixed already “before I formed you in the belly,” so the tzaddik must not suppose that his own striving is the cause — “the essence of whatever good he has is only from Him.”Maharal parallel - Netivot Olam, Netiv HaAnavah 3:2 and 7:2: Maharal's analysis of ga'avah clarifies why R. Tzadok places kavod and self-importance among the root forces opposed to Yaakov. In Netiv HaAnavah 3, Maharal describes pride as an improper "addition" to the person and compares the baal ga'avah to an asherah that grows upward as a foreign, idolatrous excrescence; ga'avah is thus bound to avodah zarah because the person gives independent weight and elevation to the self. In ch. 7 he adds a subtler warning: Torah itself is genuinely elevated, and a talmid chacham may therefore be exposed to a refined residue of pride precisely because of the objective greatness of Torah. The corrective is to be "soft like a reed": the higher the reed grows, the more it bends. This complements R. Tzadok's pairing of Yaakov's emes with anavah. Yaakov's greatness is not self-negation born of worthlessness, but the refusal to treat any excellence as self-generated. The more truth a person receives, the less room remains for autonomous self-glorification.
notes.body_plain: Yirmeyah 1:5: “בְּטֶרֶם אֶצָּרְךָ בַבֶּטֶן יְדַעְתִּיךָ, וּבְטֶרֶם תֵּצֵא מֵרֶחֶם הִקְדַּשְׁתִּיךָ, נָבִיא לַגּוֹיִם נְתַתִּיךָ” — “ Before I formed you in the belly I knew you , and before you emerged from the womb I sanctified you; a prophet to the nations I appointed you” — God’s word to Yirmeyahu at his calling. Rashi: he was designated for prophecy from before his birth. R’ Tzadok’s use: this seals the lesson of the “ugly man” and of Avos 2:8 — “ if you have learned much Torah, do not hold the credit to yourself… for it is for this that you were fashioned [notzarta] ”: whatever a person is and attains is “from the Craftsman who made him,” fixed already “before I formed you in the belly,” so the tzaddik must not suppose that his own striving is the cause — “the essence of whatever good he has is only from Him .”Maharal parallel - Netivot Olam, Netiv HaAnavah 3:2 and 7:2: Maharal's analysis of ga'avah clarifies why R. Tzadok places kavod and self-importance among the root forces opposed to Yaakov. In Netiv HaAnavah 3, Maharal describes pride as an improper "addition" to the person and compares the baal ga'avah to an asherah that grows upward as a foreign, idolatrous excrescence; ga'avah is thus bound to avodah zarah because the person gives independent weight and elevation to the self. In ch. 7 he adds a subtler warning: Torah itself is genuinely elevated, and a talmid chacham may therefore be exposed to a refined residue of pride precisely because of the objective greatness of Torah. The corrective is to be "soft like a reed": the higher the reed grows, the more it bends. This complements R. Tzadok's pairing of Yaakov's emes with anavah. Yaakov's greatness is not self-negation born of worthlessness, but the refusal to treat any excellence as self-generated. The more truth a person receives, the less room remains for autonomous self-glorification.

notes.body_html: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:5: the Rambam confronts the classic difficulty — if the Holy One foreknows whether a person will be righteous or wicked, how can his choice be free? He answers that God and His knowledge are one (His knowing is not something added to His essence), and therefore “it is not within the power of the human mind to grasp this matter clearly”; His manner of knowing is utterly unlike ours (“ein yedi’aseinu ki-yedi’aso”) — yet, he insists, “without doubt a person’s deeds are in his own hand,” and free choice is a firm foundation of the Torah. R’ Tzadok’s use: the Rambam’s very acknowledgment that he had “no [full] resolution” — for our knowing is not like His — is itself the true resolution: [Divine] knowledge and [human] choice occupy different “places,” and both are real.

notes.body_html: Hasagos HaRa’avad (ad loc.): R’ Avraham ben David objected that the Rambam “did not act in the manner of the wise — one should not begin a matter he cannot bring to completion; he opened with questions and difficulties and left the matter in a difficulty.” R’ Tzadok defends the Rambam against the charge: far from leaving it unresolved, the Rambam disclosed “the very summit of his knowledge” in recognizing that the human intellect cannot apprehend how God’s foreknowledge and man’s free choice cohere — and that recognition is the answer itself, “for our knowing is not like His knowing.”

notes.body_html: Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef: the “secret” of yedi’ah (Divine knowledge) and bechirah (free choice) is expounded in the Kabbalah — in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, and in Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef, a work of the Arizal’s Kabbalah (its title drawn from “four hundred silver shekels,” Bereishis 23:16). There the two are set on different planes of the supernal roots: from the side of God’s knowledge (the higher unity) there is no independent “choice,” while free choice belongs to the “place” of this lower world — so that the two do not contradict. R’ Tzadok points to these as the mystical ground of the principle that “in the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice there is no grasp of His knowledge.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §47): “One must ascend to Hashem through an inquiry that is above the grasp of the intellect. For with the human intellect it is impossible to grasp the truth of this matter fully, as is known — as the Rambam wrote concerning the difficulty of [Divine] foreknowledge and [human] free choice. Only the Children of Israel, upon whom the light of Torah — ‘in which truth is written’ — has shone, grasp this: the Torah-scholars, called by the name ‘Israel,’ grasp it by way of chochmah — and this is what the name ‘Israel’ denotes, from ‘for you have striven [with the Divine and with men and have prevailed]’ (Bereishis 32:29), that he became a ‘prince’ over the angels — and this is from the complete cleaving to the ultimate truth.” And Tzidkas HaTzaddik (os 40) puts it most pointedly — citing the very same source adduced here, the Arizal at the end of Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef: “The essence of teshuvah is that Hashem so illumine a person’s eyes that the willful sins become as merits — that is, that he recognize and understand that all he sinned was, too, by the will of Hashem… and this is the matter of yedi’ah and bechirah that the Arizal explained at the end of Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef: that both are true, each in its own place — in the place of choice there is no place for [His] knowledge, and in the place of [His] knowledge there is in truth no place for choice. And when one attains this tremendous light, then all his willful sins are [seen] never to have departed from the depth of Hashem’s knowledge — He, His knowing, and His will being all One; and since Hashem willed it so, all is indeed merits, and one attains the complete atonement of Yom Kippur.”

notes.body_html: Bereishis 28:20–21: “וַיִּדַּר יַעֲקֹב נֶדֶר לֵאמֹר: אִם יִהְיֶה אֱלֹקִים עִמָּדִי וּשְׁמָרַנִי בַּדֶּרֶךְ הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ […] וְשַׁבְתִּי בְשָׁלוֹם אֶל בֵּית אָבִי, וְהָיָה ה׳ לִי לֵאלֹקִים” — “and Yaakov vowed a vow, saying: If God will be with me and guard me on this way that I go… then Hashem will be a God to me.” Yaakov’s vow as he set out for Charan (Vayeitzei). Meforshim (Rashi, Ramban): Yaakov made his service depend on God’s help and protection. notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Poked Akarim §3): “from an arousal-from-Above entirely, in the sense of ‘draw me after You, we will run,’ and like the coercion of the mountain as a barrel at Sinai — that Hashem forced them, to show that they are rooted in the very essence of their root in holiness, and cannot detach themselves from the holiness of Israel.” This is §6-5’s “superior quality Israel has over converts”: for Israel “Hashem is a God to them first, and only then ‘and they’” — He draws them after Him (“draw me after You”), for their root is in Him; the convert, lacking that, must let his own effort come first.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ ״מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה״
notes.body_html: Shir HaShirim 1:4: “מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה” — “Draw me after You, we will run” (treated more fully at Siman 5 §5). In the love-allegory of the Holy One and Knesses Yisrael, Israel asks God to draw her first, and only then does she “run” after Him — the initial arousal must come from Above. R’ Tzadok’s use here: this is Israel’s superiority over converts — for Israel, Scripture places Hashem “as a God to them” first and “they [a people to Me]” only afterward (Kiddushin 70b); Israel apprehends that God alone directs “every detail of a person’s thoughts,” so the drawing precedes — whereas the convert reckons that his own effort came first.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Korach 2; Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 69:1: This se'if's yedi'ah-bechirah tension is central to Izhbitz, and the school itself supplies an important boundary against misunderstanding it. Mei HaShiloach, Korach 2, explains Korach's claim that at the deepest level "everything is in the hands of Heaven, even fear of Heaven." The teaching then says that Hashem specifically conceals this depth in olam ha-zeh so that human beings experience themselves as baalei bechirah and avodah can exist; if Divine direction were fully transparent, no meaningful human service would grow. Beit Yaakov, Bereshit 69:1, develops the same point through Kayin. Kayin argues "hashomer achi anochi" as though the overwhelming anger that led to Hevel's death proved that he had no choice. Hashem rejects that defense: the crying blood demonstrates that the deficiency lay in Kayin and that he did possess bechirah. These sources are a precise complement to R. Tzadok. "In truth all is from Hashem" is a truth disclosed from the deeper Divine perspective and, ultimately, after the avodah and teshuvah; it is not a practical heter before the act. Within the lived world of Torah, a person must treat the choice before him as real, binding, and his responsibility.

notes.body_html: Zohar, Vayeitzei (on “and Hashem saw that Leah was hated”): the editor adduces this passage for the importance of the matter — why was she hated? surely the children of a hated wife are not worthy children, yet we see that all the good sons issued from Leah! Rather, Leah corresponds to the concealed upper world (the Yovel / Binah / the world of teshuvah), all of whose matters are hidden; therefore her doings were hidden from Yaakov. Rachel corresponds to the revealed lower world (Malchus), the beginning of the ascent through the rungs. Yaakov cleaved by his outward will to the revealed (Rachel), in the secret of “and he shall cleave to his wife” — yet the “good sons” issue from the hidden root (Leah); for Yaakov corresponds to Zeir Anpin, son of Imma Ila’ah (Binah), and Rachel to the Nukva of Zeir Anpin (Malchus), called “daughter” to the supernal Abba and Imma.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 84:19: On “וַיָּשָׁב רְאוּבֵן אֶל הַבּוֹר” (Bereishis 37:29), the Midrash asks where Reuven had been, and answers that he was occupied “בְּשַׂקּוֹ וּבְתַעֲנִיתוֹ” — in his sackcloth and fasting, doing teshuvah for the matter of Bilhah (Bereishis 35:22). The Holy One said to him: “מֵעוֹלָם לֹא חָטָא אָדָם לְפָנַי וְעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, וְאַתָּה פָּתַחְתָּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה תְּחִלָּה — never has a person sinned before Me and repented, and you are the first to open with teshuvah; by your life, a descendant of yours will arise and be the first to open with teshuvah” — and who is that? Hoshea, as it says, “שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד ה׳ אֱלֹקֶיךָ” (Hoshea 14:2). The Yefe To’ar notes that Hoshea would be the first to teach teshuvah me-ahavah — repentance from love, whereby willful sins become as merits. R’ Tzadok’s use: Leah’s firstborn Reuven, and Hoshea of his line, are those who “grasp the distaff of hoda’ah / teshuvah” — the rung of Binah, the baal teshuvah who stands higher than the perfect tzaddik.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Shem MiShmuel, Vayetzei 9:15; Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut, Entrance to the Gate of Beit Yaakov 24:3-4: Shem MiShmuel explicitly identifies Rachel with alma d'isgalya and Leah with alma d'iskasya, and explains that their differing modes of avodah correspond to revealed and concealed spiritual attainment: Rachel's side is more readily expressed through revealed "aseh tov," while Leah's hidden heights are reached through the inward work of "sur mera." This closely fits R. Tzadok's contrast between the externally beautiful, revealed tzaddik-rung of Rachel and Leah's Binah/teshuvah, whose beauty is initially hidden. Sha'ar HaEmunah deepens the identification of teshuvah with Binah: complete teshuvah returns a person to the place of Binah and thereby reaches "above time," where past, present, and future are not divided in the ordinary way and the past can be healed. The work explicitly links this to "u-miBnei Yissachar yodei binah la'itim" - those who know how to heal the time. The hidden world is therefore not merely less visible than Rachel's world; it is the level from which a person's apparently fixed history can be reread and repaired.
notes.body_plain: Bereishis Rabbah 84:19: On “וַיָּשָׁב רְאוּבֵן אֶל הַבּוֹר” (Bereishis 37:29), the Midrash asks where Reuven had been, and answers that he was occupied “בְּשַׂקּוֹ וּבְתַעֲנִיתוֹ” — in his sackcloth and fasting, doing teshuvah for the matter of Bilhah (Bereishis 35:22). The Holy One said to him: “מֵעוֹלָם לֹא חָטָא אָדָם לְפָנַי וְעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, וְאַתָּה פָּתַחְתָּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה תְּחִלָּה — never has a person sinned before Me and repented, and you are the first to open with teshuvah; by your life, a descendant of yours will arise and be the first to open with teshuvah” — and who is that? Hoshea, as it says, “שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד ה׳ אֱלֹקֶיךָ” (Hoshea 14:2). The Yefe To’ar notes that Hoshea would be the first to teach teshuvah me-ahavah — repentance from love, whereby willful sins become as merits. R’ Tzadok’s use: Leah’s firstborn Reuven, and Hoshea of his line, are those who “grasp the distaff of hoda’ah / teshuvah” — the rung of Binah , the baal teshuvah who stands higher than the perfect tzaddik.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Shem MiShmuel, Vayetzei 9:15; Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut, Entrance to the Gate of Beit Yaakov 24:3-4: Shem MiShmuel explicitly identifies Rachel with alma d'isgalya and Leah with alma d'iskasya, and explains that their differing modes of avodah correspond to revealed and concealed spiritual attainment: Rachel's side is more readily expressed through revealed "aseh tov," while Leah's hidden heights are reached through the inward work of "sur mera." This closely fits R. Tzadok's contrast between the externally beautiful, revealed tzaddik-rung of Rachel and Leah's Binah/teshuvah, whose beauty is initially hidden. Sha'ar HaEmunah deepens the identification of teshuvah with Binah: complete teshuvah returns a person to the place of Binah and thereby reaches "above time," where past, present, and future are not divided in the ordinary way and the past can be healed. The work explicitly links this to "u-miBnei Yissachar yodei binah la'itim" - those who know how to heal the time. The hidden world is therefore not merely less visible than Rachel's world; it is the level from which a person's apparently fixed history can be reread and repaired.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 29:31: “וַיַּרְא ה׳ כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה, וַיִּפְתַּח אֶת רַחְמָהּ, וְרָחֵל עֲקָרָה” — “And Hashem saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb, while Rachel was barren” (Vayeitzei). Rashi: “hated” cannot mean Yaakov literally hated her — rather, He saw that the deeds of Esav were hateful to her (she had wept and prayed lest she fall to Esav’s lot), and rewarded her with children first. This verse is the axis of the whole se’if: the “hatred” is not Yaakov’s toward Leah — which would violate “lo sisna” (Vayikra 19:17) — but Leah’s inward loathing of Esav’s evil; and yet the plain sense stands too (“ein mikra yotzei midei peshuto”).

notes.body_html: Vayikra 19:17: “לֹא תִשְׂנָא אֶת אָחִיךָ בִּלְבָבֶךָ, הוֹכֵחַ תּוֹכִיחַ אֶת עֲמִיתֶךָ, וְלֹא תִשָּׂא עָלָיו חֵטְא” — “You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely reprove your fellow, and bear no sin because of him.” Rashi (from Sifra): the Torah forbids specifically hatred in the heart — concealed enmity — which is worse than open rebuke. Rambam (Hilchos De’os 6:5) counts it as a discrete prohibition. R’ Tzadok’s use: it is unthinkable (“God forbid”) that Yaakov Avinu transgressed “lo sisna es achicha bilvavecha” — and “over nothing,” toward his own wife no less — so “senuah Leah” cannot mean that he hated her.

notes.body_html: Devarim 21:15–17: “כִּי תִהְיֶיןָ לְאִישׁ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים, הָאַחַת אֲהוּבָה וְהָאַחַת שְׂנוּאָה… וְהָיָה הַבֵּן הַבְּכוֹר לַשְּׂנִיאָה” — the law of the “beloved” and the “hated” wife: the double portion of the firstborn goes to the bechor even when he is the son of the senuah (the less-loved wife). Meforshim (Rashi, Ramban): “senuah” here means less-beloved, not despised. R’ Tzadok’s use: were Leah truly Yaakov’s “hated” wife, her sons would be “bnei senuah” in this technical sense — yet her firstborn Reuven holds the bechorah’s “opening” (as in §6); the resolution is that the “hatred” was never Yaakov’s, but Leah’s own repudiation of Esav’s deeds.

notes.body_html: Shabbos 63a (and Yevamos 24a): “אֵין מִקְרָא יוֹצֵא מִידֵי פְּשׁוּטוֹ” — “a verse never departs from its plain meaning.” The principle that even where Chazal expound a verse midrashically (derash), its peshat is not thereby annulled but remains in force alongside the derash. R’ Tzadok invokes it for balance here: though the Sages expound “senuah” as the deeds of Esav were hateful to her (Bava Basra 123a), the plain sense — that Leah experienced herself as the less-loved wife — also holds, “ein mikra yotzei midei peshuto gam ken.”

notes.body_html: The Name Elokim as a term of “power/might”: the grammarians and the Kuzari derive Elokim / E-l from the root of “ayil” — strength, ram, mighty one (cf. “אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ,” Yechezkel 17:13, “the mighty of the land”). Ibn Ezra and Radak (Sefer HaShorashim, root אול/איל) explain E-l as denoting power; the Kuzari (IV:1–3) treats Elokim as “the Master of all the forces” — the Governor of all the powers of nature. R’ Tzadok’s use: because Elokim is the “baal ha-kochos,” it is the Name of Gevurah — holy might, the conquering of the yetzer (Avos 4:1); and when a single “power” is “severed off” from Him and declared independent, that same term becomes “Elohim acheirim,” the root of idolatry and of the evil Gevurah of anger and bloodshed.

The Sages (Chagigah 15a) derive from “zeh l’umas zeh” that for every holy potency the Holy One made a corresponding force in the sitra achra. R’ Tzadok’s use: the holy Gevurah — the Name Elokim, “asher asah ha-Elokim” — has its opposite “this-against-that”: the “Elohim acheirim” of idolatry, the counterfeit “power” that spreads out into anger and bloodshed.

notes.body_html: “Let him of whom ‘I fear God’ is said come and exact payment from him of whom ‘he feared not God’ is said”: R’ Tzadok pairs two verses that share the phrase yarei Elokim. Of Yosef it is said “אֶת הָאֱלֹקִים אֲנִי יָרֵא” — “I fear God” (Bereishis 42:18); of Amalek it is said “וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹקִים” — “and he feared not God” (Devarim 25:18). Yosef — of Rachel’s seed, bearing “the rung of Yitzchak” (holy Gevurah, the fear of Heaven) — is the one fit to overthrow Amalek, the God-denier: middah k’neged middah. The idiom “yavo… ve-yipara” (“let him come and exact payment”) is the Sages’ standard formula for such fitting retribution. (On Amalek falling only to Rachel’s seed, see Bava Basra 123b, cited just above.)

notes.body_html: Megillah 13a: “כָּל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי” — “whoever repudiates idolatry is called a Yehudi.” The Gemara asks why Mordechai, a Binyaminite, is called “אִישׁ יְהוּדִי” (Esther 2:5), and answers that anyone who denies avodah zarah is called by the name Yehudi (after Yehudah). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the very root of Yehudah, son of Leah — the inward denial, “in the heart,” of every “power” set up against Hashem; Leah’s whole superiority lies in this root-level repudiation of idolatry, deeper than and prior to any outward deed.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chag HaPesach §14): “(Shabbos 105b) ‘the el zar in a person’s body — this is the yetzer hara,’ that is, it is a foreign power — this is ‘a foreign god’; and the matter of the erasure of Amalek is to empty the evil from the heart.” This is the flip side of §6-7’s “denier of idolatry is called a Yehudi”: Amalek is the “foreign god” lodged within man, and Leah’s root — the heart that “utterly rejects the thing” — is the erasing of that foreign power, the inward Yehudah who holds “no belief in any power against Hashem.”Tanya and Maharal parallel - Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25; Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv HaAnavah 3:2: Tanya's treatment of anger gives a strong conceptual parallel to R. Tzadok's association here of anger, avodah zarah, and the failure to recognize Divine rule. Iggeret HaKodesh 25 explains the dictum that one who becomes angry is "as though he serves idolatry": in ordinary worldly matters, anger arises when a person loses sight of the fact that the event confronting him has come through Divine providence. At the same time, Tanya carefully preserves the realm of yiras Shamayim and the obligation to prevent issur; the recognition of providence does not erase Torah responsibility. Maharal similarly describes ga'avah as an idolatrous growth, an asherah-like elevation of the self. Together they illuminate R. Tzadok's Leah-Esav contrast. Leah's hatred of "ma'aseh Esav" is rejection of the inner posture that grants independent ultimacy to force, rage, or self. Her teshuvah-root is therefore the opposite of avodah zarah: it acknowledges both the reality of human responsibility and the deeper truth that no power, including one's own anger or strength, possesses independent being before Hashem.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 109:4: “תַּחַת אַהֲבָתִי יִשְׂטְנוּנִי, וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה” — “In return for my love they accuse me, but I am [all] prayer.” Rashi: “I — my whole being is prayer to You.” Radak / Metzudos: even as they persecute him, David turns himself wholly to prayer. The Sages take “va-ani tefillah” as David’s very rung — he made himself into prayer, the paradigm of one who knows “he has nothing except what he receives from Hashem.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the exact antithesis of Yerovam’s haughtiness — David’s recognition that “all is from Hashem,” the rung of the King Mashiach (see the Resisei Layla parallel that follows).

notes.body_html: Melachim I 12:28–30: After the kingdom split, Yerovam ben Nevat feared that pilgrimage to the Beis HaMikdash would draw Israel back to the house of David; “so the king took counsel and made two calves of gold, and said… ‘Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt,’” setting one in Beis-El and one in Dan — “and this thing became a sin.” Meforshim (Rashi, Radak): Yerovam did not truly believe in the calves; his aim was political — to secure his throne. R’ Tzadok’s use: Yerovam “introduced avodah zarah into Israel,” yet “in truth he too did not believe in idolatry”; his root was gaavah and kavod, not conviction — “whoever is haughty is as one who serves idols.”

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 101b–102a: Rav Nachman said: the arrogance in Yerovam drove him from the world. For he reasoned (I Melachim 12), “now the kingdom will return to the house of David: if this people go up to offer sacrifices in the House of Hashem in Jerusalem [and see Rechavam seated while I stand, since only Davidic kings may sit in the Temple courtyard], they will say ‘this is the king and that is the servant,’ and they will kill me” — so at once “he took counsel and made two golden calves.” And (102a): “‘after this matter Yerovam did not turn back from his evil way’ (I Melachim 13) — what is ‘after’? R’ Abba said: after the Holy One grasped Yerovam by his garment and said, ‘repent, and I and you and the son of Yishai will stroll together in Gan Eden.’ He asked, ‘who will be at the head?’ ‘The son of Yishai at the head.’ [Yerovam] said, ‘if so, I do not want it.’”

notes.body_html: The two “root” inclinations — idolatry and arayos: the Men of the Great Assembly first captured and blinded the yetzer of avodah zarah, and then prayed that the yetzer of arayos (illicit relations) be delivered into their hands as well (Yoma 69b; cf. Sanhedrin 63b–64a). These are the two “great” inclinations that Chazal single out. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely two — “for it was only from Avraham and Yitzchak that the ‘dross’ emerged” (Yishmael, the root of arayos; Esav, the root of avodah zarah, whose branches are anger and haughtiness); from Yaakov, the third Patriarch, no such “dross” issued.

notes.body_html: Melachim I 11:26: “וְיָרׇבְעָם בֶּן נְבָט אֶפְרָתִי מִן הַצְּרֵדָה, וְשֵׁם אִמּוֹ צְרוּעָה אִשָּׁה אַלְמָנָה” — “And Yerovam son of Nevat, an Efratite of Tzeredah — his mother’s name was Tzeru’ah, a widow.” The name Tzeru’ah echoes tzaraas / metzora, and the meforshim read such names as hinting at trait and destiny. R’ Tzadok’s received teaching: since tzaraas stems from anger (Arachin 16a), Yerovam’s blemish — traced “by way of his mother [Tzeru’ah — ‘the stricken one’]” — was the trait of anger, from which his fatal haughtiness was drawn.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 28:9: “וַיֵּלֶךְ עֵשָׂו אֶל יִשְׁמָעֵאל, וַיִּקַּח אֶת מָחֲלַת בַּת יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אַבְרָהָם אֲחוֹת נְבָיוֹת עַל נָשָׁיו לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה” — “And Esav went to Yishmael and took Machalas the daughter of Yishmael… in addition to his [other] wives, as a wife.” (Bereishis Rabbah 67:13 reads Machalas as “nimchalu — his sins were pardoned” on his wedding day.) R’ Tzadok’s use: Esav’s truly fitting mate — the “female” of the inclination of arayos, matching his “male” of anger and idolatry — was Machalas, of Yishmael’s line (the root of arayos), not Leah; the crowd’s saying “the elder [Leah] for the elder [Esav]” mistook Leah’s inward loathing of evil for kinship with it.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos §4): “‘the sins are like the thorn that surrounds the lettuce — and not in the root’; and this is from the side that our root is from Yitzchak… and thereby [Israel] becomes an actual merkavah, ‘children of the living God.’” This is §6-8’s Leah, “the root of the supernal holiness of Knesses Yisrael”: even should they “multiply iniquities,” the sins are only “thorns that encircle the myrtle” — peripheral, never the root — so that their inmost heart stays bound to God, and they remain “children of the living God.”

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 44a: “אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא — יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא” — “even though he has sinned, he remains Yisrael.” R’ Abba explained it by the folk-saying: “a myrtle that stands among thorns [hizmei] — its name is still ‘myrtle,’ and people [still] call it a myrtle.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel’s sins are “but like thorns that encircle the myrtle” — the hotzim surround and prick the surface but never reach the fragrant myrtle-essence within, whose root “stays bound to God”; this is Leah’s trait of teshuvah, whereby even multiplied iniquities cannot sever the root that loathes Esav’s deeds and denies idolatry. (The same Gemara is cited at Siman 1.)

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, אֲפִילּוּ בִּגְנוּת בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה לֹא דִיבֵּר הַכָּתוּב, אֶלָּא שֶׁהָיְתָה בּוֹכָה כו׳
notes.body_html: the editor notes: R. Tzadok’s wording indicates the Gemara Bava Basra 123a (cited in fn. 10), and that the matter is brought in brief in Bereishis Rabbah 70:16. The underlying principle — that Scripture will not utter a disparaging word even of an impure animal (cf. Bereishis 7:8) — is stated in Pesachim 3a.Maharal and Tanya parallel - Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv HaAnavah 3:2; Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25: R. Tzadok's contrast between David's "va-ani tefillah" and Yeravam's fall through kavod is sharpened by Maharal and Tanya. Maharal writes that the baal ga'avah is comparable to an asherah: pride is an alien growth because it treats the self as possessing an independent height. This is why Chazal can compare ga'avah itself to avodah zarah. Tanya makes the related point with anger: when a person experiences the human cause in front of him as an autonomous power, he forgets the Divine source of the event and enters the logic of idolatry. David's "I am prayer" represents the reverse posture. Tefillah is the admission that life, kingship, success, and even the power to serve are received rather than possessed. The more a king knows that his authority is a shefa entrusted to him, the more his malchus becomes a vessel for Malchus Shamayim; the more he claims the honor as his own, the more kingship becomes an idol of self. Thus R. Tzadok's two root-inclinations are opposite answers to the question: from where does one's power come?

notes.body_html: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:1 (on “עֵינַיִךְ יוֹנִים מִבַּעַד לְצַמָּתֵךְ” — “your eyes are doves from behind your veil”): “כָּל כַּלָּה שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ יָפוֹת — אֵין כָּל גּוּפָהּ צָרִיךְ בְּדִיקָה; וְשֶׁעֵינֶיהָ טְרוּטוֹת — כָּל גּוּפָהּ צְרִיכָה בְּדִיקָה” — “any bride whose eyes are beautiful, her whole body needs no examination [she is surely fit]; but one whose eyes are bleared, her whole body requires examination.” (The Midrash applies the “eyes” to the Sanhedrin — the seeing “eyes” of the congregation.) R’ Tzadok’s use: the eyes are “the essential [point] in a woman,” for they disclose the inner state — hence the whole se’if turns on the meaning of Leah’s “tender eyes.”

notes.body_html: Shir HaShirim 6:5: “הָסֵבִּי עֵינַיִךְ מִנֶּגְדִּי שֶׁהֵם הִרְהִיבֻנִי” — “Turn your eyes away from Me, for they have overwhelmed Me.” In the love-song of the Holy One and Knesses Yisrael, God, as it were, says that her gazing “overwhelms” Him. Rashi: “hirhivuni” — they have emboldened Me, stirred a rush of feeling within Me. R’ Tzadok reads “hirhivuni” as “they brought into Me [an aspect of] greatness and loftiness [gadlus ve-geius]” — the “eye” being the wellspring of both desire and pride, which is why He says “hasebi” (turn them away).

notes.body_html: Bereishis 3:6: “וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה כִּי טוֹב הָעֵץ לְמַאֲכָל וְכִי תַאֲוָה הוּא לָעֵינַיִם, וְנֶחְמָד הָעֵץ לְהַשְׂכִּיל” — “and the woman saw that the tree was good for food and that it was a delight to the eyes…” The primordial sin begins with seeing: the eye beholds, the heart covets, and desire is born (as the Yerushalmi teaches, “the eye sees and the heart covets,” cited just above). R’ Tzadok’s use: the eye is “the onset of desire” — so mastery of the eye (Yosef, “alei ayin”) is the mastery of taavah itself.

notes.body_html: Nedarim 20b: They asked Imma Shalom, wife of R’ Eliezer, “why are your children so exceedingly beautiful?” She answered, “he does not converse with me at the beginning of the night nor at its end, but only at midnight; and when he converses, he uncovers a handbreadth and covers a handbreadth, and appears as one compelled by a demon. And when I asked him why, he said, ‘so that I not set my thoughts on another woman, and the children come to be as though mamzerim.’” [The children’s beauty flows from the sanctity and restraint of the parents.]

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev §3): “for in sleep a person requires guarding, and Hashem guards him with an encompassing light — and He is”the Supporter of all the fallen."" Exactly the se’if: what is at issue is a beauty and wholeness that a man cannot maintain by his own vigilance — it is held for him from without, which is why it survives his lapses.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 38:7: “וַיְהִי עֵר בְּכוֹר יְהוּדָה רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳, וַיְמִתֵהוּ ה׳” — “And Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Hashem, and Hashem put him to death.” Rashi (from Yevamos 34b): his “evil” was hashchasas zera — corruption of the seed, so that Tamar not conceive and lose her beauty. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the corruption of the bris is the ‘ugliness of the eyes’” — just as Er was “ra b’einei Hashem,” the pgam of the bris causes, as it were, an “evil in the eyes of Hashem” in the “matter Above”; the shared phrase “b’einei Hashem” binds the sin of the eye/desire to the sin of the covenant.

notes.body_html: Mishlei 8:13: “יִרְאַת ה׳ שְׂנֹאת רָע, גֵּאָה וְגָאוֹן וְדֶרֶךְ רָע וּפִי תַהְפֻּכוֹת שָׂנֵאתִי” — “The fear of Hashem is to hate evil; pride, arrogance, an evil way, and a mouth of perversities do I hate.” Meforshim (Rashi, Metzudos): the very definition of yiras Hashem is the hatred of evil. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is “the rung of the God-fearing one who masters his inclination, becoming a hater of evil” — precisely Leah’s trait (the deeds of Esav hateful in her eyes); “fear of Hashem” and “hatred of evil” are one and the same, the antithesis of the corrupter of the bris.

notes.body_html: Zohar, Vayeishev (I 188a; cf. I 71b): on “וַיְהִי עֵר… רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳” (Bereishis 38:7), the Zohar teaches that Er’s sin was hashchasas ha-bris — he “spilled outward” (so that Tamar not conceive), and this “spilling” is the “ra” that blemishes the supernal bris / Yesod, the channel of holiness. R’ Tzadok invokes this — “as is known in the Zohar from the verse concerning Er”: the corruption of the covenant is the true “ugliness of the eyes,” while its opposite — guarding the bris — is the “God-fearing one” who “hates evil,” over whom the [evil] eye has no dominion (the rung of Yosef).

notes.body_html: Berachos 33b: “R’ Chanina said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven except for the fear of Heaven [ha-kol biydei shamayim chutz mi-yiras shamayim], as it says (Devarim 10:12), ‘and now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you, but to fear [Him].’”Sefat Emet parallel - Eikev 24:3: Sefat Emet offers a striking parallel to R. Tzadok's equation of sight, fear, and the rectification of the eyes. On "mah Hashem Elokecha sho'el me'imach ki im le-yirah," he writes that the inward bond with Hashem is already planted in the souls of Israel, but materiality covers it; yirah opens that hidden interior. He then states explicitly, "yirah otiyot re'iyah": fear and seeing are composed of the same letters, because through yirah a person becomes able to see truth, and the Divine power concealed in the Jewish soul is revealed. He connects this to the opening of both moach and lev. This beautifully complements R. Tzadok's use of "the eye sees and the heart desires." The problem of sight is not solved merely by closing the eyes; it is rectified by transforming seeing itself. Unrectified re'iyah awakens taavah and draws the heart outward. Holy re'iyah, born of yirah, pierces the material covering and allows the heart to perceive Divine reality within what it sees. Leah's "tender eyes" can therefore become not a defect but the very place in which a higher seeing is formed through tears, fear, and teshuvah.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 122:4: “שֶׁשָּׁם עָלוּ שְׁבָטִים, שִׁבְטֵי יָהּ, עֵדוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, לְהֹדוֹת לְשֵׁם ה׳” — “for there the tribes went up, the tribes of Kah, a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the Name of Hashem.” Rashi: they are called “shivtei Kah” because the Divine Name is affixed to them, testifying to their legitimacy (cf. Bereishis Rabbah 82:11). R’ Tzadok’s use: the “precious and exalted souls, such as the tribes of Kah,” are the deep souls that come only through the rung of teshuvah (Leah / ima ila’ah) — not the “ordinary children of the world.”

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 68b (opening of Perek Ben Sorer u-Moreh): the Torah’s “ben sorer u-moreh” (Devarim 21:18) is expounded to require a “ben” in the strictest sense — “a son, and not one [already] fit to be [called] a father” (only a boy in the brief window after maturity, before he could himself beget a child). R’ Tzadok’s parallel: just as “ben” excludes one ripe to be a father, so Rachel, called “bas (daughter),” is “not one fit to be called a mother” — ima tata’ah only, the lower and revealed motherhood, as against Leah’s supernal motherhood of teshuvah.

notes.body_html: Shmuel I 16:7: “כִּי לֹא אֲשֶׁר יִרְאֶה הָאָדָם, כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם, וַה׳ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב” — “for [God does] not [see] as man sees: for man looks to the eyes, but Hashem looks to the heart.” Spoken to Shmuel at David’s anointing, as he was about to judge by Eliav’s imposing appearance. Rashi / Radak: man judges by the outward, God by the inward. R’ Tzadok’s use: “in this world the perfect tzaddik is the more esteemed” — for “man looks to the eyes” (the one whose eyes are beautiful — the revealed Rachel) — “but Hashem looks to the heart,” to the purity of thought and the depths, which is Leah’s hidden rung of teshuvah.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: ״וַה׳ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב״ לְטָהֳרַת הַמַּחְשָׁבָה וְהַמַּעֲמַקִּים שֶׁבּוֹ
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §39): “The essential holiness of thought [kedushas ha-machshavah] comes only from habit and from the effort of ‘the commandment of men learned by rote’ [mitzvas anashim melumadah] — which, though it accomplishes nothing in the heart, is the more beneficial for [the purity of] the thought. For from a feeling in the heart comes such enthusiasm that one can [scarcely] act with composure; but from the recognition of the intellect in thought, one is not [over]-inflamed, and it works properly, with a settled mind.” (Thus Leah’s rung — “purity of thought,” at which every steady increase of holiness in Israel is achieved — is reached precisely through disciplined, unspectacular toil.)

notes.body_html: Taanis 2a: “R’ Yochanan said: Three keys are in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, that are not given over to a messenger — the key of rain, the key of the woman in childbirth [mafteach shel chayah], and the key of the resurrection of the dead.” (So the ending of barrenness — the ‘opening of the womb’ — is in His hand alone.)Izhbitz-Radzin and Chiddushei HaRim parallel - Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut 24:3-4; Chiddushei HaRim on Torah, Chayei Sara 1: The Izhbitz-Radzin identification of complete teshuvah with Binah sheds light on R. Tzadok's claim that Leah's power of "birth" is rooted in teshuvah and inner thought. Sha'ar HaEmunah teaches that when a person returns fully to the place of Binah he rises above ordinary time, and therefore can "heal the earlier" - the past is no longer a sealed block that can only be regretted. Chiddushei HaRim expresses the same transformative power more existentially: through teshuvah, "in one hour and one moment," past days can be repaired as though they had been filled with mitzvos and good deeds. This makes R. Tzadok's language of holadah particularly apt. Teshuvah is not only erasure; it is generative. From the very place in which a life seemed to have been diminished, new Torah, new avodah, and even a new reading of the past can be born. Leah, the hidden Binah-world, thus represents the womb of spiritual renewal.

R’ Tzadok’s use: Reuven, Leah’s firstborn, is named for the re’iyah (“seeing”) — born “from the side of seeing,” and so the very one through whom the rung of teshuvah (which needs a prior “sin”) would first be revealed in the world.

notes.body_html: Zohar (a recurring dictum; cf. Zohar III 4a, and the Idra): Chochmah and Binah — “Abba and Imma” — are “trein re’in de-la mitpar’shin,” “two companions that never part,” ever joined in perfect union. R’ Tzadok’s use: Leah’s own rung is Binah (the source of teshuvah), but “from a still-higher level” she is joined with Yaakov and rises with him to Chochmah (the rung of “Yisrael,” the talmid chacham); and since Chochmah and Binah “never part,” the union of Yaakov and Leah is the deepest bond of all.Sefat Emet parallel - Vayeshev 33:4: Sefat Emet develops precisely the paradox R. Tzadok sees in Reuven. On "ha-yeled einenu va-ani anah ani va," he cites the Midrash that Reuven was the first to open the path of teshuvah and that Hoshea, descended from Reuven, therefore opened his prophecy with "Shuvah Yisrael." He defines complete teshuvah as the state in which, because of the sin, the person finds no place or independent existence for himself; only then does Hashem give him a new "place" of refuge. He adds that Reuven was in truth a tzaddik and that the very occurrence of his failing served so that he could teach teshuvah for the generations. This is an exceptionally close complement to R. notes.body_html: Bereishis 49:3: “רְאוּבֵן בְּכֹרִי אַתָּה, כֹּחִי וְרֵאשִׁית אוֹנִי, יֶתֶר שְׂאֵת וְיֶתֶר עָז” — “Reuven, you are my firstborn, my strength and the first of my vigor…” Rashi: “reishis oni” is Yaakov’s very first drop. R’ Tzadok’s use: Reuven, as bechor, is “the first of my strength” in whom “all those born after him are included” — the root comprising all the “true” levels of Yaakov as they spread into this world (which is also why one is obligated to honor an older brother).

notes.body_html: Kesuvos 103a (and the Arizal): the obligation to honor one’s older brother is derived from “אֶת אָבִיךָ” (Shemos 20:12) — “the word ‘es’ comes to include your older brother” (Kesuvos 103a; Rambam, Hilchos Mamrim 6:15). The Arizal gives the mystical ground: the souls of the later children are “included” within the firstborn, who is their root — so honoring him is honoring the root that contains them. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the virtue of the firstborn is that all born after him are included within him” — Reuven the bechor comprising all the levels of Yaakov.Shem MiShmuel and Sefat Emet parallel - Shem MiShmuel, Vayetzei 9:15; Sefat Emet, Vayechi 22:3: The Rachel-Leah polarity here is illuminated by Shem MiShmuel's formulation that Rachel corresponds to alma d'isgalya while Leah corresponds to alma d'iskasya. The revealed world displays beauty, deed, and ordered attainment; the hidden world contains heights whose value is not immediately visible and is reached through inward separation from evil. This helps explain why Yaakov's attachment to Rachel belongs to the structure of this world while Leah becomes his enduring partner at the root. Sefat Emet adds that "Yaakov Avinu did not die" means that Yaakov deposited his whole power within the collective of Israel, which can awaken it in every generation. R. Tzadok's point is thus not simply biographical - that Yaakov happened to be buried with Leah. At the level of eternal Israel, Yaakov's abiding force is joined to the hidden world from which teshuvah and inner renewal emerge. Rachel represents visible perfection; Leah represents the concealed source that can regenerate life after visible perfection has failed.

notes.body_html: Nazir 23a–b (on the daughters of Lot, Bereishis 19:30–38): “a person should always hasten to a matter of mitzvah, for on account of the one night by which the elder [daughter] preceded the younger, she preceded her by four generations to royalty.” The elder bore Moav (ancestress of Rus → David), and so “preceded” the younger — whose line (via Ammon → Naamah) reached royalty only later, through Rechavam. R’ Tzadok’s use: “you have nothing more degraded than the daughters of Lot,” yet because the elder “preceded in the mitzvah” of perpetuating the world, royalty issued from her — the “hidden holiness” of a seemingly base act, clarified only afterward.

notes.body_html: Yevamos 22a: “A convert who converts is like a newborn child [ger she-nisgayer k’katan she-nolad].” (Severed from his former, impure root.)Sefat Emet parallel - Vayera 30:3: Sefat Emet's explanation of "zera emes" strongly complements the discussion of enduring seed and the bris. He writes that the souls of Israel extend "from beginning to end," and that truth requires the body itself to become a fitting vessel for the light of the neshamah. Bris milah removes the "sefas sheker," the false covering introduced through sin, so that the child is born as "zera emes." Emes, in this account, is continuity: the Divine root, the embodied middle, and the final destiny must belong to one unbroken line. This gives depth to R. Tzadok's contrast between transient desire - "the bread of falsehood" - and Israel's seed of truth. Taavah seeks an immediate experience cut off from enduring purpose; bris gathers the power of desire into a line that reaches beyond the moment and bears fruit. Even where there has been failure, the root of Israel remains oriented toward that continuity, which is why teshuvah can reclaim what appeared wasted and return it to the line of emes.

notes.body_html: Devarim 33:6: “יְחִי רְאוּבֵן וְאַל יָמֹת, וִיהִי מְתָיו מִסְפָּר” — “Let Reuven live and not die, and let his men be counted” — Moshe’s blessing to Reuven. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “death is drawn from desire” (“the counsel of the serpent”), the perfection of Reuven’s rung — the rung of teshuvah, which transforms desire — is exactly what brings “chayei ad” (eternal life): “and let him not die.”

R’ Tzadok’s use: the revelation of deathless “eternal life” comes “only through the rung of Leah — that is, l’ahapcha (to transform), not [merely] l’achpaya (to subdue)” — a teshuvah that turns the evil itself into good, thereby completing the rectification of “seeing.”

notes.body_html: Nechemiah 9:6: “אַתָּה הוּא ה׳ לְבַדֶּךָ, אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם… וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם” — “You alone are Hashem; You made the heavens… and You give life to them all.” From the Levites’ great confession-prayer. notes.body_html: Bereishis 27:22: “הַקֹּל קוֹל יַעֲקֹב וְהַיָּדַיִם יְדֵי עֵשָׂו” — “the voice is the voice of Yaakov, but the hands are the hands of Esav.” Bereishis Rabbah 65:20 (cf. Gittin 57b): “kol Yaakov” is the voice [of Torah and prayer] in the synagogues and study-halls — when it is heard, “the hands of Esav” have no power. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the voice of Yaakov” is essentially the voice of Torah; Yehudah’s (David’s) “voice” is its counterpart in prayer — “prayer being the mode by which the fallen self reaches upward, as Torah is the mode by which the Divine reaches down.”Sefat Emet and Chiddushei HaRim parallel - Sefat Emet, Vayeshev 33:4; Chiddushei HaRim on Torah, Chayei Sara 1: Two Ger sources bring out the life-giving character of Reuven's teshuvah. Sefat Emet says that Reuven "opened teshuvah" and thereby became the model from whom Hoshea could proclaim "Shuvah Yisrael." The complete baal teshuvah feels that sin has left him with no independent "place," and it is precisely then that Hashem grants him a new place. Chiddushei HaRim adds that teshuvah can repair past days "in one hour and one moment" as though they had been filled with mitzvos. This combination closely fits the blessing "yechi Reuven ve-al yamus" as R. Tzadok reads it. Reuven's life is not guaranteed because no breakdown occurred; rather, his distinct contribution to Israel is that breakdown need not become death.
