notes.body_plain: Bereishis 27:22: “הַקֹּל קוֹל יַעֲקֹב וְהַיָּדַיִם יְדֵי עֵשָׂו” — “ the voice is the voice of Yaakov , but the hands are the hands of Esav.” Bereishis Rabbah 65:20 (cf. Gittin 57b): “ kol Yaakov ” is the voice [of Torah and prayer] in the synagogues and study-halls — when it is heard, “the hands of Esav” have no power. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the voice of Yaakov” is essentially the voice of Torah ; Yehudah’s (David’s) “voice” is its counterpart in prayer — “prayer being the mode by which the fallen self reaches upward, as Torah is the mode by which the Divine reaches down.”Sefat Emet and Chiddushei HaRim parallel - Sefat Emet, Vayeshev 33:4; Chiddushei HaRim on Torah, Chayei Sara 1: Two Ger sources bring out the life-giving character of Reuven's teshuvah. Sefat Emet says that Reuven "opened teshuvah" and thereby became the model from whom Hoshea could proclaim "Shuvah Yisrael." The complete baal teshuvah feels that sin has left him with no independent "place," and it is precisely then that Hashem grants him a new place. Chiddushei HaRim adds that teshuvah can repair past days "in one hour and one moment" as though they had been filled with mitzvos. This combination closely fits the blessing "yechi Reuven ve-al yamus" as R. Tzadok reads it. Teshuvah can supply a new place from which life begins again and can even restore life to the days that seemed already forfeited.

They “knew what Israel should do” not in order to teach and rule it as fixed law, “but to know by knowledge alone”; and through their knowing, all Israel too knew what to do “according to the times.”

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 17:9: “עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ” — “The heart is the most deep of all, and it is grievously sick — who can know it?” The root akov connotes the tortuous, unfathomable inner recesses. R’ Tzadok’s use: over against the Torah’s fixed outer statutes, “in the depths of the heart — which is ‘the most deep of all’ — it changes at every moment”; it is there, in the heart’s hidden Binah, that the singular “time to act” is discerned.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 119:126: “עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה׳ הֵפֵרוּ תּוֹרָתֶךָ” — “It is a time to act for Hashem — they have made void Your Torah.” The Sages read the verse in both directions and invoked it to sanction committing the Oral Torah to writing — “a time to act for Hashem” overriding the rule that oral teachings not be set down (Gittin 60a; Temurah 14b; and see Berachos 63a). R’ Tzadok’s use: the Torah proper is “fixed statutes and bounds that never change for all the days of the world,” yet “in the depths of the heart” there is at times an “eis la’asos,” a need of the very moment that does not accord with the Torah’s general rule and is entrusted to the Binah of the heart.

notes.body_html: Bamidbar 6:2: “אִישׁ אוֹ אִשָּׁה כִּי יַפְלִא לִנְדֹּר נֶדֶר נָזִיר לְהַזִּיר לַה׳” — “A man or woman who sets himself apart [ki yafli], to vow a nazirite’s vow, to abstain for Hashem.” The nazir’s vow is framed by the root פ-ל-א (hafla’ah — a wondrous setting-apart); as R’ Tzadok puts it, “nezirus was given only for hafla’ah.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the parashah of vows was entrusted precisely to the one “who knows how to set apart” — to grasp, through the Binah of the heart, the hidden “wonder” of what befits this particular soul at this particular hour, beyond the universal decree of the Torah.

notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 29:14: “הִנְנִי יוֹסִף לְהַפְלִיא אֶת הָעָם הַזֶּה הַפְלֵא וָפֶלֶא, וְאָבְדָה חָכְמַת חֲכָמָיו וּבִינַת נְבֹנָיו תִּסְתַּתָּר” — “Behold, I will further do wondrously with this people, wondrous upon wonder — and the wisdom of its wise shall perish, and the discernment of its prudent shall hide itself.” Here the same root pele denotes not revelation but withdrawal — wisdom “perishing” and “hiding.” R’ Tzadok’s use: “pele is a term of concealment”; the supernal Chochmah is hidden in this world, and only its “impression” is grasped in the heart’s Binah — the very word that names the nazir’s “wondrous setting-apart” also bespeaks the hiddenness of that wisdom.

notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 10:33: “הִנֵּה הָאָדוֹן ה׳ צְבָאוֹת מְסָעֵף פֻּארָה בְּמַעֲרָצָה, וְרָמֵי הַקּוֹמָה גְּדוּעִים וְהַגְּבֹהִים יִשְׁפָּלוּ” — “Behold, the Master, Hashem of Hosts, lops off the bough with terrible force; the tall of stature are hewn down and the lofty laid low.” The verb mesa’ef is built on sa’if (a bough), yet here it means to strip the boughs away. R’ Tzadok’s use: paired with Iyov 31:12 to establish that “every root in Lashon HaKodesh denotes a thing and its opposite” — sa’if is both “bough” and “the removal of the bough,” just as le-hafli is both “to set wondrously apart” and “to remove the setting-apart.”

R’ Tzadok’s use: because “the heart knows its own bitterness,” it “can set bounds for itself according to what is fitting for that particular soul and that particular time” — the personal, non-universal measure of Binah, entrusted to the one who can grasp the hidden “wonder according to the times.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §22): “And this is "of the sons of Yissachar, who know understanding for the times, to know what Israel should do" — that they have no fixed matter, but rather gaze at every time with the Binah that is in the heart, to know what the will of Hashem is at that time, what Israel should do.” Exactly the se’if: the written Torah has “rates and bounds that never change,” but Yissachar’s rung reads, out of the heart’s Binah, what this soul and this hour require.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut, Entrance to the Gate of Beit Yaakov 24:3-4: This source is almost a direct commentary on R. Tzadok's Yissachar-Binah structure. Sha'ar HaEmunah cites "u-miBnei Yissachar yodei binah la'itim" and explains that the possessors of Binah know how to "heal the earlier" - to heal time itself. Complete teshuvah returns a person to Binah, a level above the ordinary sequence of time, where past, present, and future are not experienced as mutually sealed compartments. From there, what preceded can be repaired. This complements R. Tzadok's distinction between revealed Chochmah and the wisdom hidden in the heart. Yissachar does not merely know more information; his Binah is a faculty for penetrating the inward meaning of the time and discovering what the present moment asks of Israel. That is why his Torah belongs naturally to Leah, the mother of teshuvah. The heart that understands the time can also reinterpret the past and direct the future.

That is why his Torah belongs naturally to Leah, the mother of teshuvah. The heart that understands the time can also reinterpret the past and direct the future.

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 31:33: “וְלֹא יְלַמְּדוּ עוֹד אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְאִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו לֵאמֹר דְּעוּ אֶת ה׳, כִּי כוּלָּם יֵדְעוּ אוֹתִי לְמִקְּטַנָּם וְעַד גְּדוֹלָם” — “and no longer shall a man teach his fellow or his brother, saying, Know Hashem — for they shall all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest.” The prophecy of the covenant of the Future, when the Torah is inscribed “upon their hearts.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the reward of the Future is the complete, limitless absorption of the words of Torah into the heart — that which is fully absorbed needs no “angel to remind” it, for one never forgets what one has wholly become.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah §5): “this alluded to the light of the holy Torah that was then bestowed — precisely that which the Greeks sought, "to make them forget Your Torah."” The se’if’s forgetting is here given its historical form: an enemy can reach only Torah that has not been absorbed inward, for what the heart has taken in cannot be made to be forgotten.Sefat Emet parallel - Eikev 24:3: Sefat Emet's treatment of moach, lev, and yirah closely parallels R. Tzadok's description of da'as as wisdom that truly enters the heart. He writes that the essential recognition of the Creator is in the moach and lev, and that yirah is the outer key that opens both; once the covering of the heart is removed, the Divine attachment already planted in the Jewish soul becomes revealed. He therefore calls yirah "re'iyah" - the capacity to see the truth. This helps distinguish the Torah that remains "from the lips outward" from Torah that becomes da'as. Information can be present in the intellect and even on the tongue without reorganizing the inner person. Yirah gives the knowledge existential weight: it opens the heart to receive what the mind knows, so that the Torah becomes part of the person's own inward reality. R. Tzadok's critique of Doeg is therefore not anti-intellectual. It is a demand that chochmah pass through the gate of yirah and enter the lev, where Chochmah and Binah are joined as da'as.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §248): “The essence of man is the longing [cheishek] in the heart, in which lies his superiority over the angels; and it is what is called ‘yetzer’ — [both] the good inclination and the evil inclination. When he strengthens his longing toward the good, this is good; and if not, [toward evil]. And the Sages said (Sukkah 52a), ‘the greater [a person], the greater his inclination’ — for the greatness of one over another is only according to the greatness of his longing for the good, that is, the power of the inclination; for the good and evil inclinations are ‘this-opposite-that’ in the two chambers of the heart, according to the longing in his heart.”

notes.body_html: Tehillim 42:3: “צָמְאָה נַפְשִׁי לֵאלֹהִים לְאֵל חָי, מָתַי אָבוֹא וְאֵרָאֶה פְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים” — “my soul thirsts for God, for the living God; when shall I come and appear before God?” R’ Tzadok’s use: this “thirst” is the very cheishek that never subsided in Leah — the longing to raise up tribes; it is the ultimate intensity of longing “which has no satiety at all,” ever renewing from the first rung, like one who finishes the whole Shas and returns to its beginning.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 68:12 (and Chullin 91b): “you are the one whose icon is engraved on high” (at hu she-ikonin shelcha chakukah le-maalah) — the “form of Yaakov” is engraved beneath the Throne of Glory, and the angels “ascend and gaze upon his image above.” R’ Tzadok’s use: because Yaakov’s form is engraved on the Throne, the tribes are “the sum of the resting of the Shechinah among the lower worlds”; so Leah’s unquenchable longing to bear tribes is a longing to extend that indwelling into this world.

notes.body_html: Shemos 20:14 (the tenth commandment): “לֹא תַחְמֹד בֵּית רֵעֶךָ, לֹא תַחְמֹד אֵשֶׁת רֵעֶךָ… וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר לְרֵעֶךָ” — “you shall not covet your fellow’s house… nor anything that is your fellow’s.” R’ Tzadok’s use: all longing “for the sake of Heaven” needs the safeguard of “lo sachmod” — not to covet what is not one’s own; and “their end is embedded in their beginning,” for one who truly recognizes the first commandment, “Anochi Hashem your God,” knows that “from Your own they give to You” and does not covet what is not his.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְזֶהוּ ״דּוּדָאִים בַּשָּׂדֶה״, דְּאַף שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ מִכָּל מָקוֹם כֵּיוָן שֶׁהוּא הֶפְקֵר יָכוֹל לַחְמֹד לוֹ
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Matos §8): “In the first utterance it says "Anochi Hashem your God" — and it was not said in the language of command… and so was engraved in the souls of Israel the revelation of Godliness, until the last utterance, "lo sachmod" — for through the revelation of Godliness in ten rungs the heart is made hollow and empty of every kind of coveting and desire of this world.” The se’if’s “lo sachmod is rooted in Anochi,” stated as a process: the ten utterances hollow the heart until nothing is left to covet.Shem MiShmuel parallel - Vaetchanan 4:15, citing Rambam, Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 2:2: Shem MiShmuel brings the Rambam's classic description of the path to love and fear: contemplation of Hashem's wondrous works first produces love, praise, and an intense desire to know Him - the state expressed by David's "tzamah nafshi l'Elokim l'El chai" - and the very same contemplation then causes the person to recoil in awe, recognizing his smallness before the Perfect Knower. This complements R. Tzadok's presentation of yirah as a gate into Leah's inward world of unending longing. The two movements are not contradictory. True longing grows precisely because the object of longing cannot be possessed or exhausted, while true yirah prevents longing from collapsing into self-satisfaction. One approaches and discovers distance; the distance itself increases thirst; the renewed thirst drives a deeper approach. That circular movement explains R. Tzadok's language that after a person reaches completion he returns again to the beginning. The "gate" is not a threshold crossed once but a permanent protection of the infinitude of the relationship.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 30:1: “וַתֵּרֶא רָחֵל כִּי לֹא יָלְדָה לְיַעֲקֹב, וַתְּקַנֵּא רָחֵל בַּאֲחֹתָהּ, וַתֹּאמֶר אֶל יַעֲקֹב הָבָה לִּי בָנִים וְאִם אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי” — “and Rachel saw that she had borne Yaakov no children, and Rachel envied her sister, and said to Yaakov, ‘Give me children — and if not, I am as dead.’” R’ Tzadok’s use: envy is the very opposite of coveting, yet Rachel “envied” this coveting — desiring the dudaim, which in truth did not belong to her; this is “coveting what is not one’s own,” and it is precisely her rectification of it (ceding the tzaddik’s couch, a “good eye”) that is the subject of this se’if.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §31): “envy is toward those who are not his beloved, yet in any case [toward those] of his acquaintance and the people of his land — for one is envious only of one who resembles him, and not of a stranger.” This sharpens the se’if’s difficulty and its answer: Rachel could envy only Leah, her very sister and like — which is why the rectification had to come by giving her what was hers.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §190): “In this, Yaakov Avinu’s bed was ‘complete’ and all his seed was truth. And in the language of the Sages, a ‘fine eye’ or a ‘good eye’ [ayin tovah] means generosity of heart and not being jealous — and so in the language of Scripture, ‘the good of eye [shall be blessed], for he has given [of his bread to the poor]’ (Mishlei 22:9); and its opposite is the ‘evil eye.’” (This defines the very rectification of the se’if: Rachel’s ceding of the couch converts jealousy into the ayin tovah — the open-handed eye that begrudges nothing to another.)

notes.body_html: Nedarim 7b: “וְתַנְיָא: כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּתְנוּ חֲכָמִים עֵינֵיהֶם — אוֹ מִיתָה אוֹ עוֹנִי” — “and it is taught: wherever the Sages set their eyes [in reproach], [there follows] either death or poverty.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the “eye” of the Sages, cast in disfavor, withholds good and brings harm — the “evil eye”; over against it stands Rachel’s “good eye,” which let Leah bear more, and it is by removing that envy that Leah merited Yissachar, “the receiving of reward.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayishlach §4): “the yetzer hara was created for the good, only that man ruins it and makes it evil. For the root of the yetzer hara is envy, desire and honor — and all of them are needed in holiness as well: envy we find, "the envy of scribes increases wisdom"…” Exactly the se’if: Rachel’s envy was not the trait’s corruption but its holy use — jealousy turned into the intensification of longing, wholly for Heaven.

notes.body_html: Eruvin 100b: R’ Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of R’ Yochanan: any woman who [modestly] solicits her husband to the mitzvah will have children the like of whom did not exist even in the generation of Moshe — Of Leah it is written (Bereishis 30), “and Leah went out to meet him and said, ‘to me you shall come, for I have surely hired you’” — and (I Divrei HaYamim 12), “and of the sons of Yissachar, those who knew understanding of the times.” This teaches that “the woman solicits with the heart and the man solicits with the mouth, and this is a good trait in women” [Rashi: she shows him affection]. [Leah’s forthright request, for the mitzvah’s sake, earned her the uniquely wise sons of Yissachar.]

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כְּטַעַם ״וַיֵּדַע אֱלֹהִים״
notes.body_html: Shemos 2:25: “וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וַיֵּדַע אֱלֹהִים” — “and God saw the children of Israel, and God knew.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Yissachar’s wisdom is the supernal Chochmah that “drips” into the Binah of the heart — grasped not as taught information but as an inner “knowing,” a felt perception, in the sense of “va-yeda Elokim” — a knowing of intimate awareness rather than mere data.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Nitzavim 6: Mei HaShiloach gives an especially fitting parallel to R. Tzadok's claim that the yetzer itself can be turned toward holiness. On "u-mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha," he explains that the very cheshek a person formerly had for things that were not good in Hashem's eyes can, after complete teshuvah, be repaired by Hashem and redirected into love of Hashem, desire for Torah, and eagerness for the mitzvos. The evil desire is not simply amputated; its energetic core is clarified and returned to its proper object. This complements R. Tzadok's discussion of Rachel's kinah and the general principle that the root of the yetzer was created for good. A middah becomes destructive when its force is attached to the wrong object or experienced as an autonomous demand. Teshuvah can uncover the holy capacity concealed in that same force - ambition as zeal for avodah, jealousy as longing for holiness, desire as cheshek for Torah. The later discovery of a holy root does not sanctify the earlier misuse; it requires the actual work of return through which the desire is reoriented and made into a servant of Hashem.

notes.body_html: Koheles 1:16: “דִּבַּרְתִּי אֲנִי עִם לִבִּי לֵאמֹר… וְלִבִּי רָאָה הַרְבֵּה חָכְמָה וָדָעַת” — “I spoke with my heart, saying… and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this “seeing of the heart” is Yissachar’s rung — the “knowing” of the heart’s Binah, attained without any revealed, external seeing; the “second beginning,” of receiving reward, in the perfection of spiritual sight.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §43): “a sage is greater than a prophet — he can attain more, only that it is not a revealed and clear attainment like the attainment of prophecy, which is called "the seer," for it is like seeing through glass and a speculum; but then it was reversed from seeing to light, as they said, "the Jews had light" — this is Torah — that the Torah should be light illumining their eyes without seeing at all.” Exactly the se’if’s glass-from-sand: what is now a seeing through a speculum becomes, in the Future, light itself.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 30:20: “וַתֹּאמֶר לֵאָה זְבָדַנִי אֱלֹהִים אֹתִי זֵבֶד טוֹב, הַפַּעַם יִזְבְּלֵנִי אִישִׁי כִּי יָלַדְתִּי לוֹ שִׁשָּׁה בָנִים, וַתִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ זְבֻלוּן” — “and Leah said, ‘God has granted me a goodly gift; this time my husband will make me his abode [yizbeleini], for I have borne him six sons,’ and she called his name Zevulun.” R’ Tzadok’s use: “yizbeleini” (an abode) is a permanent cleaving, even not at the time of union — corresponding to, yet surpassing, Levi’s “yilaveh” (joining at the time of union): the fixed indwelling of supernal Chochmah in the chambers of the heart.

notes.body_html: Melachim I 8:13: “בָּנֹה בָנִיתִי בֵּית זְבֻל לָךְ, מָכוֹן לְשִׁבְתְּךָ עוֹלָמִים” — “I have surely built You a house of abode [beis zevul], a foundation for Your dwelling forever” (Shlomo, at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash). R’ Tzadok’s use: the “zevul” of Zevulun is this fixed, enduring dwelling — that the supernal Chochmah have “a foundation for Your dwelling forever” within the chambers of a person’s heart.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §76): “‘This time my husband will dwell with me’ [yizbeleini] (Bereishis 30:20) — an expression of a dwelling-place; therefore they said in Chagigah (12b) that in [the heaven called] Zevul the Beis HaMikdash stands built, for there is ‘the foundation for Your dwelling’ — a dwelling-place for the Shechinah; and this is through Zevulun, who is its support.” (This grounds the se’if’s reading of yizbeleini as a permanent indwelling: Zevulun’s very name is the fixed ‘house of zevul’ in which the Shechinah abides.)

notes.body_html: Bereishis 49:13: “זְבוּלֻן לְחוֹף יַמִּים יִשְׁכֹּן, וְהוּא לְחוֹף אֳנִיּוֹת וְיַרְכָתוֹ עַל צִידֹן” — “Zevulun shall dwell at the shore of the seas, and he shall be a haven for ships, and his flank upon Tzidon” (Yaakov’s blessing). R’ Tzadok’s use: the “sea” denotes unquenchable longing, but Zevulun dwells at its shore — the sand-boundary (Gevurah) that stills the “roaring of the seas,” and from whose sand comes the clear glass of the aspaklaria.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כָּל הַנְּחָלִים הוֹלְכִים אֶל הַיָּם וְהַיָּם אֵינֶנּוּ מָלֵא״
notes.body_html: Koheles 1:7: “כָּל הַנְּחָלִים הֹלְכִים אֶל הַיָּם וְהַיָּם אֵינֶנּוּ מָלֵא, אֶל מְקוֹם שֶׁהַנְּחָלִים הֹלְכִים שָׁם הֵם שָׁבִים לָלָכֶת” — “all the rivers flow to the sea, yet the sea is not full; to the place where the rivers flow, there they flow again.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the sea “not full” is the longing of this world that “has no satiety” — full of turmoil, with no rest until one reaches dry land.

notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 17:12: “הוֹי הֲמוֹן עַמִּים רַבִּים כַּהֲמוֹת יַמִּים יֶהֱמָיוּן, וּשְׁאוֹן לְאֻמִּים כִּשְׁאוֹן מַיִם כַּבִּירִים יִשָּׁאוּן” — “Ah, the tumult of many peoples — they roar like the roaring of the seas — and the din of nations, that roar like the roaring of mighty waters.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the “roaring of the seas” is the tumult of the nations, sunk exceedingly in the endless, boundless desires of this world.
notes.body_plain: Yeshayahu 17:12: “הוֹי הֲמוֹן עַמִּים רַבִּים כַּהֲמוֹת יַמִּים יֶהֱמָיוּן , וּשְׁאוֹן לְאֻמִּים כִּשְׁאוֹן מַיִם כַּבִּירִים יִשָּׁאוּן” — “Ah, the tumult of many peoples — they roar like the roaring of the seas — and the din of nations, that roar like the roaring of mighty waters.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the “roaring of the seas” is the tumult of the nations, sunk exceedingly in the endless, boundless desires of this world.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל כֵּן הַיָּם רָאָה אֲרוֹנוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף, שֶׁהוּא הַהַגְדָּרָה מֵחַמְדוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וַיָּנֹס וְנַעֲשָׂה יַבָּשָׁה
notes.body_html: Tehillim 114:3: “הַיָּם רָאָה וַיָּנֹס, הַיַּרְדֵּן יִסֹּב לְאָחוֹר” — “the sea saw and fled, the Jordan turned back” (from Hallel). The Sages asked, “what did it see, that it fled?” and answered: the coffin of Yosef (Midrash — Bereishis Rabbah 87; Mechilta, Beshalach). R’ Tzadok’s use: the sea — the endless desires of this world — “fled” and became dry land before the coffin of Yosef, who is the “bounding-in” (self-mastery) that guards against the desires of this world.

notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 52:8: “קוֹל צֹפַיִךְ נָשְׂאוּ קוֹל יַחְדָּו יְרַנֵּנוּ, כִּי עַיִן בְּעַיִן יִרְאוּ בְּשׁוּב ה׳ צִיּוֹן” — “the voice of your watchmen! they raise their voice, together they sing for joy, for eye to eye they shall see when Hashem returns to Zion.” R’ Tzadok’s use: in the Future even the physical eyes will become spiritual, seeing “eye to eye” through the aspaklaria ha-me’irah — and then “fear is a small matter,” granted from Heaven without any effort.

notes.body_html: Berachos 33b: On “and now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you, but to fear [Him]” (Devarim 10:12): “Is fear of Heaven a small matter [milsa zutarta]? Yes — for Moshe it is a small matter.” (For one who has attained the rung, awe of Heaven becomes “small.”)Izhbitz-Radzin and Sefat Emet parallel - Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut 24:3-4; Sefat Emet, Eikev 24:3: The combination of Yissachar, Binah, and a form of knowledge deeper than ordinary sight is developed in Sha'ar HaEmunah, which explains "yodei binah la'itim" as the power to grasp and even "heal" time from the place of Binah. This is a knowing that does not depend on visible surface alone; it reads the inward demand of the moment. Sefat Emet adds that yirah is itself a form of re'iyah: by removing the covering from moach and lev, fear enables a person to see the Divine truth concealed within his own soul. These two formulations help clarify R. Tzadok's sequence of Reuven, Yissachar, and Zevulun. Reuven begins with rectified seeing; Yissachar reaches an inward understanding that can know what is not visible; Zevulun carries that inward bond into the changing movements of "going out" and worldly encounter. Mature avodah does not depend on constant visionary clarity. Once the heart has become a dwelling for the Divine, a person can move through concealment and still remain joined to the inner truth that Binah has taught him to recognize.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §16): “And for this [purpose] is the mitzvah of tzitzis in practice — ‘that you may remember [and do all My commandments] and not stray [after your own heart]’ (Bamidbar 15:39) — which does not remove the desire entirely, so that it should not enter the heart at all; rather, [it enjoins one] not to stray after cravings and the willfulness of his heart, but to thrust it away from his heart at once. And this [comes] by way of the remembrance that the tzitzis brings — like that student in Menachos (44a) whose very tzitzis ‘slapped him across the face’ [and stopped him from sin].” (R’ Tzadok makes explicit the mechanism of the techeiles-thread that this se’if invokes: it is not the uprooting of desire but the instant refusal to pursue it.)

notes.body_html: Yeshayahu 51:12: “אָנֹכִי אָנֹכִי הוּא מְנַחֶמְכֶם, מִי אַתְּ וַתִּירְאִי מֵאֱנוֹשׁ יָמוּת” — “I, I am He who comforts you; who are you, that you fear a mortal man.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the awe a king of Israel commands is not the fear of flesh-and-blood — of that it says “who are you, that you fear a mortal man” — but a fear drawn from the Kingship of Heaven, for “the kingship of a king of Israel is drawn from the Kingship of Heaven.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Hashanah §17): “"Zachor" corresponds to the brain on the right, and there is the place of remembering — yet even in the brain, in which there is memory, forgetting can still occur at distant intervals. notes.body_html: Tehillim 119:72: “טוֹב לִי תוֹרַת פִּיךָ מֵאַלְפֵי זָהָב וָכָסֶף” — “the Torah of Your mouth is good to me, more than thousands of gold and silver.” R’ Tzadok’s use: David HaMelech named the Torah “tov” (good) — for “tov” essentially alludes to the tzaddik, “one of good deeds, fenced-in with fear of Heaven”; hence “there is no tov but Torah,” and merely to behold such a tzaddik (David) restores one’s own Torah to memory.Sefat Emet parallel - Eikev 24:3: Sefat Emet's phrase "yirah otiyot re'iyah" gives a precise Chassidic frame for R. Tzadok's use of techeiles, seeing, remembering, and fear. He explains that the bond with Hashem is already planted within Israel, but the physical covering blocks its disclosure; yirah is the key that opens the gates of moach and lev and allows a person to see the truth. This makes "u-re'isem oto u-zekhartem" more than a mnemonic technique. Holy sight generates yirah, and yirah in turn fixes what is seen within the heart so that it is not lost to forgetfulness. R. Tzadok's claim that what truly enters the heart is not forgotten follows naturally: forgetting is a sign that the knowledge remained external, while yirah converts perception into an inward orientation. The techeiles-thread thus stands at the boundary between revealed sight and hidden memory. One sees a finite physical sign, but the purpose is to awaken a fear that opens the heart to the infinite Divine reality toward which the sign points.

notes.body_html: Yerushalmi Peah 2:4: “Even that which a seasoned student [talmid vasik] is destined to teach one day before his master was already said to Moshe at Sinai.”Kedushas Levi — the Oral Torah is the gift of Israel’s own chiddush: Kedushas Levi, Yisro §22, describes the two Torahs in a manner remarkably close to this se’if. Torah shebiksav was entrusted through Moshe in fixed written form, whereas Torah shebe’al peh includes the interpretation transmitted to Moshe together with “כל שתלמיד ותיק עתיד לחדש.” He then draws the consequence: Hashem gave Israel such authority out of His love and choice of them that, according to the Torah as the tzaddikim of the generation truly interpret it, so the Divine order is conducted. This does not mean that a chacham invents a second Torah detached from Sinai; the very novelty he uncovers was rooted at Sinai, yet it becomes “his Torah” only through the labor of his own mind and heart. That formulation sharpens R’ Tzadok’s distinction here. The greatness of Torah shebe’al peh is precisely that the received Divine word becomes a personal acquisition without ceasing to be Divine. “Lo bashamayim hi” is therefore not a distancing of Torah from Heaven but the completion of the matanah: Heaven wills that the earthly chacham grasp, interpret, and decide. In this sense the talmid’s chiddush is the point at which the gift is fully received — the Torah is no longer merely before him as Toras Hashem, but lives within him as toraso.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: לְשׁוֹן ״הֶבֶל״ אֵינוֹ גְּנַאי, כִּי הוּא בְּסוֹד שִׁבְעָה הֲבָלִים שֶׁאָמַר קֹהֶלֶת עַל כָּל עִנְיָינֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה
notes.body_html: Koheles 1:2: “הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים אָמַר קֹהֶלֶת, הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים הַכֹּל הָבֶל” — “vanity of vanities, said Koheles; vanity of vanities, all is hevel [vapor].” The Sages count seven expressions of “hevel” in this verse (Koheles Rabbah 1:2), corresponding to the seven lower middos and the “days of building.” R’ Tzadok’s use: “hevel” is no disparagement — this world is the “vapor” (hevel) rising from the pot, which carries the taste of the dish still cooking; a true “sample” of the enduring World to Come.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְהָאֱמֶת שֶׁבּוֹ שֶׁהִשְׁלִיךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַרְצָה הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם
notes.body_html: Daniel 8:12: “וְצָבָא תִּנָּתֵן עַל הַתָּמִיד בְּפָשַׁע, וְתַשְׁלֵךְ אֱמֶת אַרְצָה, וְעָשְׂתָה וְהִצְלִיחָה” — “and a host was set over the daily [offering] through transgression, and it cast truth to the ground, and it acted and prospered.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this world is “the world of falsehood,” for the truth within it — which Hashem “cast to the earth” — is in utter concealment; even the Torah’s full truth is disclosed now only as a faint “vapor” of the Torah of Mashiach.Tanya — the Written Torah is revealed, yet its inner will remains sealed until Torah shebe’al peh: Tanya, Iggeres HaKodesh §29, explains that the ratzon ha-elyon clothed in the mitzvos of the Written Torah is itself “מופלא ומכוסה, טמיר ונעלם,” and becomes disclosed only through Torah shebe’al peh. His example is tefillin: the written verse commands “ukeshartam” and “totafos,” but leaves the concrete form, location, materials, dimensions, and details concealed until the Oral Torah interprets them. The same is true, he says, of all positive and negative commandments. This is a precise Chabad parallel to R’ Tzadok’s phrase that Torah shebiksav is at once “galui v’sasum.” Its words are exposed to every reader, yet the Divine will embedded in those words is not exhausted by their surface. Torah shebe’al peh supplies the “handle” by which the hidden content can actually be grasped and lived. The comparison also clarifies R’ Tzadok’s use of hevel. The revealed word is not false or deficient; like breath carrying unarticulated letters, it bears within itself an abundance not yet unfolded. The future Torah of Mashiach is therefore not a replacement of the present Torah, but the fuller disclosure of what its present letters already contain in concealment — the truth cast into this world becoming transparent rather than hidden beneath its outward form.

notes.body_html: “Oraysa v’Kudsha Brich Hu chad” — the Torah and the Holy One are one (Zohar; cf. Tanya, Likutei Amarim ch. 4): the Torah is not a mere instrument that God fashioned, but an emanation of His own wisdom and will, which are utterly one with Him. Background and meforshim: the Tanya (ch. 4) draws the contrast — a mortal king is grasped only through his garments and decrees, which are separate from him, whereas the Holy One “and His wisdom are one,” so that whoever grasps a halachah of the Torah thereby embraces God Himself; the Nefesh HaChaim (Sha’ar 4) develops the same principle at length. R’ Tzadok’s use: because “Oraysa v’Kudsha Brich Hu chad,” calling Yehudah “mechokeki” (“who inscribes Me”) is no mere figure of speech — to inscribe the Torah on the hearts of Israel is to inscribe the Divine Presence itself within them; this is the ultimate perfection of the Future.

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 31:32 (Sefaria 31:33): “כִּי זֹאת הַבְּרִית אֲשֶׁר אֶכְרֹת אֶת בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל אַחֲרֵי הַיָּמִים הָהֵם נְאֻם ה׳, נָתַתִּי אֶת תּוֹרָתִי בְּקִרְבָּם וְעַל לִבָּם אֶכְתְּבֶנָּה” — “for this is the covenant I shall make with the House of Israel after those days, says Hashem: I have set My Torah within them, and upon their heart I will write it.” Background: this is Yirmeyah’s prophecy of the “new covenant” of the Redemption — the Torah so internalized that, as the very next verse says, “they shall no longer teach one another… for they shall all know Me,” never again to be forgotten. Meforshim: R’ Tzadok’s wording “on the tablet of their heart” fuses this verse with Mishlei 3:3, “כָּתְבֵם עַל לוּחַ לִבֶּךָ” — “write them upon the tablet of your heart.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this future inscribing-upon-the-heart is the work of Yehudah/Mashiach — the perfected Oral Torah, engraved so deep within that it can never be forgotten.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §13): “The Oral Torah was not written down, for the Oral Torah is [the teacher’s] very heart — and what is in the heart cannot be written; as they said in Sanhedrin (35a). Only the mouth is ‘the pen of the heart,’ [and by it] one is able to bring [Torah] into the heart of his fellow and his student — for ‘words that come from the heart enter the heart.’” (Precisely the se’if’s picture of Yehudah/Mashiach who “inscribes the Torah on the heart”: the Oral Torah is by nature heart-written, passing living from heart to heart rather than from page to page.)

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא ״כְּצֵל יָמֵינוּ עֲלֵי אָרֶץ״
notes.body_html: Divrei HaYamim I 29:15: “כִּי גֵרִים אֲנַחְנוּ לְפָנֶיךָ וְתוֹשָׁבִים כְּכָל אֲבֹתֵינוּ, כַּצֵּל יָמֵינוּ עַל הָאָרֶץ וְאֵין מִקְוֶה” — “for we are strangers before You, and sojourners like all our fathers; our days upon the earth are like a shadow, and there is no hope [of escaping death].” Background: David’s public confession at the great assembly where Israel donated gold and silver for the future Beis HaMikdash — all wealth is truly God’s, and man is only a passing sojourner. Meforshim: Rashi (citing Midrash Koheles Rabbah 1:2) sharpens the image — our days are not even like the lasting shadow of a tree, nor like the momentary shadow of a bird in flight, but “like the shadow of a bee’s wings, which has wings yet casts no shadow at all”; and “there is no mikveh” means “there is none who has any hope that he will not die.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the shadow is but a “sample” and outline of the true form — the soul that endures into the World to Come; hence the guidance of this shadow-world is “halachah,” the conduct of “walking” through it.

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 31:21 (Sefaria 31:22): “עַד מָתַי תִּתְחַמָּקִין הַבַּת הַשּׁוֹבֵבָה, כִּי בָרָא ה׳ חֲדָשָׁה בָּאָרֶץ נְקֵבָה תְּסוֹבֵב גָּבֶר” — “how long will you hide yourself, O backsliding daughter? For Hashem has created a new thing on the earth: a female shall encircle a male.” Background: the prophet calls wayward Israel (“the backsliding daughter”) to return, promising a “new creation” — a reversal of the natural order. Meforshim: Rashi offers two readings — by the plain sense, the “female” (Israel) will court the “male” (the Holy One), going about to seek Him (in the idiom of Shir HaShirim 3:2, “I will seek him”); and in the name of R’ Yehudah HaDarshan, the “female” who until now takes only a small share like a daughter will in the end inherit everything “like a firstborn son who inherits all.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the future revelation in which the Oral Torah (Malchus, the “female”) will “encircle” and openly manifest — the receiving rung rising to be “felt to the eye” like the giver, no longer in concealment.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: מִכָּל מָקוֹם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא נֶחְשָׁב לְהַשָּׂגַת אָדָם
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §77): “for even one who is fit for prophecy and ruach ha-kodesh receives it only by way of the greatest of the generation, as it says of the elders, "and I shall draw from the spirit that is upon you."” The se’if’s paradox exactly: a person’s true chiddushim are concealed ruach ha-kodesh, yet they come through a human channel and are therefore reckoned, in this world, as a human attainment.Kedushas Levi — when prophecy recedes, the light of Torah shebe’al peh begins to shine: Kedushas Levi, Homily for Purim §22, reads “kiyemu v’kiblu” as the historical turning-point from prophecy to the revealed flowering of the Oral Torah. Until Mordechai, he writes, “היה מאיר אור תורה שבכתב”; from Mordechai onward, as prophecy ceased, “התחיל להאיר אור תורה שבעל פה,” and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah began to establish the order of prayer. His point is not that the earlier generations lacked an Oral tradition. Rather, while nevuah remained openly available, the dominant light descended from Above in a form that could be written as the word of the prophet; when that channel closed, the hidden light began to appear through Israel’s own interpretive labor. This complements R’ Tzadok’s Levi–Yehudah structure exactly. Levi/Moshe represents Torah brought down from Heaven; Yehudah/David/Mashiach represents the Torah engraved into the human heart and spoken from within it. The disappearance of open revelation is therefore also the condition for a new form of revelation: what appears to be the chacham’s own halachic judgment can carry concealed ruach ha-kodesh, while still being reckoned to him as genuine attainment and responsibility. The Divine voice has not vanished; it has entered the human mouth and heart deeply enough that the words can truly be called his Torah.

Levi/Moshe represents Torah brought down from Heaven; Yehudah/David/Mashiach represents the Torah engraved into the human heart and spoken from within it. The disappearance of open revelation is therefore also the condition for a new form of revelation: what appears to be the chacham’s own halachic judgment can carry concealed ruach ha-kodesh, while still being reckoned to him as genuine attainment and responsibility. The Divine voice has not vanished; it has entered the human mouth and heart deeply enough that the words can truly be called his Torah.

notes.body_html: “Toviah ganiz b’gaveih” — “its good is stored away within it”: R’ Tzadok cites this Aramaic dictum in the name of Chazal to define the very nature of this world — its good does not lie on the surface but is hidden deep within, disclosed only through a person’s own effort (as the se’if continues, “only through his effort does he choose the good”). Background and parallel: the same principle underlies the primordial light that the Holy One “stored away” (ganuz) for the righteous of the Future (Chagigah 12a) — the good is concealed precisely so that it must be quarried out by toil. R’ Tzadok’s use: this concealment is the engine of avodah, and therefore the deepened concealment that followed the churban (forgetting) does not diminish but expands the Oral Torah — each generation compelled to delve the more.

notes.body_html: Eichah 2:1: “אֵיכָה יָעִיב בְּאַפּוֹ אֲדֹנָי אֶת בַּת צִיּוֹן, הִשְׁלִיךְ מִשָּׁמַיִם אֶרֶץ תִּפְאֶרֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְלֹא זָכַר הֲדֹם רַגְלָיו בְּיוֹם אַפּוֹ” — “how the Lord in His anger has beclouded Bas Tziyon; He cast down from heaven to earth the glory [tiferes] of Israel, and did not remember His footstool on the day of His anger.” Background: the opening of the second kinah of Eichah — the churban, in which God hurled Israel’s glory down from its heavenly height. Meforshim: Rashi explains “from heaven to earth” — “after He had raised them up to the heavens, He cast them to the earth all at once, not little by little — from a high roof to a deep pit (mei-igra rama le-vira amikta)”; and “His footstool” is the Beis HaMikdash. R’ Tzadok reads “tiferes Yisrael” as the Torah (which is called tiferes, as is known), so the verse speaks of the Torah “cast down” — the onset of forgetting. R’ Tzadok’s use: the churban’s casting-down of the glory brought forgetting, and precisely that forgetting forced Israel to delve the deeper — so the Oral Torah expands with each generation’s concealment.

notes.body_html: Pirkei Heichalos (ch. 27–28): R’ Yishmael said in the name of R’ Akiva citing R’ Eliezer: from the day the Torah was given until the last Temple was built, “the Torah was given, but its splendor was not given” — its radiance, its might, and its glory were not given until the last Temple was built and the Shechinah rested within it. And there (ch. 28) [the Holy One said:] “I know what you seek — you seek abundant Torah, and long for a wealth of Talmud and many halachic traditions — to multiply halachos like the sand of the sea — and to establish yeshivos in the gates to expound what is forbidden and permitted” — and in the end the Holy One consented to their request. [The Torah’s full “radiance,” its Oral expansion, was granted with the Second Temple and increased in the generations after.]Tanya — galus and concealment create the work of halachic birur: Tanya, Iggeres HaKodesh §26, gives a conceptual explanation for the phenomenon R’ Tzadok traces historically. The Alter Rebbe identifies the exile of the Shechinah with Malchus being clothed in kelipas nogah, and says that precisely then “עיקר עסק התורה” is the labor of iyun and pilpul in halachah — separating permitted from forbidden and pure from impure. A halachah whose reason was previously hidden is, through the earthly scholar’s analysis, lifted out of the concealment that covered it. He adds that the supernal beings themselves come to hear the chiddushei Torah of those below, because only embodied human beings can perform this particular birur. Thus the darkness is not merely an unfortunate background against which Torah happens to survive. It creates the very task through which new depths of Torah are disclosed. This closely complements R’ Tzadok’s sequence from churban and forgetting to the increased expansion of Torah shebe’al peh. Forgetting forces a descent into difficulty, machlokes, kushya, and sustained analysis; but those are also the places where hidden chochmah is recovered. R’ Akiva’s superiority in certain depths to what Moshe initially apprehended is not a contradiction to Sinai: the later generation encounters layers of concealment that demand, and therefore elicit, forms of Torah disclosure that the earlier revealed order did not yet require.

notes.body_html: Bamidbar Rabbah 19:6 (the sefer brackets it as “Vayikra Rabbah”; the extant midrash is Bamidbar Rabbah 19:6, and Midrash Tanchuma, Chukas 8): on the Parah Adumah, Hashem tells Moshe “to you I reveal the reason of the cow, but to others it is a chok,” adding that matters concealed now will be beheld in the Future — “דְּבָרִים שֶׁלֹּא נִגְלוּ לְמֹשֶׁה נִגְלוּ לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וַחֲבֵרָיו; וְכָל יְקָר רָאֲתָה עֵינוֹ — זֶה רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וַחֲבֵרָיו” — “things not revealed to Moshe were revealed to R’ Akiva and his colleagues; ‘and his eye beheld every precious thing’ (Iyov 28:10) — this is R’ Akiva and his colleagues.” Meforshim / source-note: the “eye that saw” is drawn from Iyov 28:10, “v’chol yakar ra’asah eino.” R’ Tzadok’s use: as concealment deepened after the churban, the later sages had to see “more” than the earlier — R’ Akiva, founder of the Oral Torah’s principles and details, perceived what even Moshe did not, for he was the “armor-bearer of Mashiach,” the vessels of whose Torah he prepared.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְאָז אַחַר כָּךְ מִתְגַּלֶּה אוֹר דִּזְבוּלוּן, שֶׁהוּא כְּטַעַם ״כְּצֵל הַחָכְמָה בְּצֵל הַכֶּסֶף״
notes.body_html: Koheles 7:12: “כִּי בְּצֵל הַחָכְמָה בְּצֵל הַכָּסֶף, וְיִתְרוֹן דַּעַת הַחָכְמָה תְּחַיֶּה בְעָלֶיהָ” — “for [to be] in the shade of wisdom is [to be] in the shade of money; and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its possessor.” Background: Koheles teaches that wisdom shelters a person much as wealth does — yet wisdom is the superior shelter, for it “gives life.” Meforshim: the commentators read the two clauses as a comparison — as money casts a protective “shade,” so does wisdom, and wisdom’s advantage is that “techayeh be’aleha,” it keeps its owner alive. R’ Tzadok’s use: the two shades are two rungs — the “shade of money” is Zevulun (the longing to serve God even amid worldly commerce), and the “shade of wisdom” is Yissachar’s Torah, the greater; in the World to Come it is disclosed that the mitzvos-masters’ service was but a “shade” beside the Torah-masters.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הִקְדִּים זְבוּלוּן לְיִשָּׂשכָר ״בְּצֵאתְךָ וְיִשָּׂשכָר בְּאֹהָלֶיךָ״
notes.body_html: Devarim 33:18: “וְלִזְבוּלֻן אָמַר: שְׂמַח זְבוּלֻן בְּצֵאתֶךָ, וְיִשָּׂשכָר בְּאֹהָלֶיךָ” — “and of Zevulun he said: rejoice, Zevulun, in your going out, and Yissachar, in your tents.” Background: part of Moshe’s parting blessing to the tribes. Meforshim: Rashi (from Bereishis Rabbah 99) explains that Zevulun and Yissachar formed a partnership — Zevulun dwells at the seashore, sails out for commerce, and “puts food into the mouth of Yissachar,” who sits and toils in Torah; Moshe therefore placed Zevulun first, “for Yissachar’s Torah came about through Zevulun.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Zevulun’s “going out” — remaining cleaved to God even amid worldly affairs — is a greater level than Yissachar’s inwardness, hence its precedence; yet the essential wisdom is Yissachar’s, hidden in the heart, while Zevulun’s is the revealed joy, perceptible even to the nations.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Masei §4): "“for you are coming to the land of Canaan” — in the Midrash: “what is Canaan? A land of commerce [perakmatya], in which they trade,” as you say, “whose merchants are princes.”" Exactly the se’if: the Land itself is named for commerce, so Zevulun’s worldly engagement is no descent from Yissachar’s tent but the appointed setting in which cleaving must be achieved.Sefas Emes — Zevulun carries Torah specifically into the place of ‘going out’: Sefas Emes, Sukkos 2:11, asks the obvious question on “שמח זבולון בצאתך”: why should Zevulun rejoice in the very portion that takes him away from the beis midrash into commerce? He answers that the joy and longing for Torah established before the departure protect the person after he has gone out. Even merchants who cannot remain occupied with Torah throughout the year can fix Torah in the heart so deeply that their worldly engagement does not become total forgetfulness. This is an especially apt complement to R’ Tzadok’s elevation of Zevulun above a merely sheltered spirituality. Yissachar’s holiness is visible in the tent; Zevulun’s test is whether the same inward bond survives “betzeisecha,” when attention is dispersed among markets, money, travel, and ordinary responsibility. The Sefas Emes makes the transition itself the avodah: a person goes outward while carrying an inward point that he refuses to abandon. Thus worldly occupation need not be a second, spiritually neutral life alongside Torah. When the departure is governed by prior attachment, the commerce becomes the arena in which Torah proves that it has entered the person rather than remaining only in his surroundings. This gives content to R’ Tzadok’s claim that true deveikus can be greater precisely amid the affairs of olam hazeh.

Meforshim: Rashi glosses “amim” as [the peoples] “of the tribes of Israel” who gather to Har HaMoriah; R’ Tzadok, by contrast, reads “amim” as the nations of the world, who apprehend only the outward “mountain” — a height “marked and conspicuous by being higher than all around it.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the nations reach only the revealed “har” (as Avraham named the place a “mountain”), whereas Israel alone possess the inner “house.”

notes.body_html: Bereishis 22:14: “וַיִּקְרָא אַבְרָהָם שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא ה׳ יִרְאֶה, אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר הַיּוֹם בְּהַר ה׳ יֵרָאֶה” — “and Avraham called the name of that place ‘Hashem yireh,’ as it is said this day, ‘on the mountain of Hashem He will be seen.’” Background: after the Akeidah, Avraham names the future Temple site. Meforshim: the Gemara (Pesachim 88a) contrasts the three patriarchs — Avraham called the place a “mountain” (har), Yitzchak a “field” (sadeh), and Yaakov a “house” (bayis); the ultimate name is Yaakov’s “house.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Avraham, “the father of a multitude of nations,” named it “har” — the outward height that the nations, too, can reach; the higher, inner “house” belongs to the seed of Yaakov.

notes.body_html: “Sihara b’ashlemusa” — “the moon at its fullness”: a Zoharic idiom. In Kabbalah the moon symbolizes Malchus — the Davidic kingship and the Shechinah — which waxes and wanes like the moon. Background: Shlomo’s reign was the peak of the Jewish monarchy, “the moon at its fullness,” when the Beis HaMikdash stood and the kingdom was whole. R’ Tzadok’s use: yet this fullness lasted only “for a brief time, in his generation” — Shlomo himself became “king and then a commoner” (Sanhedrin 20b), and straightaway the kingship of the House of David was split; the full and enduring indwelling of the Shechinah in the “house” belongs to the days of Mashiach.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַסִּימָן לְמִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּקִרְבּוֹ אוֹצָר שֶׁל יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Masei §9): “"I have a good gift in My treasury and its name is Shabbos" — and one must understand: did they not say that the Holy One has nothing in His treasury but the treasury of the fear of Heaven alone, and of that it cannot be said that it is a good gift to give to Israel, since the fear of Heaven is in a person’s hand alone, as they said, "all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven"?” This is exactly the se’if’s two-way link: fear is the one thing left to man’s effort, and yet it is what Heaven keeps in its treasury — so that each side needs the other.Mei HaShiloach — chochmah and yirah must continually generate one another: Mei HaShiloach I, Beshalach §2, explains the Mishnah “אם אין חכמה אין יראה, אם אין יראה אין חכמה” as a dynamic balance. Chochmah gives a person tokef — inner firmness and confidence — but without yirah that very strength can become the delusion that his wisdom stands independently of Hashem. Conversely, a person who possesses only fear without the strengthening clarity of chochmah has not yet reached true yirah; his fear can remain imagination and anxiety rather than awe of God. The Ishbitzer therefore reads “bayam bayabashah” and “bayabashah besoch hayam” as the required interpenetration of the two states: the sea signifies yirah and tefillah, the dry land signifies the firmness of Torah, and each must be found within the other. This deepens R’ Tzadok’s two-directional account here. The first yirah is the human gate — the small opening of submission by which one enters. Chochmah is then given from Above; but that chochmah itself produces a higher yirah, now born from perception rather than mere restraint. The cycle continues. Hence the Shechinah’s dwelling in the heart is neither achieved by human effort alone nor simply imposed from Heaven. The person opens the treasury through yirah; the Divine chochmah that enters enlarges his capacity for awe, and the enlarged awe becomes a still deeper vessel for wisdom.

notes.body_html: Rema (R’ Moshe Isserles), in his gloss at the opening of Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 1:1, teaches on the verse “I have set Hashem before me always” (Tehillim 16:8) that “this is a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God.” A person’s conduct when alone in his house is not as it is before a great king; and when one takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed is He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, “immediately the awe and the submission in the fear of Him reach him” (the Rema citing Rambam, Moreh Nevuchim III:52) — the fear that “reaches him of itself” to which R’ Tzadok alludes here.

notes.body_html: Devarim 26:8: “וַיּוֹצִאֵנוּ ה׳ מִמִּצְרַיִם בְּיָד חֲזָקָה וּבִזְרֹעַ נְטוּיָה וּבְמֹרָא גָּדֹל וּבְאֹתוֹת וּבְמֹפְתִים” — “and Hashem brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and with great awe, and with signs and wonders.” Background: this verse is from the “Arami oved avi” passage of the first-fruits declaration (Devarim 26:5–10), which the Pesach Haggadah expounds phrase by phrase. Meforshim: the Haggadah (Magid), darshening this verse, teaches “u-v’mora gadol — this is the revelation of the Shechinah,” deriving it from the parallel “great awesome deeds” (mora’im gedolim) said of the Exodus in Devarim 4:34. R’ Tzadok’s use: “great awe” is the fear that descends from a revealed Divine Presence — and since “gadol” (great) connotes a spreading-forth without end, it is a fear from which one can never come to forget, unlike the lesser fear a person must generate by his own effort (“the gate”).

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah §5): “"three good gifts" — Eretz Yisrael, Torah, and the World to Come — all of them through sufferings; and they are in the merit of the three Avos, who bequeathed the root of their good traits to their children, to be fixed in the depths of their hearts: the three holy points… "and the fear of Hashem is the beginning of wisdom."” The se’if’s two-way link precisely: fear is “the beginning of wisdom,” yet it is itself an inheritance fixed in the depths of the heart — so neither side stands without the other.

notes.body_html: “The whole world was created for the sake of Israel”: a foundational teaching of Chazal. Rashi, in his opening comment on the Torah (Bereishis 1:1), explains that God created the world “for the sake of Israel, who are called reishis, and for the sake of the Torah, called reishis”; the midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 36:4) likewise teaches that the world endures in the merit of Israel. R’ Tzadok’s use: because the world thus “belongs” to Israel, its abundance is theirs to elevate — to “absorb the power of holiness that sustains it and brings it into being”; but should they sink into it as an end in itself, they sever both it and themselves from its Source.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כְּטַעַם ״שָׁמַנְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר וַיִּטּוֹשׁ [אֱלוֹהַּ עָשָׂהוּ]״ וְגוֹמֵר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְרָם לְבָבֶךָ וְשָׁכַחְתָּ [אֶת ה׳]״
notes.body_html: Devarim 32:15: “וַיִּשְׁמַן יְשֻׁרוּן וַיִּבְעָט, שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ כָּשִׂיתָ, וַיִּטֹּשׁ אֱלוֹהַּ עָשָׂהוּ, וַיְנַבֵּל צוּר יְשֻׁעָתוֹ” — “and Yeshurun grew fat and kicked — you grew fat, thick, gross — and he forsook the God who made him, and spurned the Rock of his salvation.” Background: from the song of Ha’azinu — Moshe’s warning that material abundance would lead Israel to rebel. Meforshim: the verse itself traces the descent — satiety (“you grew fat”) breeds “kicking” against Heaven, which ends in forsaking God; wealth ungoverned by gratitude produces rebellion. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the danger of “sinking oneself” into the abundance of this world alone — one is thereby “sundered from His unity”; only Zevulun’s fear (the techeiles-thread) lets a person absorb the holiness within the abundance without being severed from its Source.Noam Elimelech — techeiles and the sea teach a yirah that sets a holy boundary: Noam Elimelech, Shelach §18, develops Chazal’s chain “techeiles resembles the sea, the sea the firmament, and the firmament the Throne of Glory.” He reads the sea as yirah: Hashem placed a boundary for it, and despite the force of its waves it does not pass the limit decreed for it. The firmament, by contrast, expresses a joyous love; together the two repair the person’s ‘wings.’ This illuminates R’ Tzadok’s use of Zevulun, the sea, the sand, and the thread of techeiles. The issue is not to destroy the sea’s abundance — desire, commerce, physical vitality, and the wealth of the world — but to give it a boundary that makes its energy serve rather than overwhelm. Yirah is therefore not withdrawal from shefa; it is the capacity to receive shefa without losing the distinction between the gift and its Source. The sand holds back the sea, and the techeiles draws the eye from sea to sky to Kisei HaKavod. In R’ Tzadok’s terms, that is what permits Zevulun to draw from “shefa yamim” while extracting only the kedushah concealed in it. Without the boundary, abundance becomes “vayishman Yeshurun vayiv’at”; with the boundary, the same abundance is absorbed into avodah.

notes.body_html: Devarim 8:14: “וְרָם לְבָבֶךָ וְשָׁכַחְתָּ אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ, הַמּוֹצִיאֲךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם מִבֵּית עֲבָדִים” — “and your heart grows haughty, and you forget Hashem your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.” Background: Moshe warns that prosperity in the Land — “you shall eat and be satisfied” — can breed a haughty heart. Meforshim: the verse pairs “haughtiness of heart” directly with “forgetting”; the commentators note that self-sufficiency (as the next verses put it, ascribing success to “my own strength and the might of my hand”) is the very root of forgetting God. R’ Tzadok’s use: forgetting is the fruit of a heart “grown haughty” over worldly abundance — the exact opposite of the fear (the techeiles-thread) that “removes forgetting.”

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 5:22: “הַאוֹתִי לֹא תִירָאוּ נְאֻם ה׳… אֲשֶׁר שַׂמְתִּי חוֹל גְּבוּל לַיָּם חָק עוֹלָם וְלֹא יַעַבְרֶנְהוּ, וַיִּתְגָּעֲשׁוּ וְלֹא יוּכָלוּ וְהָמוּ גַלָּיו וְלֹא יַעַבְרֻנְהוּ” — “will you not fear Me, says Hashem…? I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an eternal decree it cannot pass — though its waves toss, they cannot prevail; though they roar, they cannot pass it.” Background: the prophet rebukes Israel’s lack of fear, pointing to the standing wonder that mere sand holds back the raging sea — a testimony to God’s power that ought to evoke awe (the verse opens, literally, “Me you do not fear?”). Meforshim: the commentators note the marvel that the frailest barrier — loose grains of sand — restrains the mightiest force, by Divine decree alone. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel are that “sand” — the boundary that keeps the “sea” of the nations’ desires from flooding the world (as it did in the generation of the Flood); their very lowliness and concealment is what holds the line.

notes.body_html: Sukkah 29a: in the passage on the significance of eclipses, the Gemara teaches that “Israel reckon [their calendar] by the moon, while the nations of the world reckon by the sun.” Background: Israel’s festivals follow the lunar cycle — the moon, which waxes, wanes, and is at times wholly covered. R’ Tzadok’s use: the moon is the emblem of Israel’s “concealment” — like the moon that is periodically hidden, Israel’s greatness is veiled in this world and revealed only in the Future; and it is precisely this hiddenness (monin la-levanah) that is their power to draw the holy spark unseen from the “sea” of worldly abundance.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 25:26: “וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן יָצָא אָחִיו וְיָדוֹ אֹחֶזֶת בַּעֲקֵב עֵשָׂו, וַיִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ יַעֲקֹב” — “and afterward his brother emerged, his hand grasping the heel of Esav, and he called his name Yaakov.” Background: at the twins’ birth Yaakov is named for the “heel” (akev) of Esav that his hand held. Meforshim: the Sages take the grasping hand as a sign that Yaakov would ultimately seize what was Esav’s (as the midrash develops on this very phrase). R’ Tzadok’s use: Yaakov’s very name expresses a “grip” on Esav’s heel — the point at which even Esav has “some hold” within holiness, and conversely the place where the hidden root of Yaakov (and of David) lies.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §13): “And in Kiddushin (18a) it is brought that Esav is a ‘Yisrael mumar’ [an apostate Jew] — meaning that before he went out to evil ways the name ‘Israel’ rested upon him, and he was circumcised at eight days, except that [afterward] he apostatized. And although with a Jew, even an apostate, ‘though he has sinned, he is [still] a Jew’ — this [inseverability] is only in the seed of Yaakov, in whom the ‘cord of inheritance’ is already fixed with ‘three strands’ [the three Avos] and can no longer be severed; but in the seed of Yitzchak [i.e., Esav], although he was at first called by the name Israel, once he apostatized [he was cut off].”

notes.body_html: Bereishis 25:28: “וַיֶּאֱהַב יִצְחָק אֶת עֵשָׂו כִּי צַיִד בְּפִיו, וְרִבְקָה אֹהֶבֶת אֶת יַעֲקֹב” — “and Yitzchak loved Esav, for game [tzayid] was in his mouth, and Rivkah loved Yaakov.” Background: by the plain sense, Yitzchak favored Esav because Esav brought him venison. Meforshim (Kabbalah): the Arizal reads “tzayid be-fiv” as a hint that great souls were “trapped” — tzayid, a hunt — within Esav, among them the soul of R’ Akiva, foundation of the Oral Torah. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why Esav bore the name “Yisrael” from birth — truly great souls were hidden in him; but only “in his heels,” the lowest rung, whereas in Yaakov they are the very essence.Me’or Einayim — Yaakov’s hand on Esav’s heel is a work of extraction, not identification: Me’or Einayim, Toldos §24, citing the Arizal, explains Yitzchak’s perception of “tzayid befiv” as an apprehension of holy souls trapped within Esav — specifically mentioning the soul of R’ Akiva. He then asks why Yaakov and Esav had to be joined so closely from conception. His answer is a principle of birur: to lift something fallen below, one must be able to reach the place where it lies. Yaakov therefore entered the same womb and “his hand grasped the heel of Esav” in order to seize and elevate the sparks of holiness embedded there. The heel is the point of contact, not the definition of Yaakov’s identity. This fits R’ Tzadok’s formulation with unusual precision. Esav can possess a genuine Israelite spark and can even conceal within himself a soul as exalted as R’ Akiva, while still not becoming ‘Yisrael in essence.’ The holy point in Esav is precisely what Yaakov is destined to reclaim. This also explains why the relationship must be spoken of carefully: the existence of a buried spark does not sanctify the shell that imprisons it. On the contrary, Yaakov’s task is to distinguish the two. The future emergence of Torah and Mashiach from places apparently belonging to Esav is therefore the completion of “yado ochezes ba’akev” — the hidden kedushah is extracted from the heel and returned to the root to which it truly belongs.

notes.body_html: Gittin 56a: the Gemara relates that Nero Caesar, sent against Yerushalayim, saw omens that he would be held to blame for its destruction, so he fled, converted, “and R’ Meir descended from him.” R’ Tzadok’s use: that R’ Meir — the anonymous voice of the Mishnah, the essence of the Oral Torah — issued from the very line of Rome/Esav shows how the holiest attainment lay hidden in Esav’s “heel,” waiting to be drawn out.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 86a: R’ Yochanan taught that the anonymous rulings of the Oral Torah all stem from R’ Akiva’s school — “an anonymous Mishnah is R’ Meir, an anonymous Tosefta is R’ Nechemiah, an anonymous [teaching in] Sifra is R’ Yehudah, an anonymous [teaching in] Sifrei is R’ Shimon — and all of them are according to R’ Akiva.” R’ Tzadok’s use: since “an anonymous Mishnah is R’ Meir” — and R’ Meir sprang from Esav’s line — the very backbone of the Oral Torah (the anonymous Mishnayos, the fixed “halachos”) traces to the great souls hidden within Esav.

notes.body_html: Mishlei 5:5: “רַגְלֶיהָ יֹרְדוֹת מָוֶת, שְׁאוֹל צְעָדֶיהָ יִתְמֹכוּ” — “her feet descend to death; her steps take hold of She’ol” (said of the seductress, the ishah zarah). Background: Mishlei warns that following the “strange woman” leads downward to death and the grave. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “feet” — the lowest rung of a person’s “stature” — are where sin lodges, “her feet descend to death”; correspondingly, in Esav (a “base man”) only the “heel” holds any good, his essence being the reverse.

notes.body_html: Koheles 3:1: “לַכֹּל זְמָן, וְעֵת לְכָל חֵפֶץ תַּחַת הַשָּׁמָיִם” — “for everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven.” Background: Koheles’ meditation that all things have their appointed time. R’ Tzadok’s use: “under heaven” is the realm of time; David’s complete rectification (emerging together with Yaakov) could in principle have been “at once,” but “a time for every purpose” — the constraint of a time-bound world — deferred it.

notes.body_html: Koheles 8:9: “…עֵת אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַט הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם לְרַע לוֹ” — “…a time when one man ruled over another to his detriment.” Background: Koheles observes the harm of one person dominating another. R’ Tzadok’s use (per the Arizal’s Sefer HaGilgulim): this “time when man ruled man” is the dominion of the “base man” — and it was this that turned David’s potential into Esav instead, so that David’s soul “did not yet emerge from the balance.”

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 63:9: on “his hand grasping the heel of Esav,” a Roman hegemon asked a sage of the House of Siloni, “who will seize the kingdom after us?” He took a blank sheet, wrote “and afterward his brother emerged, his hand grasping the heel,” and they marveled, “old words from the mouth of a new elder!” — meaning that after Esav’s (Rome’s) dominion, Yaakov’s line will grasp the kingship. R’ Tzadok’s use: it is precisely “at the heel” — after Esav — that Mashiach, the hidden root of David, will rise to seize the kingship; for the “heel” corresponds to the World of Asiyah [Action], “the perfection of the deed.”

notes.body_html: Bava Basra 10b: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked his students the meaning of “charity exalts a nation, but the kindness of the peoples is sin” (Mishlei 14:34). The answers held that the charity and kindness the nations perform is “sin” for them, since they do it only for self-aggrandizement; and R’ Nechunya ben HaKanah’s reading was deemed best — that charity and kindness are for Israel, and for the nations a “sin[-offering]” — for “just as the sin-offering atones for Israel, so charity atones for the nations of the world.”
notes.body_plain: Bava Basra 10b: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked his students the meaning of “charity exalts a nation, but the kindness of the peoples is sin” (Mishlei 14:34). The answers held that the charity and kindness the nations perform is “sin” for them, since they do it only for self-aggrandizement; and R’ Nechunya ben HaKanah’s reading was deemed best — that charity and kindness are for Israel, and for the nations a “sin[-offering]” — for “just as the sin-offering atones for Israel, so charity atones for the nations of the world.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §28): “for the ten utterances comprise ten holy middos, whose opposite is the ten nations given to Avraham, who cleaved to their opposite in holiness; and "the first of the nations is Amalek" — the beginning and the keser of the kelipah.” This grounds the se’if’s reversal: the husk has its own “crown,” an outward summit that mimics the holy order precisely in order to be mistaken for it.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּ״שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם״ הָיָה לְרַע לוֹ
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Sukkos §21): “for all the force of their generosity and giving is not in the innermost heart, but only to arouse accusation against Israel — "the kindness of the nations is a sin"; unlike Israel, whose… giving is in joy, in the innermost point of the heart, as it says, "and you shall draw water in gladness."” Exactly the se’if: the nations’ mitzvos are real deeds with a hollow interior — done for self-aggrandizement, they become an accusation rather than a merit.Sefas Emes — Esav’s falsehood survives only by borrowing a beginning of truth: Sefas Emes, Toldos 26:3, reads “וידו אוחזת בעקב עשו” through the maxim that falsehood has no legs. A lie that contains no truth at its beginning cannot endure at all; therefore Esav must possess “something at his head,” but his end is “adei oveid.” Yaakov, by contrast, is “Sefas emes tikon la’ad” — truth that reaches and repairs all the way to the heel and the end. This supplies a sharp conceptual complement to R’ Tzadok’s image of the swine stretching out its split hoof. The deception works only because it displays a real-looking point of purity. Similarly, the nations may perform acts that resemble mitzvos or kindness; the outward form can contain enough truth to sustain the claim. The falsehood lies in making that partial truth represent the whole while the hidden interior remains directed to self. Yaakov’s response is not to deny that there is any true point in Esav. His hand takes hold of precisely that point and carries truth through to its conclusion. The distinction between Yaakov and Esav is therefore not simply ‘truth versus zero truth,’ but enduring truth versus borrowed truth that cannot survive to the end. What is holy in Esav is destined to be gathered into Yaakov; what is merely the pose of holiness is ultimately exposed.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְדַרְגָּא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל — רְצֹה לוֹמַר תַּלְמִיד חָכָם דְּאָחִיד בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא — זֶה ״לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי״
notes.body_html: Tehillim 147:20: “לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי, וּמִשְׁפָּטִים בַּל יְדָעוּם, הַלְלוּ יָהּ” — “He has not done so for any [other] nation; and His statutes — they know them not. Halleluyah.” Background: the closing verse of the psalm — God gave His word, His laws and statutes, to Yaakov/Israel alone; no other nation was granted them. Meforshim: by the plain sense, the Torah’s mishpatim are Israel’s unique portion, and “the nations do not know them” — which is why the verse crowns the psalm with praise. R’ Tzadok’s use: the rung of “Yisrael” — the talmid chacham who “grasps the Torah” from within — is that of which “He has not done so for any nation”; only the outer rung of “Yaakov” (bare mitzvah-deed, seen by the eye) has any counterpart among the nations and in Esav.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר ״אֵיךְ נֶחְפְּשׂוּ עֵשָׂו נִבְעוּ מַצְפֻּנָיו״
notes.body_html: Ovadiah 1:6: “אֵיךְ נֶחְפְּשׂוּ עֵשָׂו, נִבְעוּ מַצְפֻּנָיו” — “how Esav has been searched out, his hidden treasures laid bare!” Background: from Ovadiah’s single-chapter prophecy of the downfall of Edom (Esav) — his concealed stores will be ransacked and exposed, with nothing left hidden. Meforshim: by the plain sense, Esav’s secret hoards of wealth are plundered and brought to light. R’ Tzadok’s use: though Esav borrowed Israel’s “power of concealment” to mask his evil — “his secrets hidden” — that veil is only skin-deep; “how Esav was searched out, his hidden things laid bare” — in truth he is “empty of everything,” his emptiness revealed to all.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 25:27: “וַיִּגְדְּלוּ הַנְּעָרִים, וַיְהִי עֵשָׂו אִישׁ יֹדֵעַ צַיִד אִישׁ שָׂדֶה, וְיַעֲקֹב אִישׁ תָּם יֹשֵׁב אֹהָלִים” — “and the lads grew up, and Esav became a man who knew hunting, a man of the field, while Yaakov was a wholesome man [ish tam], dwelling in tents.” Background: the two brothers’ contrasting natures — Esav the hunter of the open field, Yaakov the “tam” who sat in the tents [of study]. Meforshim: Rashi glosses “tam” — “he was not expert [in deceit]; as his heart, so his mouth; one who is not sharp to deceive is called tam.” R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because Yaakov is “tam” — his inner heart matching his outward conduct — he appeared to the world’s eye to lack Esav’s “power,” so that people supposed Leah “belonged” to Esav; yet in the hidden depths Yaakov is inwardly “his brother in cunning,” and the true rung of “Yisrael” is the concealed wisdom of the heart, which no outward eye perceives.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְרַק דַּרְגָּא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מַעֲמַקֵּי הַחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב שֶׁ״אִישׁ תְּבוּנוֹת יִדְלֶנָּה״ דְּאֵין נִגְלֶה לְפֹעַל
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeitzei §10): “"where the birds nest" — in what place? In Lebanon — and these are the two birds spoken of in several places, the upper ones, which issue from Lebanon, which is the concealed [world].” The se’if’s alma d’iskasya precisely: Leah’s perfection is rooted in the upper, hidden place from which the revealed pairs issue — never visible in the order the eye reads.Leah and the hidden world — why the baal teshuvah can reveal a root deeper than visible purity: Shem MiShmuel, Vayeitzei 9:15, explicitly identifies Rachel with alma d’isgalya and Leah with alma d’iskasya. He associates Rachel’s revealed illumination with aseh tov and Leah’s higher hidden illumination with sur me’ra. The Ishbitz teaching on Berachos 34b (Mei HaShiloach II) adds the teshuvah dimension: the tzaddik gamur has a more purified body, but the soul of the baal teshuvah is hewn from a higher place; through the cry and broken heart of teshuvah it can reach an ‘omek amok’ beyond ordinary human daas. These sources clarify R’ Tzadok’s paradox that Leah, apparently the side whose affinity was misunderstood and assigned to Esav, is in her depth wholly alien to him and can culminate in the very perfection of teshuvah. Alma d’iskasya means that the decisive truth of the person is not always readable from the visible history. Yet the hidden root is not a shortcut around avodah. It becomes manifest through sur me’ra, brokenhearted return, and transformation. This is why R’ Tzadok can speak of the baal teshuvah’s sins eventually becoming merits without confusing him with Esav’s concealment of evil. Esav hides corruption beneath an outward claim; Leah’s world hides a holiness that is uncovered by genuine correction. One concealment falsifies the surface, while the other reveals that the surface was never the final measure of the soul.

notes.body_html: Yechezkel 37:19: “הִנֵּה אֲנִי לֹקֵחַ אֶת עֵץ יוֹסֵף אֲשֶׁר בְּיַד אֶפְרַיִם וְשִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל חֲבֵרָיו, וְנָתַתִּי אוֹתָם עָלָיו אֶת עֵץ יְהוּדָה, וַעֲשִׂיתִם לְעֵץ אֶחָד, וְהָיוּ אֶחָד בְּיָדִי” — “behold, I take the wood of Yosef, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his companions, and I will set them upon it — the wood of Yehudah — and make them into one wood, and they shall be one in My hand.” Background: from Yechezkel’s prophecy of the “two sticks” (37:15–19) — the prophet takes two pieces of wood inscribed for Yosef (Ephraim) and for Yehudah and joins them into one, a sign of the future reunification of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah into one people under one king (Mashiach). Meforshim: the commentators read the two sticks as the two monarchies — the ten tribes under Ephraim/Yosef, and Yehudah — to be reunited in the Redemption; R’ Tzadok’s phrase “one to the other” (echad el echad) is drawn from the adjacent verse (37:17), “and bring them near one to another into one stick.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the full “clarification” that Yosef and Yehudah — who appear as opposites in this world — are truly one root will be revealed “before all eyes” only in the Future, when God joins “the wood of Yosef and Yehudah, one to the other, to be companions.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §15): “to instruct before him — and it is brought in the Midrash,”to establish for him a house of study."" Exactly the se’if: Yosef and Yehudah appear opposed — deed against heart — yet the first thing sent ahead into exile is the house of study, in which the two are already one.Shem MiShmuel — the future joining of Yosef and Yehudah repairs the root of their apparent opposition: Shem MiShmuel, Korach 2:21, reads Yechezkel’s two sticks — the wood of Yosef and the wood of Yehudah becoming ‘one in My hand’ — as the final tikkun of the root from which later divisions grew. He links that future unity to the healing of the sale of Yosef and cites the parallel promise that Ephraim will no longer envy Yehudah and Yehudah will no longer oppress Ephraim. This is a close complement to R’ Tzadok’s insistence that the two lines are one at their source even though this world presents them as opposites. Yosef is the visibly guarded yesod, the tzaddik whose sanctity is expressed through restraint and purity; Yehudah is the line in which failure, confession, and teshuvah become the road to Malchus. If one judges only by the revealed form, each can seem to invalidate the other. The prophetic future does not erase either model. It makes them ‘one wood’: the tzaddik’s purity and the baal teshuvah’s depth are seen as two expressions of one Divine root. This also frames the difficult material that follows concerning Yehudah, Shimon, and bris. R’ Tzadok is not lowering the Torah’s prohibitions; he is tracing how the very line whose revealed history contains grave failure can, through teshuvah and clarification, disclose a unity with Yosef that was hidden all along.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §90): “"concerning the matter of Peor and concerning the matter of Kozbi"… for they were fenced-in as regards forbidden relations, only that they reasoned there is no prohibition with the nations, as with the daughter of Yisro — yet in any case he begets a child for idolatry.” Exactly the se’if’s point: the prohibition of cohabiting with a gentile woman is the one the Torah left implicit, and its true severity lies in what is begotten, not in the act alone.

notes.body_html: “The Torah did not decree punishment without first issuing a warning” (a governing rule of the Gemara; see, e.g., Yoma 81a; Sanhedrin 54a): a fixed principle that no act is punishable under the Torah unless the Torah first stated an explicit prohibition (azharah) against it — so wherever Scripture records only a punishment, the Gemara must seek out the corresponding warning. R’ Tzadok’s use: since the two “corruptions” here — bris-corruption and cohabiting with a gentile woman — carry only a stated punishment and no explicit prohibition, the very halachah “was hidden” (even from Moshe, until Pinchas recalled it); this reflects that, in the deepest truth, the seed of Israel has no real “connection” to a gentile woman at all — there is, as it were, nothing there to formally forbid.

He said, “son of Amram — is this one forbidden or permitted? and if you say forbidden — who permitted the daughter of Yisro to you?” The halachah was hidden from him [Moshe] — And it is written, “and Pinchas saw” — what did he see? Rav said: “he saw the deed and remembered the halachah.” He said to [Moshe], “great-uncle, did you not teach us on your descent from Sinai, ‘one who cohabits with an Aramean woman — zealots may strike him’?” [The prohibition was left unstated, and the halachah “was hidden” until Pinchas recalled it.]
