notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 85 (on the wife of Potifar): [R’ Yehoshua ben Levi said] she saw by her astrology that she was destined to raise up a child from [Yosef], but did not know whether from herself or from her daughter — and the union was fulfilled through her daughter Osnas. Avodah Zarah 20a (on R’ Akiva): he saw the wife of the wicked Turnusrufus — and he spat, laughed, and wept: spat, for she came from a putrid drop; laughed, for she was destined to convert and he would marry her; and wept, that such beauty would ultimately decay in the dust. [R’ Akiva’s reaction shows the “longing” was one-sided and future-oriented — she would convert and marry him.]

notes.body_html: The source is the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach), R’ Tzadok’s rebbe. R’ Tzadok’s “v’shamati” (“and I heard”) characteristically signals a teaching received from his teacher, R’ Mordechai Yosef Leiner of Izhbitz, author of the Mei HaShiloach. The idea here — that even the “accursed” gentile does not truly desire the union, and that a gentile’s apparent “longing” masks a hidden root-connection disclosed only in the Future — is the Ishbitzer’s teaching on Zimri and Kozbi. See Mei HaShiloach, Parashas Balak (on “v’hinei ish mi-bnei Yisrael… ha-Midyanis”): before the deed he is called “a man of the Children of Israel,” but afterward “a man of Israel” — “for in the Future the Holy One will clarify that this soul was bound to him at his root, as is brought in the writings of the Arizal”; and Mei HaShiloach, Parashas Pinchas (on “va-yar Pinchas”): “she was his soulmate (bas zug) from the six days of creation, as explained in the writings of the Arizal… but the depth of the root of the matter was hidden from [Pinchas].” R’ Tzadok’s continuation here — the Arizal on Shechem (“chashkah nafsho”), reincarnated in Zimri — draws directly on these passages.

notes.body_html: Menachos 44a: A man scrupulous in the mitzvah of tzitzis heard of a harlot overseas who took four hundred zuz as her fee; he sent it and set a time. When he came and sat upon the bed, “his four tzitzis came and slapped him across the face”; he slipped down and sat upon the ground, and she did likewise. She pressed him to explain, and he told her of the mitzvah of tzitzis — “which testified before me four times, ‘the Torah of Hashem my God.’” In the end she sought out his beis midrash, converted, and married him — “and the very couches she had spread for him in prohibition, she [now] spread for him in permission.”

notes.body_html: Menachos 43b: the source of the morning identity-blessings — the beraisa (R’ Meir / R’ Yehudah) that a person must bless each day “she-asani Yisrael,” and in the accepted nusach “shelo asani goy,” “shelo asani ishah,” “shelo asani bur/aved.” Background: these blessings affirm the distinctiveness of the Jew’s very being. R’ Tzadok’s use: the negative wording “who did not make me a goy” (rather than “who made me a Jew”) already hints at his point — that some Jewish souls do descend, by way of gilgul, into gentiles; hence one thanks God that he was not “made a gentile.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi §15): “to provoke the good inclination against the evil inclination, and to prevent a person from forbidden acts; and the utterance "Anochi" — which is to bring holiness into the heart — was not said in the language of command, but in the language [of statement].” Exactly the se’if: the convert’s root is kelipas nogah, which turns toward the good — and what turns it is not a command imposed from without but a holiness brought into the heart.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: שֶׁהוּא סוֹד ״נֹגַהּ לוֹ סָבִיב״
notes.body_html: Yechezkel 1:4: “וָאֵרֶא וְהִנֵּה רוּחַ סְעָרָה בָּאָה מִן הַצָּפוֹן, עָנָן גָּדוֹל וְאֵשׁ מִתְלַקַּחַת וְנֹגַהּ לוֹ סָבִיב, וּמִתּוֹכָהּ כְּעֵין הַחַשְׁמַל מִתּוֹךְ הָאֵשׁ” — “and I saw, and behold, a stormwind came from the north, a great cloud and a flashing fire, with a brightness [nogah] round about it, and from its midst like the gleam of chashmal from within the fire.” Background: the opening of Yechezkel’s Merkavah vision. Meforshim: in Kabbalah “nogah” is the intermediate kelipah — the “brightness” encircling the holiness, half-good and half-evil, able to be “turned” wholly to good. R’ Tzadok’s use: converts are rooted in kelipas nogah, the “nogah lo saviv” — the shell that surrounds the holy and can be flipped from evil to good.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 12:9: “סָבִיב רְשָׁעִים יִתְהַלָּכוּן, כְּרֻם זֻלּוּת לִבְנֵי אָדָם” — “the wicked walk round about, when vileness is exalted among men.” Background: the psalm laments an age in which the wicked hold sway. R’ Tzadok’s use: read with the nogah imagery, the wicked “walk round about” the holiness — positioned at its periphery, like the shell encircling the fruit.

notes.body_html: Eichah 1:17: “פֵּרְשָׂה צִיּוֹן בְּיָדֶיהָ אֵין מְנַחֵם לָהּ, צִוָּה ה׳ לְיַעֲקֹב סְבִיבָיו צָרָיו, הָיְתָה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם לְנִדָּה בֵּינֵיהֶם” — “Tziyon spreads out her hands, there is none to comfort her; Hashem has commanded concerning Yaakov that his foes be round about him; Yerushalayim has become a niddah among them.” Background: from the first kinah of Eichah — Yaakov hemmed in by his enemies “round about.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this too is the “surrounding” of holiness by the shell — the foes set around Yaakov, at his boundary, as kelipas nogah that encircles the holy.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּמֵהֶם הֵם הַגֵּרִים, דְּגָלוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל זֶה — לְהוֹסִיף גֵּרִים
notes.body_html: Pesachim 87b: “R’ Elazar said: The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel among the nations only in order that converts be added to them [ela kdei she-yitosfu aleihem gerim], as it says (Hoshea 2:25), ‘and I will sow her for Me in the land.’”Tanya — kelipas nogah is a mixed middle that can be clarified and raised: Tanya, Likutei Amarim ch. 7, defines kelipas nogah as an intermediate realm between the three completely impure kelipos and kedushah. It contains good mixed with evil; therefore at times it descends and is included with the impure side, and at times its good is separated and it rises into holiness. The Alter Rebbe illustrates this with ordinary permitted physical things: when used merely for bodily appetite they remain in nogah, but when directed to avodas Hashem their vitality can itself ascend. This provides a useful conceptual parallel to R’ Tzadok’s language here about converts and the extraction of holiness from a mixed exterior. The categories should not simply be equated — R’ Tzadok is discussing the origins of souls and geirus, while Tanya is explaining the spiritual status of permitted worldly vitality — but the underlying structure is similar. A mixed domain is not fixed by its present location. Its hidden good can be separated from the evil surrounding it and incorporated into kedushah. That model helps explain why R’ Tzadok can describe a soul or spark as caught in an alien environment without treating the environment itself as holy. The point of the descent is birur: once the good is truly detached from the old identification, it does not remain a sanctified fragment of the shell; it rises into a new belonging.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §13): “on the verse "and be whole" — [the parable of] the noblewoman: "there is no dross in you except the nail of the little finger; pare it a little and be whole."” The se’if’s kelipas nogah exactly: what stands between a soul and Israel is not its substance but a thin outer rim — pared away, what remains was whole all along.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §15): “for Avraham was the first of the converts — that he was born of the nations according to natural descent, and afterward recognized [his Creator] and converted; and with regard to the nations, recognition through one’s own striving is called "what a person illumines"… yet Avraham merited afterward the name "ezrachi," that he is not a convert, and they said, "Avraham is called Yisrael."” Exactly the se’if: the convert’s soul comes from “another chamber,” and its whole ascent is the passage from a self-kindled light to a native one.

notes.body_html: Megillah 3a: “Even though [a person] himself does not see, his mazal sees [iyhu lo chazi, mazalei chazi].” (One is affected even by what he does not consciously perceive — hence Bilaam’s power to sense.)

notes.body_html: Tiferes Yehonasan (Parashas Pinchas) — R’ Yonasan Eybeschutz asks why Moav sent the daughters of Midyan to entice Israel rather than their own daughters, and explains (per his approach) that Balak — a greater diviner than Bilaam — foresaw that from a union of an Israelite with a daughter of Moav would issue the one destined to “remove wickedness from the world”: namely Boaz and Ruth the Moabite, from whom came David HaMelech, who would “cast Moav to the ground.” R’ Tzadok cites this to show that even those apparent “sins” were, at root, “for the sake of Heaven” (see there at length).

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּרַק בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא וְהִיא מִזֶּרַע קֹדֶשׁ וּדְבוּקִים בִּקְדֻשָּׁה וּקְרוּאִים ״בְּנֵי אֵל חָי״, כָּל מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם הֵם פְּעוּלַת צַדִּיק לְחַיִּים וְדָבוּק בְּחִיּוּת חֵי הָעוֹלָמִים
notes.body_html: Hoshea 2:1: “וְהָיָה מִסְפַּר בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּחוֹל הַיָּם… וְהָיָה בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם, יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם בְּנֵי אֵל חָי” — “and the number of the Children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea… and it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, ‘you are not My people,’ it shall be said to them, ‘sons of the living God.’” Background: Hoshea’s word of consolation — Israel, though rebuked, will be restored and named “sons of the living God” (the Sages take this as proof that even when called “not My people” they remain His children). R’ Tzadok’s use: only among Israel — both partners “of holy seed,” called “sons of the living God” — is a marital union “the deed of a tzaddik, unto life,” bound to the vitality of the Life of the worlds.

notes.body_html: Mishlei 10:16: “פְּעֻלַּת צַדִּיק לְחַיִּים, תְּבוּאַת רָשָׁע לְחַטָּאת” — “the wage of a tzaddik is unto life; the produce of a wicked man is unto sin.” Background: Mishlei contrasts the fruits of the righteous (life) with those of the wicked (sin). R’ Tzadok’s use: he reads “peulas tzaddik l’chaim” of the marital act itself — among Israel it is “a deed of a tzaddik, unto life”; but with “the daughter of a foreign god” the same act becomes “tevu’as rasha l’chatas,” bound to the side of death.

notes.body_html: Malachi 2:11: “בָּגְדָה יְהוּדָה… כִּי חִלֵּל יְהוּדָה קֹדֶשׁ ה׳ אֲשֶׁר אָהֵב, וּבָעַל בַּת אֵל נֵכָר” — “Yehudah has dealt treacherously… for Yehudah has profaned the holiness of Hashem which He loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god.” Background: Malachi rebukes the returnees for intermarriage — “marrying the daughter of a foreign god.” Meforshim: the Sages apply “bas El neichar” to the gentile woman and to the very charge of the Zimri episode (Sanhedrin 82a). R’ Tzadok’s use: cleaving to “the daughter of a foreign god” is “from the side of death” — it brought death upon the 24,000, for the offspring “is like her” and never counts as the “seed of Israel.”

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 106a: “‘Come, I will counsel you [what this people will do to your people]’ (Bamidbar 24:14) — [Bilaam advised Balak:] the God of these [Israel] hates immorality; set out women before them in harlotry [and they will stumble].” (The “counsel of harlotry” — the daughters of Moav and Midyan.)Mei HaShiloach — a holy potential does not become permissible before its proper time, person, and place: Mei HaShiloach I, Shemini §5, formulates a principle especially important for this se’if: a person must discern “העת והנפש והמקום” so that an act is aligned with the will of Hashem, because a middah or act that is right in one setting is not thereby fit at all times. He illustrates this from Pinchas: the law of kana’in pog’in bo applied only at the exact moment of the act; had the circumstances changed, the legal and spiritual judgment would have changed with them. The Ishbitzer therefore demands not only intensity but exact timing, and the ability to leave a middah immediately when its proper moment passes. This is a powerful safeguard for R’ Tzadok’s discussion of Bilaam’s counsel. Bilaam perceived a future truth — that kedushah, Davidic kingship, and ultimately Mashiach would emerge through Moav — and weaponized that truth by forcing it into the wrong time and form, before conversion and outside the Torah’s permitted order. The later holiness of Rus does not retroactively make the earlier union permissible. It proves the opposite: a potential that belongs to Divine purpose must still arrive through the divinely appointed gate. In Ishbitz terms, knowing a hidden root is never enough; one must also know the et, nefesh, and makom. Otherwise a glimpse of future holiness becomes precisely the temptation by which a person attaches himself to the side of death.

notes.body_html: Zohar, Yisro 68a: R’ Abba said: it is not written of Yisro “priest of On” but “priest of Midyan” — it is all one; at first he was called “priest of On” [Yosef’s father-in-law], and afterward “priest of Midyan” — and “priest of Midyan” hints at the secret of “the woman of strife [eishes medanim].” Likkutei Torah (of the Arizal), beginning of Parashas Yisro: Know that there is in the Sitra Achra a “priest of Midyan,” corresponding to Yesod Abba of holiness; for there in holiness it is love, but in the kelipah it is enmity and strife — and no light was granted to unite them, and they remained in separation — this is “the workers of iniquity shall be scattered”; whereas above, in the secret of Abba and Imma, “they never part.” [Yesod Abba is the root of undivided love; its counterfeit in the kelipah is “the woman of strife,” whose “workers of iniquity are scattered.”]

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 105a: in Perek Chelek, the “expounders of impressions” (dorshei reshumos) taught that all of the seed of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov have a share in the World to Come — Bilaam alone excepted (cf. the Mishnah’s list of exceptions, Sanhedrin 90a). R’ Tzadok’s use: “reshumos” (impressions) denotes the rung of Chochmah, above Binah — the “World to Come”; the supernal Chochmah of the mind is not itself “felt,” only its “impression” is felt in the heart. From the side of that Chochmah there is no “dross” in Yaakov’s seed at all — the discerning one perceives that, however their deeds appear on the surface, the depths of their hearts cleave wholly to God.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Bamidbar §2): “the number of the hosts of the Torah and the hosts of the Mishkan — the union of the Holy One and His Shechinah; and it is brought in the Zohar, the secret of the unification is like the encircling of the altar.” The se’if’s “two companions that never part” in its structural form: the counting itself is an act of binding, so that what is numbered is held in a single, unbreakable union.Sefas Emes — Yosef’s own tikkun transformed the way he saw the other shevatim: Sefas Emes, Vayeishev 7:6, gives a striking reading of “vayavei Yosef es dibasam ra’ah.” A tzaddik’s task, he writes, is to raise the good deeds of Israel before the Creator. Yosef had not yet reached his full perfection; before his descent and his nisayon he could still bring their negative report. After the ordeal, when he became ‘Yosef HaTzaddik,’ he raised only their good, and then the brothers could once again be together with their father. This complements R’ Tzadok’s distinction between Yosef’s initial surface judgment and the deeper truth of the tribes. Yosef’s mistake was not that standards of bris and holiness are unreal. His own later life proves how absolute those standards are. Rather, his perfection required learning how to see the covenantal good beneath another Jew’s confusing outward state without abolishing judgment of the act. The mature tzaddik becomes an advocate who uncovers the point fit to be elevated. That is closely related to R’ Tzadok’s Yesod Abba: a deeper daas in which the shevatim’s various paths no longer appear as mutually excluding identities. The higher union is not blindness to sin; it is sight deep enough to distinguish the sin from the indestructible root of the sinner.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §12): “The elevation of the yesod of the male to Yesod Abba comes afterward, on Sukkos — the culmination of Rosh Hashanah — for from the intensity of fear comes the intensity of the joy of ‘the season of our rejoicing,’ whence they draw ru’ach ha-kodesh at the Simchas Beis HaSho’evah: a spirit from the supernal holiness, which is Chochmah Ila’ah [the supernal Wisdom].” (This locates the se’if’s Yesod Abba: it is drawn from Chochmah Ila’ah — the “opening of the gate of Chochmah” that stands above teshuvah — which is why it effects the total, unbreakable union that Yesod Ze’er [deed] cannot.)

notes.body_html: Mishlei 10:25: “כַּעֲבוֹר סוּפָה וְאֵין רָשָׁע, וְצַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם” — “when the storm passes, the wicked is no more, but a tzaddik is the foundation of the world.” Background: Mishlei contrasts the fleeting wicked with the enduring righteous. Meforshim: the Sages (Yoma 38b) take “tzaddik yesod olam” to mean that the world stands upon the righteous — even one tzaddik sustains it. R’ Tzadok’s use: the sefirah of Yesod is this very “foundation” — the bond joining Israel to their Father in Heaven, “upon which the whole edifice of creation stands,” just as Noach (“ish tzaddik”) remained to re-found the world after the Flood.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §209): “They instituted [before the Amidah] ‘A-D-N-Y, open my lips’ (Tehillim 51:17) — for the Name A-D-N-Y denotes His Shechinah that is within the hearts of the Children of Israel; and we ask that She open the mouth — not that the mouth speak of itself, but only what the heart opens within it. And the Holy One is ‘the heart of Israel,’ as it says, ‘the Rock of my heart’ (Tehillim 73:26).” (This grounds the se’if’s reading of A-D-N-Y as Malchus / Knesses Yisrael: the Name is the Shechinah indwelling Israel’s hearts, and its constriction in exile is the din the se’if traces.)

notes.body_html: Tehillim 84:12: “כִּי שֶׁמֶשׁ וּמָגֵן ה׳ אֱלֹהִים, חֵן וְכָבוֹד יִתֵּן ה׳, לֹא יִמְנַע טוֹב לַהֹלְכִים בְּתָמִים” — “for Hashem God is a sun and a shield; grace and glory Hashem gives; He withholds no good from those who walk in wholeness.” Background: the closing praise of the psalm — God gives light like a sun and protects like a shield, withholding no good from the upright. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “sun” is the trait of “day,” corresponding to the Name Havayah (twelve permutations); over against it, the Nukva (Knesses Yisrael) is “night” — the moon that receives the sun’s light — and therefore hers are twenty-four permutations, day and night joined.

notes.body_html: Nedarim 32a (and the tradition that Avraham “chose the exiles” for his descendants): the Gemara there treats why Avraham’s children were subjected to exile, and R’ Tzadok reads it as Avraham’s own choice — that he “chose the exiles.” R’ Tzadok’s use: though Avraham’s trait is Chesed, he chose exile out of longing for the perfection of the name “father” (Av) — for a father must beget, and every begetting requires the “contraction” (Din) that exile embodies; hence the month “Av” both “begets the judgments” and, as their very root, sweetens them.

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 29:11: “כִּי אָנֹכִי יָדַעְתִּי אֶת הַמַּחֲשָׁבֹת אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי חֹשֵׁב עֲלֵיכֶם נְאֻם ה׳, מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה, לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה” — “for I know the thoughts that I think toward you, says Hashem — thoughts of peace and not of evil — to give you a future and a hope.” Background: from Yirmeyah’s letter to the Babylonian exiles — the exile itself is purposed toward a good end. R’ Tzadok’s use: all Israel’s sufferings and exiles are “to give them a good end and hope,” drawn from Chochmah — the hidden chasadim joined to the letters of “din,” whose “end” turns to the wonders of the days of Mashiach.Shelah — the din of exile is rooted in rescue and a road toward life: Shelah, Aseres HaDibros, Pesachim, Matzah Ashirah 4:46, states the principle “אין רע יורד מלמעלה”: even what appears as evil can be a rescue from a harsher consequence for which the person is otherwise exposed. He cites the Midrashic teaching that Avraham chose subjection to the kingdoms for his descendants so that they be spared Gehinnom, and then links suffering itself to “דרך חיים תוכחות מוסר.” The Shelah does not call pain pleasant, nor does he deny that it must be experienced as judgment. His point is that the judgment can be ordered toward preservation and life. This fits R’ Tzadok’s insistence that the dinim of galus are born from a root of Chesed — Av, the fatherly source, ‘begetting’ contraction precisely for the sake of an achris v’tikvah. The contraction is real: exile limits, separates, and obscures. Yet if its root is chesed, then the final meaning of the contraction is not destruction but formation. A child can exist as a distinct child only because unlimited expansion makes room for boundary; similarly, Israel’s history can pass through din in order to emerge with a clarified and enduring form. The sweetness of the din is therefore not found by denying the darkness, but by returning it to the Av-source from which its good purpose descends.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 49:9: “גּוּר אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה, מִטֶּרֶף בְּנִי עָלִיתָ, כָּרַע רָבַץ כְּאַרְיֵה וּכְלָבִיא מִי יְקִימֶנּוּ” — “Yehudah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have risen; he crouches, lies down like a lion, and like a lioness — who shall rouse him?” Background: Yaakov’s blessing to Yehudah, the royal tribe, likened to a lion. R’ Tzadok’s use: the lion (aryeh) is Yehudah, the kingly “singular of the tribes”; and Dan, too, is called “aryeh” — the “tail of the lion” — everywhere joined to Yehudah, so that beginning and end meet as one.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 49:16: “דָּן יָדִין עַמּוֹ, כְּאַחַד שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל” — “Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel.” Background: Yaakov’s blessing to Dan. Meforshim: Rashi reads “k’echad” as “like the singular [k’meyuchad] of the tribes” — i.e., Dan’s judge (Shimshon) will be like David, of Yehudah. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why Dan, though the “tail” and rearmost of the camp, is bound to Yehudah the “head” — as in the Mishkan (Betzalel of Yehudah, Oholiav of Dan) — the “circle” in which beginning and end are joined as one.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [לו] וְשִׁמְשׁוֹן וּשְׁלֹמֹה שְׁנֵיהֶם נָשְׂאוּ נָשִׁים נָכְרִיּוֹת, וְעַיֵּין בָּרַמְבָּ״ם [הִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה (פי״ג יד—טז)] שֶׁגִּיְּירוּם עַיֵּין שָׁם
notes.body_html: Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Biah 13:14–16: the Rambam cautions, “Let it not enter your mind that Shimshon the savior of Israel, or Shlomo king of Israel who was called ‘beloved of Hashem,’ married gentile women in their gentile state” — rather, these women were converted (13:16: “Shlomo converted women and married them, and so too Shimshon converted and married”). Background: the Rambam (13:14–15) explains that a beis din did not accept converts throughout the days of David and Shlomo — suspecting ulterior motives — yet many converted before laymen, and the great court “neither pushed them away nor drew them close, until their end be seen.” R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because these wives were converts, Shimshon’s and Shlomo’s whole intent was to “subdue” the nations and bring them into holiness — a foretaste of the work of Mashiach, who “will come to teach Torah and mitzvos to the nations,” while Israel will need no teacher.Be’er Mayim Chaim — drawing the distant good into kedushah: Be’er Mayim Chaim, Bereishis 1:2:7, explains Chazal’s statement that Israel were exiled among the nations in order that converts be added to them as a process of birur: holy sparks situated in foreign environments are themselves in exile, and when Israel reaches those places the concealed holiness is drawn toward its own kind — ‘מצא מין את מינו וניעור.’ He reads ‘עת אשר שלט האדם באדם לרע לו’ in the familiar Lurianic sense that the apparent dominion of the other side ultimately becomes ‘to its own detriment,’ because Israel departs carrying out the vitality that had been trapped there. This supplies an illuminating conceptual background to R’ Tzadok’s reading of Shimshon and Shlomo. Their aim, as he has grounded it in the Rambam’s insistence that the women were converted, was not to blur Israel’s boundary but to draw what could genuinely enter beneath the wings of the Shechinah. The Be’er Mayim Chaim makes the direction of the movement decisive: holiness may descend into a distant place in order to extract what belongs to it, but it must return with the spark rather than become absorbed by the shell. That distinction is exactly what keeps R’ Tzadok’s account from becoming a license for assimilation. The future conquest of evil by Malchus is not a sanctification of foreignness as foreignness; it is the disclosure and ingathering of whatever can truly be converted into service of Hashem.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §20): “This is the whole matter of Shlomo HaMelech in marrying foreign women: he wished that all should recognize the power of Your kingship, as it will be in the Future. And this is the reason for his prayer — that the nations too should come to recognize the holiness of the Mikdash, that they turn to pray toward it, until, by force of that recognition, they too should have some power in prayer, that they be answered.” (Precisely the se’if’s account of Shimshon and Shlomo: the marriages to ‘foreign women’ were an effort to draw the nations under the wings of the Shechinah — the future work of Mashiach’s Malchus.)

notes.body_html: Esther 1:22: Achashverosh’s decree, sent to every province, that “…לִהְיוֹת כָּל אִישׁ שֹׂרֵר בְּבֵיתוֹ וּמְדַבֵּר כִּלְשׁוֹן עַמּוֹ” — “…that every man should rule in his own house and speak the tongue of his people.” Background: the edict issued after Vashti’s fall (the Sages, Megillah 12b, note how petty it seemed). R’ Tzadok’s use: he draws on the verse’s plain phrase — that “every man rules in his own house” — to explain that a king exercises “kingship” (the conduct of Din) only over others; within his own home he is merely a father, and there his children “cleave to the very essence of the King,” untouched by the ruling-rod of Malchus.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 107a: in the same sugya, after the episode of Bas Sheva, when David pleaded to be wholly forgiven, “the Holy One said to him: Accept sufferings upon yourself — and he accepted them upon himself” (kabel alecha yissurin — kibel alav); and Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav that “for six months David was afflicted with tzara’as, the Shechinah departed from him, and the Sanhedrin withdrew from him.” Background: the daf opens with the warning that “a person should never bring himself to a test,” for David had asked, “Examine me, O Hashem, and test me” (Tehillim 26:2), and stumbled. R’ Tzadok renders David’s acceptance in fuller aggadic dress — “why does the strap hang idle? Flog me!” — reading it as David’s willing embrace of yissurin as the very price of “life”: for as the root of Malchus — Knesses Yisrael “poor and lowly,” who owns nothing of herself — his own “side” is to receive suffering and thereby merit the World to Come.

notes.body_html: Chagigah 9b: Eliyahu said to Bar Hei Hei: what is [the meaning of] “behold, I have refined you, but not with silver; I have chosen you in the crucible of affliction” (Yeshayah 48)? It teaches that the Holy One went through all the good traits to give to Israel, and found none [as fitting] as poverty — as people say, “poverty befits Israel like a red trapping on a white horse.” Berachos 5a: It was taught, R’ Shimon ben Yochai says: three good gifts did the Holy One give Israel, and all of them He gave only through afflictions — these are: the Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 91a–b: Antoninus said to Rebbi that body and soul could each escape judgment — the body pleading, “the soul sinned, for from the day it left me I lie still as a stone,” and the soul, “the body sinned, for from the day I left it I fly in the air like a bird.” Rebbi answered with a parable: a king set two watchmen over his orchard, one lame and one blind. The lame said, “I see fine figs — carry me and we will bring them”; the lame rode upon the blind, and they brought and ate. When the owner demanded the figs, the lame said, “have I legs?” and the blind, “have I eyes?” — so he set the lame upon the blind and judged them as one. So too the Holy One brings the soul, casts it into the body, and judges them together.Mei HaShiloach — the neshamah remains pure, while bechirah operates in the embodied person: Mei HaShiloach, Anthology, Collectanea, Siddur §1, explains the daily declaration ‘נשמה שנתת בי טהורה היא’ by distinguishing nefesh, ruach, and neshamah. ‘לנשמה אין שום חטא ופגם מגיע’ — no sin or blemish reaches the neshamah itself; nefesh remains bound to the body, while ruach signifies the human power of bechirah, through which one can choose good and reject evil. This is a precise Izhbitz complement to R’ Tzadok’s use of the blind-and-lame parable. The purity of the soul does not acquit the person, because the moral subject in this world is the joined human being: the soul supplies life and vision, the body supplies the instruments of action, and ruach is the arena in which choice is exercised. Thus R’ Tzadok can simultaneously maintain that the deepest Jewish soul is intrinsically pure and that the embodied person is fully answerable for what he does. The distinction is especially important in this siman, where retrospective descriptions of an unblemished root could otherwise be misunderstood as denying responsibility. Izhbitz itself preserves both truths: the neshamah is never transformed into evil, but the person’s bechirah remains real precisely in the level through which that holy life is translated into action. Yissurin can therefore refine the embodied partnership without implying that the essential soul had ceased to be holy.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 102:1: “תְּפִלָּה לְעָנִי כִי יַעֲטֹף, וְלִפְנֵי ה׳ יִשְׁפֹּךְ שִׂיחוֹ” — “a prayer of the poor man [ani] when he faints, and pours out his plea before Hashem.” Background: the superscription of the psalm — the archetypal prayer of the “poor man.” R’ Tzadok’s use: David HaMelech, though a wealthy king, “called himself ani,” in the secret of “a prayer of the poor man” — the inner poverty of one who knows he owns nothing of his own, and therefore “pours out his plea” before God.Yismach Moshe — David’s poverty is the consciousness that everything is received: Yismach Moshe, Re’eh 16:1, asks how a person should understand giving tzedakah and answers that no one should imagine that he gives from property that is independently ‘his.’ Every human being enters the world empty-handed, and the Creator sustains all creatures through His tzedakah; the wealthy person is therefore a messenger through whom what Hashem has already designated reaches the recipient. He then explains David’s repeated self-description as ‘עני ואביון’: David could say this even as a king because he understood himself as one who only receives a greater measure of the Divine gift. This is almost a prose commentary on R’ Tzadok’s definition of oni in this se’if. The poverty that rectifies sight is not necessarily absence of possessions. It is the collapse of the illusion of autonomous ownership — the inner opposite of ‘כחי ועוצם ידי עשה לי את החיל הזה.’ A person may possess wealth, power, vision, or kingship, yet remain an ani when he sees all of it as entrusted rather than self-generated. In that state the eye no longer converts Divine gifts into grounds for self-expansion. It looks upward to the Giver. David’s poverty therefore belongs intrinsically to Malchus: the king who holds everything can still know that nothing is ‘from himself,’ and this recognition is itself the tikkun of the faculty that otherwise covets and claims.

notes.body_html: I Divrei HaYamim 22:14: “וְהִנֵּה בְעָנְיִי הֲכִינוֹתִי לְבֵית ה׳…” — “and behold, in my affliction [b’onyi] I have prepared for the House of Hashem…” — David’s words as he readied the gold, silver, and materials for the Temple that Shlomo would build. Meforshim: the commentators ask how David, of vast wealth, could speak of “my affliction,” and explain “onyi” as travail and toil, or (as here) an inner “poverty.” R’ Tzadok’s use: David “took upon himself the sufferings of the poor man,” calling even his Temple-preparations “b’onyi” — the affliction of the soul that recognizes it has nothing of its own.

notes.body_html: Avos 4:1: “Ben Zoma says: Who is rich? He who rejoices in his portion [ha-sameach b’chelko], as it says (Tehillim 128:2), ‘when you eat the labor of your hands, you are praiseworthy and it is well with you.’”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §175): “As the Sages said of David HaMelech, ‘your hands are sharp and decisive, to rule with them over His world’; and it says of him ‘admoni’ (ruddy) — like Esav — ‘but with beautiful eyes’ [yefeh einayim]: [he shed blood] only by the ruling of the Sanhedrin (Bereishis Rabbah 63); and therefore he merited kingship. And Shaul was removed because he became ‘merciful to the cruel’ — for the trait of Malchus is [that of] stern judgment.” (This is the se’if’s David: ‘ruddy’ like Esav yet ‘of beautiful eyes’ — his sight is rectified, seeing not by his own craving but by the da’as of the Sanhedrin, which is why ‘poverty’ of the eye does not apply to him.)

notes.body_html: II Shmuel 12:3: in Nathan the prophet’s parable, “וְלָרָשׁ אֵין כֹּל, כִּי אִם כִּבְשָׂה אַחַת קְטַנָּה” — “but the poor man had nothing, save one little ewe lamb.” Background: Nathan’s rebuke of David after the episode of Bas Sheva — the rich man who seizes the pauper’s single lamb. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the essence of poverty is when ‘the pauper has nothing’ and lacks everything” — real, bodily destitution, which is “a bad trait” — as opposed to Israel’s spiritual “poverty,” which lacks nothing but knows that all it has is from the King.

notes.body_html: Nedarim 66a: a man vowed against benefiting from his unattractive niece; they brought her into R’ Yishmael’s house and beautified her, and R’ Yishmael — seeing the vow thereby void — “wept and said: the daughters of Israel are comely, only that poverty disfigures them” (banos Yisrael na’os hen, ela she-ha-aniyus menavaltan). Background: the Gemara’s poignant teaching that the true beauty of Israel’s daughters is merely masked by want. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel’s poverty is no true blemish but “like a red trapping on a white horse” — a beauty; the “disfigurement” is only the outward want, while inwardly “the daughters of Israel are comely.”

notes.body_html: Bereishis 33:11, 33:9: Yaakov pressed his gift upon Esav, saying “כִּי חַנַּנִי אֱלֹהִים וְכִי יֶשׁ לִי כֹל” — “for God has favored me, and because I have everything [kol]” (33:11) — whereas Esav had said only “יֶשׁ לִי רָב,” “I have much [rav]” (33:9). Meforshim: Rashi contrasts them — Yaakov says “all my need,” the tzaddik content with his portion, while Esav’s “much” is the boast of one still lacking. R’ Tzadok’s use: “yesh li kol” is the rung of Yaakov, who lacks nothing; Esav’s “rav” betrays that he “still lacks” — “and the belly of the wicked shall want” (Mishlei 13:25) — for the righteous are satisfied with their portion, but the wicked, however rich, are “great paupers.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: אֲבָל צַדִּיקִים שְׂמֵחִים בְּחֶלְקָם וּשְׂבֵעִים וְאֵין חָסֵר לָהֶם כְּלוּם
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar §6): “there is no satiety, as it is written, "one who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver," and it is brought, "a person does not leave the world with half his desire in his hand"; but "satisfied with favor" means that Hashem bestows ratzon [contentment] within him, and through this he is [satisfied].” Exactly the se’if’s “poverty”: the lack that matters is never material, and its remedy is not acquisition but a God-given contentment — “who rejoices in his portion.”

notes.body_html: Koheles 10:7: “רָאִיתִי עֲבָדִים עַל סוּסִים, וְשָׂרִים הֹלְכִים כַּעֲבָדִים עַל הָאָרֶץ” — “I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking like servants on the ground.” Background: Koheles’ lament at an overturned order. R’ Tzadok’s use: following the Tikkunei Zohar on this verse, the “horse” is the body upon which the soul “rides”; a “white horse” is a body “clean and full of chasadim” — yet even the finest horse needs the “rod and strap,” the “red” of Din, which upon the white horse becomes a grace and a beauty.

notes.body_html: Mishlei 26:3: “שׁוֹט לַסּוּס, מֶתֶג לַחֲמוֹר, וְשֵׁבֶט לְגֵו כְּסִילִים” — “a whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.” Background: Mishlei’s image of the instruments of discipline. R’ Tzadok’s use: he distinguishes the whip — “made only to strike,” a bare blow (the “rod for the back of fools”) — from the leather strap, “which is also made for adornment”; Israel’s chastening is the beautifying red strap, not the fool’s whip.

notes.body_html: Esther 5:11: “וַיְסַפֵּר לָהֶם הָמָן אֶת כְּבוֹד עָשְׁרוֹ וְרֹב בָּנָיו…” — “and Haman recounted to them the glory of his riches and the multitude of his sons…” Background: Haman boasting to his friends and wife at the summit of his fortune — just before his fall. R’ Tzadok’s use: Haman typifies the nations’ “wealth” — the conceit that “my strength and the might of my hand made this valor,” boasting of riches as self-made — whereas in truth “all is in the hands of Heaven,” decreed before one is even formed.

notes.body_html: Mishlei 27:1: “אַל תִּתְהַלֵּל בְּיוֹם מָחָר, כִּי לֹא תֵדַע מַה יֵּלֶד יוֹם” — “do not boast about tomorrow, for you know not what a day may bring forth.” Background: Mishlei’s caution against presuming upon the future. R’ Tzadok’s use: joined to “let a person not trust in himself until the day of his death” (Avos 2:4), this seals the point — the God-fearing man lives “all the days of his life in this affliction [oni],” owning nothing and presuming nothing, “for he knows not what a day may bring forth.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [לט] וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית הַיִּסּוּרִין שֶׁזּוֹכֶה עַל יָדָם לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Noach §2): "“only you have I known [therefore I shall visit upon you]” — His beloved He exacts from little by little; and also to arouse for the future, as it says, “he who withholds [the rod hates his son], and he who loves him seeks him with chastisement.”" Exactly the se’if: sufferings are the price and preparation of Olam Haba — exacted “little by little” precisely from the beloved, which is why even the covenant of milah is a “suffering of love.”

notes.body_html: Berachos 17a: “A pearl [teaching] in the mouth of Rav: The World to Come is not like this world. In the World to Come there is no eating and no drinking, no envy and no hatred and no competition; rather, the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah [neheninnin mi-ziv ha-Shechinah].”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §7): “"Shabbos is one sixtieth of the World to Come"… and the World to Come is the absence of doing — for "today to do them" [is this world] — only that the righteous… derive pleasure from the radiance of the Shechinah.” Exactly the se’if: the reward is not a further act but the cessation of acting — a state in which the soul only receives, and therefore nothing can part it from the light.

notes.body_html: Devarim 17:20: among the laws of the king — “לְבִלְתִּי רוּם לְבָבוֹ מֵאֶחָיו, וּלְבִלְתִּי סוּר מִן הַמִּצְוָה יָמִין וּשְׂמֹאול” — “that his heart not be raised above his brothers, and that he not turn aside from the commandment, right or left.” Background: the Torah’s charge to the king, who writes and carries a Sefer Torah “to learn to fear Hashem” and remain humble despite his power. Meforshim: the Sifrei and Rashi stress that even a king may not lord himself over “his brothers.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is “the essence of the kingship of Israel” and “the perfection of the king” — the mitzvah unique to a king is precisely the guard against “raising of the heart”; hence David, root of Malchus, is the dalet of lowliness, who “recognizes his lowliness and lack.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: רַק הָ״ו״ בָּאֶמְצַע אוֹת אֱמֶת מַבְרִיחַ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה — דַּרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב ע״ה
notes.body_html: Shemos 26:28: of the Mishkan’s wall-boards — “וְהַבְּרִיחַ הַתִּיכֹן בְּתוֹךְ הַקְּרָשִׁים, מַבְרִחַ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה” — “and the middle bar, within the boards, shall reach from end to end.” Background: the central crossbar running the full length of the Mishkan’s wall, binding all the boards together (per the Midrash, miraculously bending around all three sides). Meforshim: in Kabbalah this “middle bar” that “reaches from end to end” is Tiferes — the trait of Yaakov, “truth,” which mediates and joins the extremes. R’ Tzadok’s use: the vav in the middle of “David” is this “letter of truth” that “reaches from end to end” — the rung of Yaakov, “whose form is engraved on the Throne of Glory,” through whom the trait of Malchus is drawn only by cleaving to the very essence of the King.Sod Yesharim — the two dalets of David enclose the vav of connection: Sod Yesharim, Hoshana Rabbah 13:2, gives an unusually direct parallel to R’ Tzadok’s letter-symbolism. The name דוד, he writes, begins with a dalet because David knew ‘דלית ליה מגרמיה כלום’ — he possessed nothing from himself. The vav signifies the explicit connection Hashem then illuminates to the one who recognizes that dependence; precisely because David knows he has no independent power, Hashem shows him the bond through which all blessing reaches him. Yet after all his victories and revelations David still says ‘כי עני ואביון אנכי’ and ‘ה׳ לא גבה לבי ולא רמו עיני’; this continued self-nullification is the second dalet. The Sod Yesharim thus sharpens R’ Tzadok’s point that the vav of emes stands between two dalets. The first lowliness is not merely the condition before receiving Divine abundance, to be discarded once a person succeeds. The second dalet proves that even after the vav — after connection, strength, kingship, and salvation — the recipient has not converted the gift into self-possession. That is why Davidic Malchus can receive endlessly without becoming a rival sovereignty. Its greatness is real, but its truth is the knowledge that every greatness flowing through it remains the King’s. The structure of the name itself becomes a discipline of teshuvah: lack, connection, and then renewed lack even after illumination.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim §4): “and among the tribes too we find [Shemos Rabbah 40], "you have none greater than the tribe of Yehudah, and none lower than [the tribe of] Dan."” Exactly the se’if: Dan is the collective’s “tail” — the extreme opposite pole to Yehudah, which is why kingship belongs to the one and judgeship alone to the other.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְנוֹדָע דְּכַעַס הָאֲרִי מְעוֹרָב בְּרַחְמָנוּת גַּם כֵּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ הַטִּבְעִיִּים, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן חֲמַת ״זוֹחֲלֵי עָפָר״ וּנְחָשִׁים, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נָאֶה לוֹ הַמְּלוּכָה
notes.body_html: Devarim 32:24: in Ha’azinu — “וְשֶׁן בְּהֵמֹת אֲשַׁלַּח בָּם, עִם חֲמַת זֹחֲלֵי עָפָר” — “and the teeth of beasts I will send against them, with the venom of crawlers of the dust.” Background: among the punishments Moshe foretells — the “crawlers of the dust” are serpents. R’ Tzadok’s use: he contrasts the “wrath of the lion,” which “the naturalists said” is mingled with mercy (and so befits kingship), with the pure venom of the serpent, the “crawler of the dust” — and since Dan is likened in Yaakov’s blessing to a serpent, “kingship does not befit him,” only judgeship.

Exactly the se’if: Dan is the root of Din, and his is the “judging” power that must estimate what cannot be read off the words — the serpent’s discernment, which is not the open authority of kingship.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסִפְרֵי] עַל פָּסוּק ״פֶּן יֵשׁ בָּכֶם מִשְׁפָּחָה אוֹ שֵׁבֶט [אֲשֶׁר לְבָבוֹ פֹנֶה]״ — זֶה שֵׁבֶט דָּן
notes.body_html: Sifrei, on Devarim 29:17: the Torah warns, “פֶּן יֵשׁ בָּכֶם… מִשְׁפָּחָה אוֹ שֵׁבֶט אֲשֶׁר לְבָבוֹ פֹנֶה הַיּוֹם מֵעִם ה׳” — “lest there be among you… a family or a tribe whose heart turns away this day from Hashem” — and the Sifrei comments, “this is the tribe of Dan.” Background: the Danite associations with idolatry — the graven image of Michah (whose Levite served within Dan’s domain) and, later, one of Yerovam’s golden calves set in Dan. R’ Tzadok’s use: Dan, as the “root of Din,” is likewise the “root of the existence of idolatry in Israel” — for “from anger one comes to coarseness,” and the two are “branches of the drive for idolatry.”Tanya — anger becomes a form of avodah zarah when it attributes independent power to the event: Tanya, Iggeres HaKodesh §25, returns explicitly to Chazal’s statement that anger is ‘as though one worshipped idolatry.’ The Alter Rebbe explains that in ordinary worldly matters the root error of anger is failure to recognize that ‘הכל בידי שמים חוץ מיראת שמים’: the circumstance that provoked the person did not acquire an independent sovereignty outside Divine providence. He carefully limits this principle, noting that in matters of Heaven one may indeed protest wrongdoing in order to separate someone from an issur, as Moshe himself became angry. This distinction complements R’ Tzadok’s movement from Dan’s Din to anger, coarseness, and avodah zarah. Anger becomes spiritually related to idolatry when it experiences the offending person or event as an autonomous force that has displaced Hashem from the field. The issue is not that all forcefulness is forbidden; Din itself is holy, and zeal for Torah can be required. The corruption begins when gevurah ceases to be an instrument of yiras Shamayim and becomes the assertion of a separate center of power. This also explains why R’ Tzadok can trace idolatry to a distortion of Din rather than to an intellectual doctrine alone: the emotional act of rage can already enact the same metaphysical falsehood — treating a created force as though it stood on its own.

notes.body_html: Shemos 24:10: at the vision of the elders at Sinai — “וַיִּרְאוּ אֵת אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְתַחַת רַגְלָיו כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר, וּכְעֶצֶם הַשָּׁמַיִם לָטֹהַר” — “and they saw the God of Israel, and beneath His feet was like the work of a sapphire brick [livnas ha-sapir], and like the very heavens in purity.” Meforshim: Rashi (from the Midrash) explains that this “brick” recalled the bricks of Israel’s Egyptian bondage — set before Him throughout the enslavement as a remembrance of their affliction. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “brick,” “beneath His feet,” is “below the entire stature” — the lowest, most material rung (Michah, “pressed into the building”); yet “in the secret of an encompassing light” it is refined until it becomes “sapphirine,” translucent.

notes.body_html: Yevamos 24b: “the Sages taught: we do not accept converts in the days of the Mashiach — just as they accepted no converts in the days of David or of Shlomo.” Background: formal conversion is suspended in eras where ulterior motive is suspected. R’ Tzadok’s use: yet in the Future there will be “self-attached converts [gerim gerurim],” who join of their own accord; Moshe, longing for a complete tikkun already in his own days, “accepted the converts of the erev rav” in that very spirit — reaching to rectify even them.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §44): “Moshe Rabbeinu taught Torah to Israel — and even the erev rav and the converts from the nations, once they had converted, are ‘established’ in the name of Israel. But Avraham Avinu taught the nations of the world; for of all the converts he made and ‘the souls they made [in Charan],’ none remained [reckoned] among Israel — since there was not yet a ‘name of Israel’ such that ‘a convert who converts is like a newborn child’ into Jewishness.” (This is why, as the se’if says, Moshe could take in the erev rav: through Moshe the Torah ‘establishes’ even the attached converts within Israel — the very work Moshe hoped would bring a complete tikkun in his days.)

notes.body_html: Shoftim 18:30: of Michah’s idol among the Danites — “וִיהוֹנָתָן בֶּן גֵּרְשֹׁם בֶּן מְנַשֶּׁה, הוּא וּבָנָיו הָיוּ כֹהֲנִים לְשֵׁבֶט הַדָּנִי” — “and Yehonasan son of Gershom son of Menasheh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan.” Meforshim: the nun of “Menasheh [מנשה]” is written suspended (nun teluyah), and the Sages (Bava Basra 109b) read the name as “Moshe” — Yehonasan was in truth the grandson of Moshe, the nun inserted only to shield Moshe’s honor. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is Moshe’s “connection” to Michah — since Yehonasan, of Moshe’s own seed, later served as Michah’s priest — which is why Hashem bade Moshe “bring out Michah” from the Nile mud.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל יָדוֹ נִתְבָּרֵר שֹׁרֶשׁ טָעוּתוֹ כְּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יֵיטִיב ה׳ לִי״ וְגוֹמֵר
notes.body_html: Shoftim 17:13: Michah’s words when a wandering Levite became his priest — “עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יֵיטִיב ה׳ לִי, כִּי הָיָה לִי הַלֵּוִי לְכֹהֵן” — “now I know that Hashem will do me good, for the Levite has become my priest.” Background: Michah’s private idol-shrine gains a Levite officiant. R’ Tzadok’s use: from this very verse the Sages learned that Michah “kicked at Anochi,” not at “no other gods” — for he said “Hashem [Havayah] will do me good,” a Name never applied to idolatry; he did believe in Havayah, only he “corporealized” Him upon his idol.Tanya — the basic error is imagining a created thing as possessing existence apart from the Divine power within it: Tanya, Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah ch. 2, describes the ‘root of the error’ of those who deny continuous Divine providence as the comparison of creation to a human artisan. Once a craftsman finishes a vessel, the vessel can remain after his hands leave it; but creation ex nihilo is entirely different. Were the Creator’s power to withdraw for an instant, the created being would return to absolute nothingness. Therefore ‘כח הפועל בנפעל תמיד’ — the creative force must continuously be present within the creature to sustain it. This provides a useful conceptual complement to R’ Tzadok’s diagnosis of Michah. Michah did not simply erase the Name of Hashem; he could still say ‘ייטיב ה׳ לי.’ His corruption lay in fastening Divine presence to a separate corporeal object, as though the physical form could be a self-standing bearer or localization of God. The Tanya’s account explains why such corporealization is so profound a mistake: the creature has no independent ontological platform upon which God could later ‘rest’ as an added presence. Its entire being at every moment is only the effect of the Divine word sustaining it. Thus even when the language of faith remains on the lips, treating a created thing as an autonomous locus of power already fractures yichud. R’ Tzadok’s category of Michah as gravely mistaken rather than simply atheistic becomes more intelligible against this distinction.

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 42:8: “אֲנִי ה׳ הוּא שְׁמִי, וּכְבוֹדִי לְאַחֵר לֹא אֶתֵּן, וּתְהִלָּתִי לַפְּסִילִים” — “I am Hashem, that is My Name, and My glory I will not give to another, nor My praise to idols.” Background: God declares that the honor of His Name belongs to Him alone, never to idols. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because the Name Havayah is never “given to another” — never found applied to idolatry anywhere — Michah’s applying it to his own idol was not the “invention of other gods” but the corporealizing of the true God: a “kicking at Anochi.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרָה ״דָּנַנִּי אֱלֹקִים״, רְצֹה לוֹמַר עַל שֶׁמַּגַּע הַהוֹלָדָה מִמֶּנָּה הִצְדִּיקָה הַדִּין, וְגַם ״שָׁמַע בְּקוֹלִי״ לְהִבָּנוֹת מִשִּׁפְחָתָהּ
notes.body_html: Bereishis 30:6: at the birth of Bilhah’s first son — “וַתֹּאמֶר רָחֵל, דָּנַנִּי אֱלֹהִים וְגַם שָׁמַע בְּקֹלִי וַיִּתֶּן לִי בֵּן, עַל כֵּן קָרְאָה שְׁמוֹ דָּן” — “and Rachel said: God has judged me [danani], and He has also heard my voice and given me a son; therefore she called his name Dan.” Meforshim: Rashi — “He judged me [and] found me innocent,” acquitting her. R’ Tzadok’s use: Rachel named him for “the trait of Din in her” — sensing at his birth (as the Imahos could) the “drive for idolatry and anger” whose beginning lay in her own line (Yosef’s), and thereby “justifying the judgment” that had kept her barren; yet “He heard my voice,” for through this very child the power of that drive was weakened.Be’er Mayim Chaim — ‘Dan’ itself is remembered by Chazal as a point where avodah zarah obstructs holy advance: Be’er Mayim Chaim, Bereishis 12:8:6, comments on Chazal’s reading of ‘וירדוף עד דן’ — Avraham’s pursuit stopped at Dan because he prophetically saw the idolatry that would one day stand there. The Be’er Mayim Chaim stresses the strange spiritual force of that sin: avodah zarah ‘strikes before and behind,’ and Avraham therefore built an altar and sought to interpose holiness against the future blemish. This does not supply R’ Tzadok’s specific genealogy from Rachel through Bilhah, but it gives a striking Chassidic echo to the very association on which he builds: the name and place of Dan stand in Chazal as a frontier at which the power of avodah zarah becomes capable of arresting even Avraham’s forward movement. R’ Tzadok’s contribution is to locate that danger within the inner structure of the shevatim and to explain why it appears specifically at the ‘lowest’ end of Rachel’s extension. The Be’er Mayim Chaim helps frame the severity of the point without making Dan himself synonymous with evil. Avraham’s response is to build a mizbe’ach — to establish an opposing orientation toward Hashem. So too in R’ Tzadok, the very force that can descend into Din and anger is not discarded; it must be weakened, redirected, and ultimately restored to the service of the one God.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 30:3: Rachel, still barren, gave her handmaid Bilhah to Yaakov — “הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה בֹּא אֵלֶיהָ… וְאִבָּנֶה גַם אָנֹכִי מִמֶּנָּה” — “behold my handmaid Bilhah, come to her… and I too shall be built up through her.” Background: as Sarah had done with Hagar, Rachel seeks to be “built up” through her maidservant’s children. R’ Tzadok’s use: Bilhah’s sons are “the beginning of the emergence of Rachel’s seed” — Rachel “wishing to be built up” through her handmaid while Din still decreed that she herself not yet bear; and indeed “He heard her voice,” for the harsh drive was thereby drawn off and weakened.

notes.body_html: Be’er Moshe (R’ Moshe Yechiel Epstein of Ozherov), Neviim — Shoftim, p. 246: וכן אמרו (סנהדרין קג, ב): מפני מה לא מנו את מיכה [בין] אלה שאין להם חלק לעולם הבא? מפני שפיתו מצויה לעוברי דרכים… כל העולם מתארחין אצלו The Be’er Moshe brings the Gemara’s own astonishing verdict on Michah: the man whose idol stood in Israel was nevertheless not counted among those with no share in the World to Come — because his bread was available to wayfarers. This bears directly on the se’if’s reading of Michah as “mistaken” rather than wicked: the Jewish root held, and it is the hospitality issuing from that root, not the idol, that fixed his standing.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נִקְרָא אֱלֹקֵי הָאָרֶץ, וְכֵן הַתּוֹרָה עִיקָּרָהּ בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבָּ״ן
notes.body_html: Ramban, Vayikra 18:25 (on “וַתָּקִא הָאָרֶץ אֶת יֹשְׁבֶיהָ,” “and the Land vomited out its inhabitants”): the Ramban expounds his celebrated principle that “the essence of all the commandments is for those who dwell in the Land of Hashem” — the mitzvos kept in exile being but a “sign” lest they be forgotten against the return. Background: the verse warns that the Land itself expels those who defile it. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “the inheritance of the Land is a bequest from the Avos,” the Land “spewed out all the nations and accepted only” Israel, who bear “the root of the holiness of their fathers”; hence Dan’s late inheritance signals that the root of his holiness (and its shadow-deficiency) surfaced only later.Sefas Emes — return is possible because the sin is accidental to the inherited root of Israel: Sefas Emes, Nitzavim 5:2, reads ‘אתם נצבים היום כולכם’ as describing an eternal standing of Klal Yisrael before Hashem. The work of each individual is to nullify himself to that whole. Because the Torah’s statement is itself enduring — ‘שפת אמת תכון לעד’ — even the wicked can return: ‘החטא רק במקרה שנפרש מכללות ישראל ולכן יכול לחזור לשורשו, כמאמר לירושת אבותי אני חוזר.’ Sin is a contingent separation from the collective; teshuvah is a return to the inherited root of the fathers. This is an exceptionally close complement to R’ Tzadok’s language in the present se’if. The Land is not merely territory distributed by lot but ‘ירושת אבות,’ a bequest whose reception reflects the underlying covenantal root. Dan’s delayed inheritance can therefore symbolize a delayed clarification of how his particular place belongs within that inherited holiness. The Sefas Emes also guards against reading R’ Tzadok’s discussion as though a tribe’s historical failures could erase its essential share. If sin is a separation from the klal rather than a destruction of the root, the final movement must be return — to the Avos, to the klal, and to the place that expresses that root. Eretz Yisrael can ‘vomit out’ impurity precisely because its deepest relationship to Israel is prior to and more enduring than any particular failure.

notes.body_html: Shoftim 14:4: of Shimshon’s marriage to a Philistine woman — “וְאָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ לֹא יָדְעוּ כִּי מֵה׳ הִיא, כִּי תֹאֲנָה הוּא מְבַקֵּשׁ מִפְּלִשְׁתִּים” — “his father and mother did not know that it was from Hashem, for He was seeking a pretext against the Philistines.” Background: Scripture testifies that Shimshon’s seemingly wayward choice was providential. R’ Tzadok’s use: though Shimshon “chose the daughters of the uncircumcised” and seemed to have a “connection” with them, “it was from Hashem” — to the very opposite end: to take vengeance upon them and subdue them, “to the detriment of the base man” — the pattern of Malchus Tata’ah, which consumes evil from within.

notes.body_html: Shoftim 17:6; 18:1: the account of Michah’s idol, and of the Danite migration, each opens, “בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל” — “in those days there was no king in Israel” (17:6 adds: “each man did what was right in his own eyes”). Background: the refrain of Sefer Shoftim’s closing chapters, framing an age of disorder before the monarchy. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “from the side of Malchus is the perfection of Knesses Yisrael,” a “deficiency in the root of Jewishness” (Dan’s idolatry) could arise only “when there is yet no king,” while the “edifice of the stature” of Knesses Yisrael stood incomplete.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 78:67–68: “וַיִּמְאַס בְּאֹהֶל יוֹסֵף, וּבְשֵׁבֶט אֶפְרַיִם לֹא בָחָר; וַיִּבְחַר אֶת שֵׁבֶט יְהוּדָה, אֶת הַר צִיּוֹן אֲשֶׁר אָהֵב” — “He rejected the tent of Yosef, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim; but He chose the tribe of Yehudah, Mount Zion which He loves.” Background: Asaf’s psalm — the Sanctuary passed from Shiloh (in Ephraim) to Zion (in Yehudah). R’ Tzadok’s use: Michah’s idol “stood only as long as the House of God was in Shiloh,” in Ephraim, “which He did not choose” for the permanent inheritance — before “Yerushalayim, the inheritance,” was chosen and the election of Israel fully clarified.

notes.body_html: Taanis 26b (Mishnah): “When [the month of] Av enters, we diminish in joy [mishe-nichnas Av mema’atin b’simcha].”Mei HaShiloach — the last camp of Dan is bound to the first camp of Yehudah: Mei HaShiloach II, Bamidbar §2, explains the order of the degalim by focusing on the apparent inequality between Yehudah in the east and Dan, who traveled last in the north. Yet Betzalel of Yehudah and Oholiav of Dan were both filled with wisdom for the Mishkan. The lesson of ‘איש על דגלו,’ he writes, is that each person’s true honor is to stand in the place where Hashem wills his particular revelation to occur, without jealousy. He then cites the Zohar on Moshe’s blessing ‘דן גור אריה’: Dan is deliberately tied to Yehudah so that ‘the beginning and the end’ of the four camps are bound in one place — Yehudah is ‘גור אריה יהודה,’ and Dan too becomes ‘גור אריה.’ This is a direct Izhbitz parallel to R’ Tzadok’s closing movement in the se’if. Dan’s present position as the tail is not his final definition. Precisely the last camp must eventually reveal its bond with the first, and the tribe associated with Shimshon’s serpent-like Din is destined to receive the leonine title of Yehudah. The future tikkun is therefore not the abolition of Dan’s distinct place but the revelation that the lowest edge of the camp was always organically attached to Malchus. The bitterness and distance of the present are healed when the ‘end’ knows itself as part of the same one body as the ‘beginning.’

R’ Tzadok’s use: in this “circle” (igulim), where beginning and end join as one, Dan is “joined together with Yehudah” — the very theme of the fifteenth of Av, when “the tribes were permitted to intermarry,” all becoming “one people”; and then “there will no longer be ‘bitter of soul’ at all.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [מה] וּמִשֶּׁנִּכְנַס אֲדָר שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד יוֹסֵף עַל שֵׁם ״וְיִדְגּוּ לָרֹב״
notes.body_html: Bereishis 48:16: in Yaakov’s blessing of Ephraim and Menashe — “וְיִדְגּוּ לָרֹב בְּקֶרֶב הָאָרֶץ” — “and may they multiply like fish [v’yidgu] in the midst of the land.” Meforshim: Rashi — like the fish of the sea, which the waters cover so that the evil eye has no dominion over them, so may Yosef’s seed increase. R’ Tzadok’s use: the month Adar is “opposite Yosef,” “on account of ‘may they multiply like fish’”; and just as Yosef is counted as two tribes (Ephraim and Menashe), so there are two months of Adar — for in Yosef is “the root of joy in Hashem,” and therefore “when Adar enters, we increase in joy.”Zohar — Yosef and joy are linked through the return of the Shechinah to Yaakov: Zohar, Vayeishev 3:29, states the principle that the Shechinah does not rest in a place of sadness but in a place of joy. It then proves the point from Yaakov: during the years in which he mourned Yosef the Shechinah departed from him; when the good news of Yosef arrived, ‘ותחי רוח יעקב אביהם’ — his spirit revived, and the state in which revelation could rest returned. This supplies a Zoharic foundation for R’ Tzadok’s association of Yosef with the root of simchah. Yosef is not merely the object of Yaakov’s private happiness. His being alive restores ruach and Shechinah; the disclosure of Yosef is itself the transition from atzvus to a vessel for Divine presence. That connection also helps explain why R’ Tzadok places Yosef opposite Adar, the month in which joy increases. Yosef’s characteristic kedushah is separation and guardedness, but it is not a constricted holiness. When the covenant is protected, vitality can flow without fear of being swallowed by the outside. The resulting simchah is therefore not indulgence but the spaciousness of a life reconnected to its source. Adar’s joy and Yosef’s yesod meet in this point: holiness becomes so secure in its root that Divine life can expand openly rather than remain hidden behind mourning and anxiety.

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 55:8: “כִּי לֹא מַחְשְׁבוֹתַי מַחְשְׁבוֹתֵיכֶם, וְלֹא דַרְכֵיכֶם דְּרָכָי, נְאֻם ה׳” — “for My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor your ways My ways, says Hashem.” Background: God’s assurance that His designs transcend human reckoning. R’ Tzadok’s use: when the Men of the Great Assembly “wished to count Shlomo” among those without a share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 104b), they were “informed from Heaven” by this verse — for the sages judged him “according to the revealed” of this world, whereas the truth of God’s wisdom (that Shlomo’s foreign marriages were a drawing-in, not a falling-away) will be disclosed only “in the days of Mashiach and the World to Come.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְהָ״ה״ בַּסּוֹף הִיא ״ה״ אַחֲרוֹנָה שֶׁבַּשֵּׁם שֶׁרוֹמֶזֶת לְנוּקְבָא וּשְׁכִינָה
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §42): “from the tidings of Yitzchak’s birth — that the holy trait of Gevurah would come into the world — automatically, "when this one rises that one falls," for Sedom is the dross within the trait of Gevurah, and the evil in it is to be evil to people.” Exactly the se’if: where Gevurah enters, its dross is displaced — and Leah, rendering judgment upon herself, drew that harsh Din into the very name of the child.Tzidkas HaTzadik — Leah is the hidden world of teshuvah, whose beauty is not visible on the surface: R’ Tzadok himself gives an important parallel in Tzidkas HaTzadik §164. There he explains that teshuvah belongs to ‘עלמא דאתכסיא,’ a hidden world whose preciousness and beauty are not evident to ordinary human sight. Yaakov is told ‘כי שנואה לאה,’ and the world assumed ‘the older to the older,’ associating Leah outwardly with Esav; but her tears over that very prospect are, for R’ Tzadok, ‘the secret of teshuvah.’ Rachel, by contrast, is ‘יפת תואר ויפת מראה,’ the beauty of the revealed world and the visible tzaddik. Yet he continues that the principal ‘births’ — new Torah and renewed souls for the will of Hashem — issue through Leah’s rung of teshuvah. This parallel clarifies the present se’if’s difficult movement from Leah’s Din to Dinah and then to the later revelation of Leah as the root of the holy Nukva. The apparent harshness is not the last word. Leah’s identity is hidden precisely because teshuvah itself works through what first appears deficient, rejected, or painful and reveals a deeper capacity for new life. The transformation of the fetus into Dinah can therefore symbolize contraction without implying that Leah’s essence belongs to the side of corruption. Her hidden world contains the power by which Din itself becomes the womb of future correction.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Shemos §4): “"one who guards Shabbos from profaning it" and "guards his hand from doing any evil"; and they expounded in the Mechilta that he is guarded from the transgression — and it appears that this alludes in particular to this blemish, which is called "evil."” The se’if’s difficulty exactly: what is at stake in “cohabiting with a gentile” is not one prohibition among others but the blemish the Torah names simply “evil,” from which a person must be guarded, not merely warned.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ עַל ״בֶּן הַכְּנַעֲנִית״ זוֹ דִּינָה שֶׁנִּבְעֲלָה לִכְנַעֲנִי, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה גַּם הִיא ״כְּנַעֲנִית״ כְּאִלּוּ נִדְבְּקָה בּוֹ לְגַמְרֵי חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כְּמוֹהוּ
notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 80:11: “‘And they took Dinah’ — R’ Yudan said: they dragged her out [reluctant to leave]. R’ Huna said: a woman who has cohabited with an uncircumcised man finds it hard to part [from him]. R’ Huna said: [Dinah] said, ‘and I, where shall I carry my shame?’ — until Shimon swore to her that he would take her [as a wife] (and this was before the giving of the Torah). This is [the meaning of] what is written (Bereishis 46), ‘and Shaul son of the Canaanite woman’ — the son of Dinah who had cohabited with a Canaanite — And the Rabbanan say: Shimon took her and buried her in the land of Canaan.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּב״ר] דְּאֵין ״ס׳״ בְּפָרָשַׁת בְּרֵאשִׁית עַד בְּרִיאַת הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁנִּבְרָא הַשָּׂטָן עִמָּהּ
notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 17:6: the Midrash observes that no letter samech appears in the Torah from “In the beginning” until the creation of the woman — the first samech being “וַיִּסְגֹּר בָּשָׂר תַּחְתֶּנָּה” (“and He closed up the flesh in its place,” Bereishis 2:21) — and teaches: “once the woman was created, the Satan was created with her.” Background: the samech (ס), a closed, encircling letter, marks the entry of concealment and of the adversary. Meforshim: the Midrash elsewhere (Bereishis Rabbah 17:8; and the Mishnah, Shabbos 2:6) teaches that “the woman brought death to the world” through Chava; and the Sages identify this “Satan” with the yetzer hara and the Angel of Death (Bava Basra 16a) — one adversary under three names. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why “in her is the grip of the outer forces” and “her feet descend to death” — the woman is the “vessel of contraction [tzimtzum],” the power that contracts and conceals the light; the very samech/Satan born with her is the “trait of Din” that constricts the radiance of the Shechinah.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּרַק עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִזְדַּכְּכוֹת, אֲבָל מִצַּד עַצְמָן אֵין בָּהֶם הִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר מֵאִיר
notes.body_html: Berachos 17a: Rav said to R’ Chiya, “In what do women merit? — In bringing their children to learn Torah in the beis knesses, and sending their husbands to study in the beis midrash, and waiting for their husbands until they return from the beis midrash.” Background: the Gemara assumes that women, exempt from the mitzvah of Torah study, seem to lack its great merit. Meforshim: the Iyun Yaakov and Maharsha explain that they share fully in that merit by enabling it — “one who causes a mitzvah to be done is as one who does it” — so their portion equals the learner’s own. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is exactly his point — of herself the woman has “no revelation of the light of Torah,” being the “vessel of contraction”; her light shines only “through her joining to her husband and children,” through whom she is “refined.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [מז] וְהַמְּדִינִים הֵם זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה מִבְּנֵי קְטוּרָה, וְעַל כֵּן נִכְלָלִים בִּכְלַל יִשְׁמְעֵאלִים בְּסִיפּוּר מְכִירַת יוֹסֵף
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §89): “those who atone for others — their reward is measure for measure, that they merit for their own — that is, for their seed after them; and this is "and it shall be for him and for his seed."” Exactly the se’if: the line of Keturah carries off the “dross” of Avraham’s Chesed, for what a father transmits reaches his seed by measure — and the holy line is secured only through Yitzchak.Tiferes Shlomo — extracting holy sparks requires stricter fidelity to Torah, not imitation of the shell: Tiferes Shlomo, Purim §99, develops the doctrine of birur with an important warning. When the nations are subdued, he explains, the holy sparks swallowed within them emerge and can enter Israel; but precisely because those sparks had been clothed in deeply corrupt environments, the Torah warns ‘השמר לך פן תנקש אחריהם’ — do not be ensnared by imitating the nations after their defeat. He concludes that the Divine command must be followed without adding or subtracting: one must extract the holy life without importing the alien form that had surrounded it. This distinction is highly relevant to R’ Tzadok’s description of Midyan. Midyan can possess a genuine point of affinity — a residue of Avraham’s line and therefore a desire to attach to Israel — while the form in which that desire presents itself is strife and prohibited attachment. The presence of a holy root inside a mixed structure does not make the structure holy. On the contrary, it creates the need for a more exact birur. The Tiferes Shlomo therefore supplies a useful boundary for the next se’if as well: discovering future holiness within a nation, person, or desire is never a reason to imitate its present forbidden expression. The spark is to be removed from the shell and returned to Torah; otherwise the seeker of hidden holiness can become captive to the very husk he meant to refine.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chayei Sarah §6): “"and your end shall greatly increase" — this is Avraham, who took a wife and fathered with her several sons at the last.” Exactly the se’if: Keturah’s children issue from Avraham’s later period — after the circumcision, Yitzchak, and the Akeidah — and it is this that constrains the Chesed they inherit.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְזָכָה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה גַּם לְדַרְגָּא דְּיִצְחָק כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹקִים אַתָּה״, וּלְצַמְצֵם הַחֲסָדִים שֶׁלֹּא יִתְפַּשְּׁטוּ לְמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ
notes.body_html: Bereishis 22:12: at the Akeidah, the angel stays Avraham’s hand — “כִּי עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה, וְלֹא חָשַׂכְתָּ אֶת בִּנְךָ” — “for now I know that you are one who fears God, and you have not withheld your son.” Meforshim: Rashi — “now I know” means “now I have made [it] known [to all]” that you love Me; the Ramban explains that the trial brought Avraham’s latent fear “from the potential into the actual,” so that it be rewarded as a deed and not as intention alone. R’ Tzadok’s use: through the Akeidah “Avraham merited also the rung of Yitzchak” — the trait of yirah and Gevurah — learning “to contract the chasadim so they not spread to a place where they are not needed”; hence the sons of Keturah, born to him only afterward, bear a contracted desire, called “Midyan” (from din), unlike Ishmael’s unbounded lust.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §38): “for the birth of Yishmael is the clarification of the filth of the love and longing of Avraham Avinu — meaning that he is the dross of the longings and desires, as it says in the Zohar on "He shone forth from Har Paran."” Exactly the se’if: the Midianite line carries the same “dross of Chesed” as Yishmael — the residue left when Avraham’s love is clarified.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: רַק שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת מָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה אַחַר כָּךְ דְּאוֹתָם שֶׁלֹּא יָדְעוּ אִישׁ הֶחֱיוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לָהֶם וְנִדְבְּקוּ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
notes.body_html: Bamidbar 31:18: after the war against Midyan, Moshe instructs — “וְכֹל הַטַּף בַּנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר, הַחֲיוּ לָכֶם” — “but all the young women who have not known a man’s embrace, keep alive for yourselves.” Meforshim: Rashi (from the Sifrei) — the fit ones were passed before the tzitz, whose face would pale over any who had sinned, so as to discern who “had not known a man.” R’ Tzadok’s use: those Midianite women “who had not known a man” the Children of Israel “kept alive… and they cleaved to Israel” — for as Avraham’s seed they harbor “a longing to cleave to Israel”; had they not first “known” [union] through harlotry and prohibition, they could have cleaved “in a permitted manner.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּמִצַּד הֱיוֹתָם זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אַחַר שֶׁזָּכָה לְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלִיקָּרֵא ״אֶזְרָחִי״ יֵשׁ לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת וְחֵשֶׁק לִידָּבֵק בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
notes.body_html: Bava Basra 15a: among the “ten elders” by whose hand [portions of] Tehillim were composed, the Gemara identifies “Eisan ha-Ezrachi” (Tehillim 89:1) as Avraham Avinu. Meforshim: Rashi — Eisan (“mighty”) and Ezrachi denote Avraham, mighty in the fear of God; and the ezrach is the deep-rooted “native,” as in “ezrach ra’anan,” a firmly-rooted flourishing tree (Tehillim 37:35). R’ Tzadok’s use: though Avraham began as a wandering “sojourner,” he “merited the name Israel and to be called the Ezrachi [native]” — rooted and settled in holiness; and by virtue of this very rootedness his seed, even Midyan, retain “a connection and a longing to cleave to Israel.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּדְבָרִים רַבָּה] דְּזֶה בִּלְעָם שֶׁהֶחֱלִיק לָשׁוֹן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּדֵי לְטׇרְדָן מֵהָעוֹלָם
notes.body_html: Devarim Rabbah 1 (Parashas Devarim): the Midrash contrasts Moshe, who rebuked Israel out of love, with Bilaam — “the smooth-tongued [machalik lashon]” (cf. Mishlei 28:23) — who blessed them out of hatred, “in order to drive them from the world.” Meforshim: R’ Acha bar Chanina explains that God assigned the rebukes to Moshe (their lover) and the blessings to Bilaam (their hater), lest Israel protest “an enemy rebukes us” or the nations say “their friend merely flatters them” — so that both rebuke and blessing be believed; the Midrash-commentators add that Bilaam’s very flattery was the deadlier weapon, for by exalting Israel he sought to make them haughty and fall (as they did at Shittim, Bamidbar 25). R’ Tzadok’s use: this was Bilaam’s “whole counsel” — he “revealed to them their immense elevation” (that no sin will ever separate them) precisely in order to instill license “to do whatever was in their hearts, even against the Torah,” reasoning that their inmost cleaving to the living God can be undone by no deed.Mei HaShiloach — Korach’s error is the precise antinomian inference Bilaam tries to plant: Mei HaShiloach I, Korach §2, explains Korach’s claim that a garment wholly of techeiles should require no tzitzis as a spiritual argument. Techeiles signifies yirah, and Korach reasoned from the deepest truth that ‘הכל בידי שמים’ — even human desire and action ultimately have their source in Hashem. If so, he argued, how can a person truly do something against the Divine will, and why is the external discipline of tzitzis still necessary? The Ishbitzer’s answer is crucial: in this world Hashem deliberately hides that deepest mode of providence because He desires human avodah. At the level available to the person, he must live as a baal bechirah and submit himself to yirah and mitzvah; if the total Divine determination were exposed in advance, no genuine avodah would grow. This is almost the exact theological temptation R’ Tzadok attributes here to Bilaam. Bilaam tells Israel a true statement about their ultimate inseparability from Hashem and converts it into a false permission to violate the Torah now. The Mei HaShiloach shows why that move is illegitimate even within Izhbitz itself. Hidden foreknowledge may illuminate events retrospectively, after avodah and teshuvah; it cannot be used prospectively to cancel the revealed command. ‘Everything is from Hashem’ is not a substitute for tzitzis, yirah, halachah, or bechirah in the world where man is commanded to serve.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §15): “Certainly the Torah did not write a falsehood [when Bilaam] said of himself, ‘one who knows the knowledge of the Most High’ [yodea da’as elyon]; only that all his knowledge was ‘from the lips outward,’ and once he brought it out from the lips, perforce nothing remained with him, and he was driven off and went, as it says, ‘behold, I am going [to my people]’ (Bamidbar 24:14). And even though he knew, by the knowledge of the Most High, that [Hashem] loves Israel and that they endure for all eternity — with all this he did not desist from counseling schemes to make them stumble.” (Exactly the se’if’s Bilaam: ‘the smooth-tongued,’ whose ‘knowledge’ is all lip-deep flattery; he saw Israel’s imperishable elevation and used the very seeing to try to drive them from the world.)
