notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh §12): “and it counts there, regarding Achan, all the severe transgressions he transgressed against the five books of the Torah, and he was one who drew his foreskin forward… and at first glance one must understand why they attributed to him the sins that are not explicit.” The se’if’s mechanism exactly: where a man is told his elevation is unconditional, the sins that follow are the unwritten ones — precisely those no verse had to forbid him.

notes.body_html: Megillah 12a: [R’ Shimon bar Yochai’s students asked why the Jews of that generation were liable to destruction; one answer:] “because they bowed to the image [of Nevuchadnezzar]” — but they did so only outwardly [lifnim], and so [Hashem] too dealt with them only outwardly [and did not truly destroy them].

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [מט] וְעַל כֵּן ״לְעֶבֶד״ נִמְכַּר יוֹסֵף לָהֶם
notes.body_html: Tehillim 105:17: of the descent to Egypt — “שָׁלַח לִפְנֵיהֶם אִישׁ, לְעֶבֶד נִמְכַּר יוֹסֵף” — “He sent a man before them; Yosef was sold as a slave.” Meforshim: Rashi and Radak — God “sent” Yosef ahead by means of his sale, to prepare sustenance for the family’s descent; the very selling “as a slave” was the providential instrument. R’ Tzadok’s use: Yosef was sold specifically “as a slave” — “the dominion of man over man to his detriment” — for the brothers, supposing that Yaakov’s line bore “dross” as Avraham’s and Yitzchak’s had, sold him to be subdued; yet this very subjugation set the “clarification” of Israel’s holiness in motion.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְדִימּוּ עַל יוֹסֵף כִּי רָאוּהוּ חָפֵץ לִמְשׁוֹל בָּהֶם
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek, Mishlei §1): “The Name Havayah is the essential Name of Hashem, comprising all the vitality bestowed into creation — which is the ‘middle line’ [kav emtzai] of all creation. And Yosef, too, holds fast to this rung, for ‘the radiance of his countenance resembled his father’s’; and the tzaddik is the ‘guardian of the covenant,’ the rung of Yosef, in whom the [Divine] Name prevails.” (This is why the brothers’ suspicion in the se’if fell on Yosef in particular: he embodies Yaakov’s own ‘middle line’ — the tzaddik-Yesod whose face mirrors his father’s — so that in him, of all the sons, they thought to detect the ‘dross’ of that very trait.)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeishev §10): “for the covenant of the tongue and the covenant of the flesh correspond, as is known; and after he saw what came of this — that they sold him to Egypt — then he became embittered in his soul, that he had caused it by blemishing in the trait of Yesod.” Exactly the se’if: the “evil report” and the selling are one matter — the suspicion the brothers formed and Yosef’s own speech both turn on the same trait.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 84:18 (the base cites 84:17): “R’ Yehoshua ben Baisus in the name of R’ Yehuda bar Simon: it is written (Yeshayahu 63:17), ‘why do You make us stray, Hashem, from Your ways’ — when You willed, You placed in their hearts to love, and when You willed, You placed in their hearts to hate.” (So the brothers’ hatred of Yosef was, at root, directed from Above.)

notes.body_html: Bereishis 50:20: Yosef reassures his brothers after Yaakov’s death — “וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה, אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה, לְמַעַן עֲשֹׂה כַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה לְהַחֲיֹת עַם רָב” — “and you intended evil against me, but God intended it for good, to bring about, as this day, the saving of many lives.” Meforshim: the Ramban — the brothers’ deed and the Divine plan coincided, each bearing its own reckoning, so that Yosef holds them accountable while affirming the good that came of it. R’ Tzadok’s use: once Yosef was “clarified” through the trial of Potifar’s wife, it emerged that “their thoughts for evil, God intended for good” — the sale that seemed to “connect” Yaakov’s seed to the nations in truth proved their utter separateness and holiness.Beis Yaakov — ‘God intended it for good’ is a retrospective clarification, not the brothers’ prospective license: Beis Yaakov on Torah, Vayeitzei 67:3, distinguishes two modes that are indispensable for reading ‘ואתם חשבתם עלי רעה, אלהים חשבה לטובה.’ Yaakov’s own middah is ‘לפני’: he seeks to see the will of Hashem within the act before doing it and refuses to rely on a later heavenly clarification that an outwardly troubling act will somehow be repaired. David’s line can reveal an ‘אחרי’ — a later clarification in which Hashem shows how even what was not consciously ordered can be brought into good. Yosef, whose countenance resembled Yaakov’s, therefore tells his brothers ‘התחת אלהים אני’: according to Yosef’s own path, the act as it appeared at the time was not something he could have chosen on the strength of a future tikkun; only afterward did Hashem reveal how their intention and the event were woven into life-saving good. This is a precise Izhbitz complement to R’ Tzadok’s account of the sale. Providence can take a deed born from error and make it the instrument of the Egyptian descent, Yosef’s test, and Israel’s clarification. But that retrospective Divine good does not collapse the distinction between good and evil at the moment of choice. The brothers remain accountable for what they thought, while Hashem remains sovereign over what their deed ultimately became.

notes.body_html: Berachos 9b: on “and Hashem gave the people favor in the eyes of Egypt” (Shemos 12:36), the Gemara teaches that at the Exodus Israel so emptied Egypt of its wealth that “they made it like a depth in which there are no fish [ki-metzulah she-ein bah dagim].” Meforshim: Rashi — they drained Egypt of its treasures so completely that nothing of worth remained, like a deep that has been fished out. R’ Tzadok’s use: this was the culmination of the “clarification” — after Israel were “fenced-in from immorality” through the years of servitude, they “extracted” the last vitality from Egypt, “the nakedness of the land,” leaving the husk empty, “a depth without fish,” and thereby “merited redemption.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל כֵּן מִיתַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הָיְתָה תְּלוּיָה בְּנִקְמַת הַמִּדְיָנִים, כִּי הוּא בְּסוֹד הַדַּעַת הַמְחַבֵּר חָכְמָה וּבִינָה כַּנּוֹדָע
notes.body_html: Bamidbar 31:2: God commands Moshe — “נְקֹם נִקְמַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֵת הַמִּדְיָנִים, אַחַר תֵּאָסֵף אֶל עַמֶּיךָ” — “avenge the vengeance of the Children of Israel against the Midianites; afterward you shall be gathered to your people.” Meforshim: Rashi — although Moshe heard that his death was “bound up” with this act, he carried it out “with joy, without delay”; and it was Midyan, not Moav, that was punished, for they “stirred the strife” through their daughters. R’ Tzadok’s use: Moshe’s death hinged upon avenging Midyan because he is “in the secret of Daas,” which joins Chochmah and Binah — and Midyan, the “woman of strife,” assails precisely that inner union (Yesod Abba); hence the “beginning of the base man’s dominion” after Sinai came through “the daughters of Midyan,” the “beginning of evil.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §20): “[In Egypt they were in] complete servitude — for ‘what a slave acquires, his master acquires’ — so that all the holiness of Israel was swallowed up within them; as the Midrash (Shocher Tov 107) expounds on the verse ‘a nation from within a nation’ [goy mikerev goy], that they were like a fetus in its mother’s womb — and ‘a fetus is reckoned as its mother’s thigh’ — such was the [dependent] force of Israel’s holiness within them.” (Exactly the se’if’s image: in Egypt Israel had ‘no vitality of its own,’ a fetus enclosed within the mother, its holiness wholly bound up in the husk until the time to ‘come out.’)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Sivan §4): “and Avraham our father fulfilled the whole Torah before it was given.” Exactly the se’if’s Yisro: the “priest and head” who is drawn near belongs to a world in which the name of Avraham still reaches — for a rung of Torah existed and was recognizable before Sinai, outside the camp.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §69): “what does [the soul] derive pleasure from? This is the scent — and therefore it is in the nose, for there is the dwelling of the neshamah, as it says, "the breath of life in his nostrils."” Exactly the se’if: while Israel in Egypt were “a fetus with no vitality of its own,” Moshe’s vitality had to come from outside through Tzipporah — the faintest channel, like scent, which is the soul’s own nourishment.

notes.body_html: Shemos Rabbah 1:32: Yisro was a priest of idolatry who “saw there was no substance in it,” rejected it, and resolved to repent even before Moshe came. He told his townsmen, “until now I served you [as priest]; now I am old — choose another,” and handed over the idolatrous vessels. They ostracized him — that none should associate with him, work for him, or shepherd his flocks — “therefore he sent out his daughters to shepherd.” Sotah 11a: R’ Chiya bar Abba said in the name of R’ Simai: three were party to that counsel [of “let us deal wisely with them”] — Bilaam, Iyov, and Yisro. Bilaam, who advised it, was slain; Iyov, who kept silent, was sentenced to sufferings; and Yisro, who fled, merited that among his descendants were those who sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone [the Sanhedrin].

notes.body_html: Bamidbar 24:21: beholding the Keini (the descendants of Yisro), Bilaam lifts his parable — “אֵיתָן מוֹשָׁבֶךָ, וְשִׂים בַּסֶּלַע קִנֶּךָ” — “firm [eisan] is your dwelling-place, and set your nest in the rock.” Meforshim: Rashi — the “Keini” are the children of Yisro, and Bilaam marvels at their good fortune, that they came to be “set” so firmly among Israel (some seated in the Chamber of Hewn Stone); “eisan” bespeaks strength and permanence. R’ Tzadok’s use: “his dwelling is eisan” means that there was aroused in Yisro “the root fixed in him from his origin” — that he issued from “Eisan,” Avraham Avinu (Eisan ha-Ezrachi), “the father of all converts”; hence Yisro is the “head of the righteous converts.”

notes.body_html: I Shmuel 15:6: before striking Amalek, Shaul warns the Keini — “לְכוּ סֻּרוּ רְדוּ מִתּוֹךְ עֲמָלֵקִי פֶּן אֹסִפְךָ עִמּוֹ, וְאַתָּה עָשִׂיתָה חֶסֶד עִם כָּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל” — “‘Go, depart, go down from among the Amalekite, lest I sweep you away with him’ — for you did kindness with all the Children of Israel.” Meforshim: Rashi — the “Keini” here are the descendants of Yisro, who “dwelt within Amalek”; Shaul spared them for the kindness Yisro had shown Moshe. R’ Tzadok’s use: Yisro, “the first of converts,” and Amalek, “the first of the nations,” are “adjacent in their rung” — the good and evil sides of the nations set side by side; so Yisro “dwelt within Amalek,” the good side waiting to be “extracted” and brought “beneath the wings of the Shechinah.”Mei HaShiloach — converts are still received because the cosmic birur is not yet complete: Mei HaShiloach I, Berachos 27b:3, reads the dispute over whether Ma’ariv is optional or obligatory through the unfinished work of galus. He notes that when an Ammonite convert came before the sages and was ruled eligible to enter the congregation, the very ruling demonstrated that ‘עדיין לא נגמר הבירור’ — the clarification is not yet complete. In the days of Mashiach converts will no longer be accepted, whereas now they are accepted because ‘עדיין יש ניצוצות קדושה הצריכים להתלקט,’ holy sparks still remain to be gathered. This is an exact Izhbitz parallel to R’ Tzadok’s explanation of Yisro as ‘ראשית גרים’ and of exile as the setting in which the good side of the nations can be extracted and brought beneath the wings of the Shechinah. Yisro’s adjacency to Amalek is therefore not accidental symbolism. So long as the birur is unfinished, good and evil can stand in unnerving proximity; the task is to separate them without confusing them. Yisro leaves the counsel of Pharaoh, leaves Midyan’s idolatrous priesthood, and ultimately comes to Torah. The very possibility of such movement testifies that the nations are not yet a closed, final category. Galus persists while sparks remain outside; geulah corresponds to the completion of that gathering, when the lines are finally clarified and no further conversion is needed.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §48): “The Sages said (Shabbos 89b) that it is called ‘Har Sinai’ because ‘hatred [sinah] descended upon the nations of the world’ through it — by the trait of Nitzachon (contention/triumph), which is the rung of Moshe Rabbeinu, ‘whose face was like the face of the sun’ (Bava Basra 75a).” (This is the very power the se’if traces through Moshe’s Midyan exile: Sinai — the Torah that makes Israel ‘one nation’ — of itself ‘brings down hatred’ upon the nations, the force opposed to their being drawn in.)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos §6): “and at the Giving of the Torah, when their filth ceased, they merited the first affection, from "the kisses of His mouth" — in the two utterances that were in public, as it says at the end of Zevachim, that the nations too sensed something [of it].” Exactly the se’if: Sinai both made Israel “one nation” and was felt by the nations — which is precisely why it “brought hatred to the nations,” and why that power had to be absorbed.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְעוֹרֵר יִתְרוֹ וּבָא לַמִּדְבָּר, שֶׁנִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ שֹׁרֶשׁ כֹּחַ דְּמִדְיָן מִצַּד הַבְּרִיאָה, שֶׁהוּא הָרִיחוּק הַגָּמוּר לְכָל מִינֵי כֹּחוֹת דְּאוּמּוֹת שֶׁהֵם כֹּחוֹת גּוּפָנִים דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת לִקְדֻשָּׁה כְּלָל
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Shemos §1): “he mentions there the names of the tribes on account of their allusion to the redemption, which is the purpose of the exile — and all of it a preparation for the Giving of the Torah; and as in Berachos, that three gifts [come] through sufferings.” The se’if’s Midyan exile exactly: the sojourn among the nations is not an interruption of Moshe’s mission but its preparation — the exile is how the gift is acquired.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Yitro 3; Yitro 2: The Ishbitzer gives a particularly close explanation of the same 'good power' that can be extracted from Yisro's Midyanite root. On the Midrash's contrast, 'strike the scoffer' - Amalek, but 'the simple one will become wise' - Yisro, he explains that both traits begin as deficiencies: the leitz mocks every truth, whereas the peti is open to every influence. Yet the latter defect can itself be redirected, because one who is open can eventually receive the truth and repair the root of his deficiency. Yisro therefore moves from having experimented with avodah zarah to 'atah yadati ki gadol Hashem' and conversion. In a second teaching the Ishbitzer says that even Yisro's first 'hearing' was sent to him by Hashem; nevertheless, because Yisro recognized that 'la-Hashem ha'aretz u-melo'ah' and yearned to cleave to Israel, Heaven credited the hearing to him as though it had begun from his own initiative. This closely complements R' Tzadok here: the power of Midyan is not redeemed by blurring the distinction between Israel and the nations. Its good is extracted precisely when the outsider recognizes the distinction and converts the very power of separation into a movement toward joining Israel.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 37:15: of the wicked who plot against the righteous — “חַרְבָּם תָּבוֹא בְלִבָּם, וְקַשְּׁתוֹתָם תִּשָּׁבַרְנָה” — “their sword shall enter their own heart, and their bows shall be broken.” Background: David’s psalm, in which the schemes the wicked draw against the just recoil upon themselves. Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — the very weapon the wicked unsheathe to harm the righteous turns back and pierces their own heart, their bows shattered. R’ Tzadok’s use: Moshe, root of the Yesod and of Israel’s unbreakable bond to their Father, “prevailed against” the surrounding husk of Midyan — turning its own power of strife back upon it, “their sword shall enter their own heart,” so that “all their dominion is to their own detriment.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayishlach §2): “but the wisdom of Israel is Torah in its essence — which instructs and teaches his heart the way he should go,” unlike a wisdom that does not instruct or teach the heart. Exactly the se’if’s distinction: those who “separate themselves from the nations and join with Israel” receive the outward attachment, but what is at issue is whether the Torah reaches and teaches the heart.

notes.body_html: Yevamos 47b: “R’ Chelbo said: Converts are as hard for Israel as a sapachas [a skin-affliction/scab] [kashim gerim l’Yisrael k’sapachas].”Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Berakhot 27b:3; cf. Tiferet Shlomo, Purim 99: The Ishbitzer's reading of the dispute over Ma'ariv gives a conceptual background to R' Tzadok's treatment of gerim and the erev rav. He explains that before the final birur, when the world is not yet completely clarified, converts are still accepted because 'there are still holy sparks that must be gathered'; only in the Messianic future, when the clarification is complete, will converts no longer be accepted. Thus gerus itself belongs to an unfinished world in which holiness remains intermingled outside Israel and must still be drawn home. Tiferet Shlomo develops the same language of nitzotzos but adds an important caution: when holy sparks emerge from the nations, their surrounding admixture can also accompany them, and Israel must guard itself so that the alien element is not absorbed together with the holy spark. That balance fits the present se'if with unusual precision. Moshe's acceptance of the erev rav was not a mistake in recognizing that something holy sought attachment to Israel; the danger lay in the incompleteness of the birur, so that attachment to Israel could coexist with a residue that later sought the Golden Calf. R' Tzadok's 'sapachas' image therefore describes not gerus itself, God forbid, but the danger of an incompletely clarified attachment that clings externally before the inner root has been fully transformed.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְזֶה הָיָה אוֹת רִאשׁוֹן דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה בְּנִגְעֵי יָדוֹ וְשָׁבָה כִּבְשָׂרוֹ
notes.body_html: Shemos 4:6–7: Moshe’s first sign — “וַיּוֹצִאָהּ וְהִנֵּה יָדוֹ מְצֹרַעַת כַּשָּׁלֶג… הָשֵׁב יָדְךָ אֶל חֵיקֶךָ… וְהִנֵּה שָׁבָה כִּבְשָׂרוֹ” — “he brought out his hand, and behold, it was leprous as snow… [then] ‘return your hand to your bosom’… and behold, it had returned like his [own] flesh.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Sages read the leprous hand as a rebuke — Moshe was stricken with tzara’as, the affliction of the slanderer (for having “slandered” Israel by doubting their faith), and its healing bespoke forgiveness. R’ Tzadok’s use: the sign was shown “in his hand” — “that which accepts the converts,” for “acceptance is attributed to the hand”; the hand made leprous and then “returned like his flesh” taught that the converts, like a passing lesion, “harm Israel only for a moment” and leave no lasting wound — “and therefore he did not worry, and accepted them.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״הֵן לֹא יַאֲמִינוּ לִי״, שֶׁחָשַׁד חִסָּרוֹן אֱמוּנָה בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגַם הוּא בִּכְלַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
notes.body_html: Shemos 4:1 (and Shabbos 97a): Moshe demurred — “וְהֵן לֹא יַאֲמִינוּ לִי, וְלֹא יִשְׁמְעוּ בְּקֹלִי” — “but behold, they will not believe me, nor heed my voice.” Meforshim: Reish Lakish (Shabbos 97a) — “one who suspects the worthy is smitten in his body,” for God had already attested that Israel are “believers, children of believers”; Moshe, doubting their faith, was answered, “they will believe… but you, in the end, will not believe” — and forthwith his hand turned “leprous as snow.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Moshe’s very suspicion of a “lack of faith” in Israel arose “from the husk of Midyan,” from which he had not yet fully parted — the husk whose way is precisely to suspect Israel — and from this came, too, his thought that “the converts have a connection with the Children of Israel.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §10): “this world is good mixed with evil and evil with good, and there is no oneness in it — rather every thing is compounded of two opposites; and therefore [a thing] entirely turned white is pure.” Exactly the se’if’s “good spark”: in a world where nothing is unmixed, the husk exists for the sake of the good held inside it, and Yisro is the case in which that good is drawn out and absorbed.

notes.body_html: Bamidbar 10:31: Moshe urges Chovav (Yisro) to remain — “אַל נָא תַּעֲזֹב אֹתָנוּ… וְהָיִיתָ לָּנוּ לְעֵינָיִם” — “please do not leave us… and you shall be for us as eyes.” Meforshim: Rashi offers two readings — “you shall be as beloved to us as our own eyes,” and “you shall enlighten our eyes”; the Sifrei — “whatever is hidden from our eyes, you shall illumine for us.” R’ Tzadok’s use: “the Sanhedrin are called ‘the eyes of the congregation’” — those who supervise the people; from Yisro’s seed came heads of Sanhedrins seated in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and it was fitting that he “be for us as eyes,” for the convert’s sight is a light received from without.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 44:21; Tehillim 34:16: “וְאָשִׂימָה עֵינִי עָלָיו” — “that I may set my eye upon him” (Yosef, of Binyamin), and “עֵינֵי ה׳ אֶל צַדִּיקִים” — “the eyes of Hashem are toward the righteous.” Background: two of the verses in which “eye” connotes not mere sight but watchful care. Meforshim: Rashi (on Bereishis 44:21) — “I will set My eye upon him for good”; the “eye” bespeaks attentive supervision (hashgachah). R’ Tzadok’s use: “the eye everywhere indicates supervision and the setting of the heart upon a matter” — and so the Sanhedrin, the “eyes of the congregation,” are “those who supervise” every affair of Israel, as in the eglah arufah: “our hands did not shed it” — that we did not see him and let him go.

notes.body_html: Sotah 45b (Mishnah): In the declaration of the eglah arufah, the elders say: “‘our hands did not spill this blood, nor did our eyes see’ (Devarim 21:7)” — [meaning] “he did not come into our hands and we sent him off without food, and we did not see him and leave him without escort.” (The elders are “the eyes of the congregation,” answerable for what they “see.”)

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְדָבָר זֶה חִידֵּשׁ יִתְרוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״נָבֹל תִּבֹּל״ וְגוֹמֵר
notes.body_html: Shemos 18:18: Yisro’s counsel to Moshe — “נָבֹל תִּבֹּל, גַּם אַתָּה גַּם הָעָם הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר עִמָּךְ, כִּי כָבֵד מִמְּךָ הַדָּבָר” — “you will surely wear away — both you and this people that is with you — for the matter is too heavy for you.” Meforshim: Rashi — “navol tibol” means you will wither as a leaf wilts in the heat; you cannot bear it alone, so appoint judges beneath you. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the “portion Yisro added” — the appointing of judges (the Sanhedrin). Moshe, of himself, “did not wish to appoint a Sanhedrin”; he would rather “illumine every Jew’s eyes,” that each see his own faults — the light of the Future, when “no longer will each man teach his fellow.” But that inner sight is possible only for Israel; the convert must “receive from Israel,” and so this “increment” entered the Torah through Yisro.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Yitro 1; cf. Kedushat Levi, Yitro 22: On 'Moshe listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he said,' the Mei HaShiloach remarks that Yisro himself did not know the full depth of what his own counsel contained; the words were, as it were, spoken through him, while Moshe perceived their true reach. This is an especially fitting complement to R' Tzadok's 'you shall be for us as eyes.' Yisro can introduce the counsel that produces the system of judges, but its Torah-depth is grasped and established through Moshe. Kedushat Levi adds a second dimension: Torah shebe'al peh includes 'all that a seasoned student will one day innovate,' and Hashem entrusted Israel with the extraordinary power that the Torah as interpreted by the righteous sages of the generation becomes the operative halachic word. The two sources together sharpen R' Tzadok's distinction. Yisro's contribution is neither accidental nor merely administrative; it becomes a vessel for the 'eyes of the congregation.' Yet the 'eye' is not an autonomous wisdom imported from outside. The counsel is absorbed into Moshe's Torah, and from there into the Sanhedrin, whose vision is the Torah's own inner perception. This explains how the good spark of a convert can genuinely add to the revealed structure without becoming an independent source alongside Sinai.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Emor §8): “this is the trait of Keser, which is above apprehension and human intellect — and then "He made darkness His covering"; and from the beginning of the utterance "let there be light" is the first trait, called supernal Chochmah, as it says, "wrapped in light like a garment" — teaching that He wrapped Himself.” The se’if’s “conceals and hides the true light” precisely: the garment is the condition of any revelation at all, and above it the light has no garment because it has no receiver.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin, os ו–ז): on the sugya of R’ Meir (Eruvin 13a–b), R’ Tzadok writes: “This is what they said [in Bereishis Rabbah 20], that in R’ Meir’s Torah was written ‘kasnos or’ [with an alef] — for the ‘garments [kasnos]’ are the clothing that conceals the body, and ‘or’ with an alef means that even through the garment [the light] illumines and makes the body shine.” And he explains R’ Meir’s very name: he is called “Meir” [Hebrew, “illumines”] because “he illumines the eyes of the sages in the revealed halachah,” and “Nehorai” [Aramaic] for the hidden light of Torah, “which the ministering angels do not grasp” — “his name bespeaks the surpassing measure of his radiance, which is in the concealed and the deep.” (Precisely the se’if’s theme: the Torah of this world is clothed in “garments of skin,” yet the one who is himself “full of light” perceives the inner radiance even through the garment.)

notes.body_html: Bereishis 3:21; Bereishis Rabbah 20:12: after the sin, “וַיַּעַשׂ ה׳ אֱלֹהִים לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם” — “and Hashem God made for Adam and his wife garments of skin [or, with an ayin], and clothed them.” Meforshim: the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 20:12) reports that “in R’ Meir’s Torah scroll it was found written ‘kasnos or’ with an alef — garments of light,” the luminous garments Adam had worn before the sin, exchanged afterward for “garments of skin.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this world is one in which “or (skin) was substituted for or (light)”; correspondingly, the Torah of this world — “from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil” — is “clothed in garments of skin and parchment” (a scroll of ink upon hide), its inner light concealed, until the Future, when “upon the tablet of their heart I will write it.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Beha’alotcha §10): “"Woe to the people who say that the Torah comes to relate mere narratives and commonplace words"… "in this manner, the Torah has a body and [garments]."” Exactly the se’if: the Torah’s essence was written into a portion bearing a convert’s name because in this world the light must arrive clothed — the garment is not the Torah, but without it the Torah could not be given here at all.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §53): “R’ Meir was able to distinguish and separate the inner [kernel] from the husk, for he was ‘full of light’ [me’ir], as his name implies — which is why in his Torah scroll it was written ‘garments of light’ [kasnos ohr] with an aleph (Bereishis Rabbah, end of §20): that even the ‘garment of skin’ [kasnos or] was full of light. And this is like the light of a torch, which draws to itself every small light that comes near it — so [R’ Meir] could draw toward himself the inner light that was within Acher. Therefore one should contemplate teshuvah before study, for then he is called a tzaddik (Kiddushin 49b) and merits the ‘light sown [for the righteous]’ — that what he learns be sown within his heart, to sprout abundant light within him.”Further Chassidic context - Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Yitro 5; Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 29:22-24: The Ishbitzer explicitly asks why Yisro's arrival is written before Matan Torah even according to the opinion that he actually came afterward. He answers that the Torah wished to demonstrate, before describing Revelation itself, how far the power of Torah can reach: even Yisro, who had been exceedingly distant and had served every form of idolatry, could through genuine longing draw so near that the parashah of Matan Torah bears his name. He reads the name Yisro as a hint to 'chemlah gedolah vi-yeseirah' - an additional compassion by which the Divine light spreads even to the distant. This directly supports R' Tzadok's play on Yisro as 'surplus': the surplus is not extraneous matter alongside Torah, but Torah's capacity to clothe and extend its light to a place that previously stood outside. Tanya supplies the complementary side of the garment metaphor. The Alter Rebbe explains that the supernal Will clothed in the Written Torah is often sealed and hidden until Torah shebe'al peh reveals its concrete form - tefillin, Shabbos labor, and the detailed halachic structure. Thus a garment is not merely a concealment of the light; it is also what makes the hidden will usable and knowable below. R' Tzadok's formulation that gerim attain the 'garments' can therefore be read as a real mode of attachment, while still preserving his distinction between the garment and the innermost root.
notes.body_plain: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §53): “R’ Meir was able to distinguish and separate the inner [kernel] from the husk, for he was ‘full of light’ [ me’ir ], as his name implies — which is why in his Torah scroll it was written ‘garments of light’ [ kasnos ohr ] with an aleph (Bereishis Rabbah, end of §20): that even the ‘garment of skin’ [ kasnos or ] was full of light. And this is like the light of a torch, which draws to itself every small light that comes near it — so [R’ Meir] could draw toward himself the inner light that was within Acher. Therefore one should contemplate teshuvah before study, for then he is called a tzaddik (Kiddushin 49b) and merits the ‘light sown [for the righteous]’ — that what he learns be sown within his heart, to sprout abundant light within him.”Further Chassidic context - Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Yitro 5; Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 29:22-24: The Ishbitzer explicitly asks why Yisro's arrival is written before Matan Torah even according to the opinion that he actually came afterward. He answers that the Torah wished to demonstrate, before describing Revelation itself, how far the power of Torah can reach: even Yisro, who had been exceedingly distant and had served every form of idolatry, could through genuine longing draw so near that the parashah of Matan Torah bears his name. He reads the name Yisro as a hint to 'chemlah gedolah vi-yeseirah' - an additional compassion by which the Divine light spreads even to the distant. This directly supports R' Tzadok's play on Yisro as 'surplus': the surplus is not extraneous matter alongside Torah, but Torah's capacity to clothe and extend its light to a place that previously stood outside. Tanya supplies the complementary side of the garment metaphor. The Alter Rebbe explains that the supernal Will clothed in the Written Torah is often sealed and hidden until Torah shebe'al peh reveals its concrete form - tefillin, Shabbos labor, and the detailed halachic structure. Thus a garment is not merely a concealment of the light; it is also what makes the hidden will usable and knowable below. R' Tzadok's formulation that gerim attain the 'garments' can therefore be read as a real mode of attachment, while still preserving his distinction between the garment and the innermost root.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 82a–b: Rav Sheishess said: her name was not Kozbi but Shveilnai bas Tzur; why was she called Kozbi? — because she “deceived [kizvah]” through her father. The tribe of Shimon came to Zimri ben Salu, “we are judged with death-penalties and you sit silent?” He gathered 24,000 and went to Kozbi, saying, “yield to me.” She replied, “I am a king’s daughter; my father commanded me to yield only to the greatest among them.” He said, “I too am a tribal prince, and greater than [Moshe].” He seized her forelock and brought her before Moshe: “Ben Amram — is this one forbidden or permitted? and if you say forbidden — who permitted Yisro’s daughter to you?” The halachah “was hidden from him,” and all wept — “and behold they were weeping at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.” “And Pinchas saw” — Rav said: “he saw the deed and remembered the halachah,” and said, “great-uncle, did you not teach me on your descent from Sinai that ‘one who cohabits with a gentile woman — zealots may strike him’?” [Moshe] answered, “let the reader of the letter be its agent.” And Pinchas was a grandson of Yisro, for Elazar had married a daughter of “Putiel” — Yisro.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Matot 6: The Ishbitzer returns to the episode of Midyan and makes the safeguard in R' Tzadok's discussion explicit. When Moshe rebuked Pinchas and the army for keeping the Midianite women alive, the Mei HaShiloach says that Moshe showed Pinchas that he too had momentarily touched the same error as Zimri: perceiving that a soul contains a holy point and therefore concluding that it may already be brought into holiness through one's own present action. Zimri's claim, 'who permitted Yisro's daughter to you?,' was based on his conviction that Kozbi possessed a real root of holiness, just as Moshe had known that Tzipporah belonged to him. The Ishbitzer does not deny the hidden root; he says that in this world 'the Holy One did not choose this matter,' and that Moshe, in the later war, saw that the apparently salvageable Midianite women were forbidden at that moment despite an underlying connection. This is precisely the distinction needed for R' Tzadok's language of the Torah's dinim as garments. The garment of halachah is not a lower truth that may be discarded once a person senses a deeper spark. It is the authoritative disclosure of how the Divine will is to be lived now. Pinchas' greatness was that he remembered the halachah at Shittim; Moshe's rebuke later taught him that even holy perception must remain subordinate to that present halachic boundary.

notes.body_html: Devarim 25:19: the command against Amalek — “תִּמְחֶה אֶת זֵכֶר עֲמָלֵק מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמָיִם, לֹא תִּשְׁכָּח” — “you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under the heavens; do not forget.” Meforshim: because Amalek is “the root of all evil,” his very “memory” must be erased; and the Mechilta teaches that “we do not accept converts from Amalek.” R’ Tzadok’s use: since Amalek’s evil is total, “it is impossible to absorb the holy sparks within him except by compulsion and unintentionally,” never willingly — and only through a woman (“the ground of the world”), where a gentile comes upon a bas Yisrael and the child is kosher, as indeed “of the descendants of Haman, some taught Torah in Bnei Brak” (Gittin 57b).

notes.body_html: Vayikra 24:10: of the blasphemer — “וַיֵּצֵא בֶּן אִשָּׁה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית, וְהוּא בֶּן אִישׁ מִצְרִי, בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל” — “and the son of an Israelite woman went out — and he was the son of an Egyptian man — among the Children of Israel.” Meforshim: Rashi (from the Midrash) — he was the son of the Egyptian taskmaster whom Moshe had slain, born to Shelomis bas Divri of the tribe of Dan; the child of a gentile father and a Jewish mother is a kosher Jew, yet Scripture still calls him “son of an Egyptian man.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the one narrow channel by which a holy spark is reclaimed from the nations — “a gentile upon a bas Yisrael,” where “the child is kosher and is a Jew,” yet is “also called the son of the gentile”; whereas “a Jew upon a gentile woman — her child is like her.”

notes.body_html: Megillah 7b: Rava’s dictum — “חַיָּיב אִינִישׁ לְבַסּוּמֵי בְּפוּרַיָּא עַד דְּלָא יָדַע בֵּין אָרוּר הָמָן לְבָרוּךְ מָרְדֳּכַי” — “a person is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know [the difference] between ‘cursed is Haman’ and ‘blessed is Mordechai’.” Meforshim: the commentators explain that on Purim one reaches a rung “beyond knowing,” where even Haman’s [Amalek’s] evil is subsumed within the praise of God. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the sole mode in which the holy sparks may be drawn out of Amalek — “by compulsion and unintentionally,” in a state of “not knowing,” beyond the deliberate mind; Zimri’s error was to imagine that one might reclaim Midyan’s sparks willingly, in full consciousness, which is impossible.

notes.body_html: Rashi, Devarim 27:24 (citing R’ Moshe HaDarshan): “there are here eleven verses beginning with ‘arur [cursed]’ — corresponding to the eleven tribes; but for Shimon he did not write ‘arur,’ because [Moshe] did not wish to bless him before his death, when he blessed the other tribes — and so he did not wish to curse him either.” Background: the arurim of Ki Savo (Devarim 27:15–26) number eleven, Shimon alone unmentioned. Meforshim: Rashi elsewhere (Devarim 33:7) gives the reason Moshe withheld Shimon’s blessing — “he held [the deed of] Shittim against him.” R’ Tzadok’s use: each “arur” marks the root-deficiency of a tribe (as he “heard”); Shimon’s is left unwritten because his deficiency — the deed of Shittim (Zimri) — “is a matter that cannot be clothed in writing,” too concealed to appear on the revealed page.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְכֵן תּוֹרָה כָּתְבָה בּוֹ לְשׁוֹן ״וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ״, ״לְמַטֵּה אֲבוֹתָיו יִדְבָּקוּ״ וְכַדּוֹמֶה
notes.body_html: Bereishis 2:24; Bamidbar 36:7: the Torah reserves the language of “cleaving [deveikus]” for a true, bonded union — “וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ, וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד,” “and he shall cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (2:24); and “אִישׁ בְּנַחֲלַת מַטֵּה אֲבֹתָיו יִדְבְּקוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,” “each shall cleave to the inheritance of his fathers’ tribe” (36:7). R’ Tzadok’s use: union with “the daughter of a foreign god” is a “complete cleaving,” for the two “become one flesh,” a body in which both are partners — unlike idolatry, which “the Midrash likens to one who embraces a eunuch,” a barren act that begets nothing. Hence the deficiency of Shittim, were it truly as it appears, would be an unthinkable “cleaving” of Israel — who cleave to the living God — to its very opposite.Izhbitz clarification - Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Balak 9: On Zimri's challenge to Moshe, the Ishbitzer gives one of the clearest formulations of the prospective/retrospective distinction that is essential when reading this entire passage. Zimri argued that just as Moshe knew Tzipporah had a portion in the World to Come, he too saw that Kozbi had a future holy root. The Mei HaShiloach answers with 'do not boast of tomorrow, for you do not know what a day will bring': even if one perceives that in the future a matter will be clarified for good, one still does not know 'how Hashem conducts the present.' Moshe's union with Tzipporah was permitted because Hashem illuminated for him how to act in the present; Zimri had no such authorization. Only afterward can Heaven disclose that a hidden soul-root was genuinely connected. This exactly complements R' Tzadok's assertion that Shittim cannot represent the true root of Shimon. The hidden holiness explains why the fall is not the tribe's essence; it does not retroactively give a person license to enact the fall. Before and during action the Torah's revealed command and the obligation of bechirah govern absolutely. Only after the fact, and only through Divine clarification and teshuvah, may a deeper providential root be uncovered. The source therefore protects R' Tzadok's very daring language from an antinomian reading while preserving the Izhbitz claim that the outward appearance is not always the final truth.

notes.body_html: I Shmuel 16:7: as Shmuel comes to anoint David, God warns him not to judge by appearance — “כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם, וַה׳ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב,” “for man looks upon the eyes [the outward], but Hashem looks upon the heart.” Meforshim: Rashi — a person perceives only what is outwardly visible, whereas God discerns the inner intent. R’ Tzadok’s use: even though “Hashem sees the heart” and perceives the hidden, “there is still a distinction between seeing and hearing” — sight grasps the visible surface, but hearing reaches “what the heart conceals”; hence at Reuven’s birth, from the side of seeing, only “affliction” and “a lack of love” were named — not “hatred,” which belongs to the deeper realm of hearing (Shimon).

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §25): “[Man’s completion is] from Hashem, who created man as a being of deficiency requiring completion. And this is the root of Israel, who ‘count by the moon’ — for they are ‘in a state of deficiency,’ and their completion is upheld from Hashem. But the nations of the world ‘count by the sun,’ which has no deficiency; since they have nothing to complete, it seems to them that they lack nothing — until they say, ‘I will ascend above the heights of the cloud, I will liken myself to the Most High’ (Yeshayahu 14:14), to resemble the sun; and this is the whole craving of the nations.” (This is the se’if’s contrast exactly: Israel are the ‘poor’ moon, owning nothing of themselves and awaiting completion from Hashem, while the nations are the self-sufficient sun that ‘imagines it needs nothing.’)

notes.body_html: Bereishis 8:21: after the Flood, God resolves — “לֹא אֹסִף לְקַלֵּל עוֹד אֶת הָאֲדָמָה בַּעֲבוּר הָאָדָם, כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו” — “I will not again curse the ground for man’s sake, for the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” Meforshim: Rashi — “mi-ne’urav” [from his youth]: from the moment the child stirs to emerge into the world, the yetzer hara is set within him. R’ Tzadok’s use: this “evil inclination” presses upon Israel more than the nations — for the yetzer “leaves the nations and provokes Israel” (Sukkah 52a) — precisely because Israel “have no power of their own to defeat it,” and must look to God’s help alone.

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 66:2: God declares whom He regards — “וְאֶל זֶה אַבִּיט, אֶל עָנִי וּנְכֵה רוּחַ, וְחָרֵד עַל דְּבָרִי” — “but to this one I look: to the poor and broken-spirited, who trembles at My word.” Meforshim: the Radak — of all His creation, God “looks” upon the humble and lowly of spirit, not the mighty. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the gaze of Hashem’s eyes is only upon [Israel], on account of their poverty” — for they own nothing of themselves and their “eyes look only to Him,” unlike the nations, whose self-sufficiency turns their gaze away from Heaven.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְזֶהוּ הַתְחָלַת הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַבָּא בְּלֵב הָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי בַּת קוֹל הַיּוֹצֵא בְּכָל יוֹם ״שׁוּבוּ בָּנִים שׁוֹבָבִים״
notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 3:14: the call to return — “שׁוּבוּ בָנִים שׁוֹבָבִים נְאֻם ה׳, כִּי אָנֹכִי בָּעַלְתִּי בָכֶם” — “return, O wayward children, says Hashem, for I am your Master.” Background: the Sages teach that a Heavenly voice (bas kol) “issues forth each day” proclaiming, “return, O wayward children” (Chagigah 15a). R’ Tzadok’s use: this daily voice is “the beginning of the arousal that comes into the heart of man” — for God, “seeing into the depths of Israel’s heart,” recognizes their root, “that their eyes look only to Him,” and rouses them “to recognize their affliction and await His service.”Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Sod Yesharim, Hoshana Rabba 13:2; cf. Yismach Moshe, Re'eh 16:1: Sod Yesharim reads the very name David as a pattern of holy poverty: the dalet signifies 'לית ליה מגרמיה כלום' - that he has nothing of his own - while the vav signifies the explicit bond Hashem illuminates for one who recognizes that nothing is self-generated; remarkably, after all David's victories he still says, 'for I am poor and needy.' The work contrasts this with Gog, whose defining error is to seize strength as self-generated power. This is a striking parallel to R' Tzadok's description of Israel as the moon: their poverty is not spiritual weakness but the truth that all light is received. Precisely that confession can become the source of immense courage, because the person no longer relies on a finite power of his own. Yismach Moshe makes the same point in the practical realm of tzedakah. Even the wealthy giver is fundamentally poor, since no one brought anything into the world; the money destined for the poor was placed in his hands by Hashem, and he is merely the shaliach who transfers it. David could therefore call himself poor while king. Together the sources illuminate the paradox in this se'if: Israel's lack is itself their closeness. 'I am Yours' means that the absence of independent possession turns the eyes upward, making Hashem's salvation not an external rescue but the completion of the very form in which Israel was created.
notes.body_plain: Yirmeyah 3:14: the call to return — “ שׁוּבוּ בָנִים שׁוֹבָבִים נְאֻם ה׳, כִּי אָנֹכִי בָּעַלְתִּי בָכֶם ” — “ return, O wayward children, says Hashem, for I am your Master .” Background: the Sages teach that a Heavenly voice ( bas kol ) “issues forth each day” proclaiming, “return, O wayward children” (Chagigah 15a). R’ Tzadok’s use: this daily voice is “the beginning of the arousal that comes into the heart of man” — for God, “seeing into the depths of Israel’s heart,” recognizes their root, “that their eyes look only to Him,” and rouses them “to recognize their affliction and await His service.”Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Sod Yesharim, Hoshana Rabba 13:2; cf. Yismach Moshe, Re'eh 16:1: Sod Yesharim reads the very name David as a pattern of holy poverty: the dalet signifies 'לית ליה מגרמיה כלום' - that he has nothing of his own - while the vav signifies the explicit bond Hashem illuminates for one who recognizes that nothing is self-generated; remarkably, after all David's victories he still says, 'for I am poor and needy.' The work contrasts this with Gog, whose defining error is to seize strength as self-generated power. This is a striking parallel to R' Tzadok's description of Israel as the moon: their poverty is not spiritual weakness but the truth that all light is received. Precisely that confession can become the source of immense courage, because the person no longer relies on a finite power of his own. Yismach Moshe makes the same point in the practical realm of tzedakah. Even the wealthy giver is fundamentally poor, since no one brought anything into the world; the money destined for the poor was placed in his hands by Hashem, and he is merely the shaliach who transfers it. David could therefore call himself poor while king. Together the sources illuminate the paradox in this se'if: Israel's lack is itself their closeness. 'I am Yours' means that the absence of independent possession turns the eyes upward, making Hashem's salvation not an external rescue but the completion of the very form in which Israel was created.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chayei Sarah §7): “as in the Yerushalmi, "the heart and the eye are the two agents of sin" — as it is written, "give, My son, your heart to Me, and let your eyes guard My ways"; said the Holy One: if you give Me your heart and your eyes, I know that you are Mine.” Exactly the se’if: the arousal begins where Hashem looks — at the heart — and a person’s own sense of distance is measured by an organ God is not using.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Yitro 2: The Ishbitzer's explanation of 'Vayishma Yisro' closely parallels R' Tzadok's account of the first stirrings of teshuvah. He says that the initial hearing did not actually originate in Yisro; Hashem sent him that hearing. Yet because Yisro had recognition of Hashem, a powerful desire to cleave to Israel, and the awareness that 'the earth and all it contains belongs to Hashem,' Heaven rewarded him by attributing even the beginning of the hearing to Yisro himself. The source gives a concrete Izhbitz model for the two levels operating in this se'if. The awakening toward good is a gift - the yetzer tov and the bat kol that call the person home. Nevertheless, the human response is real: the person can receive the arousal, deepen it, and turn his desire toward the Source. When he does so, the Divine gift becomes, as it were, his own avodah and receives the name of his act. This also helps define the danger R' Tzadok describes when introspection deepens into the false conclusion 'I am hated.' The true heavenly arousal is the movement toward return; the despairing interpretation is an added human distortion. But because the person continues to cry out rather than sever the bond, even that darkness can become the setting in which the original Divine summons is heard more deeply.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 3:16 (and Bereishis Rabbah 20:7): to Chava, God says — “וְאֶל אִישֵׁךְ תְּשׁוּקָתֵךְ, וְהוּא יִמְשׇׁל בָּךְ” — “and your longing shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you.” Meforshim: the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah) reads “teshukasech” [your longing] as directed to her husband alone; and the Sages (Avos d’Rabbi Nasan) observe that “all a woman’s conversation” bends toward that single desire. R’ Tzadok’s use: because “a woman’s longing is only for her husband,” her voice — issuing “from the innermost depths of the heart” — arouses his love (whence the Sages derived “kol b’ishah ervah”); and just so, “Israel’s longing is only for the Holy One,” so that their crying voice “arouses His love for them,” and the love that had been hidden is at last revealed.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §19): “a cloud screen dividing — this is "a betrothed maiden cried out and there was none to save her," which is the abundance of harlotry that stops up the heart from receiving light.” Exactly the se’if: the cry that seems unheard is not unheard — what stands between is a screen, and the “hearing” of Heaven is precisely what passes through it.Izhbitz-Radzin context - Beit Yaakov on Torah, Vayetzei 63:1: Beit Yaakov identifies Rachel with alma d'isgalya and Leah with alma d'iskasya. Rachel's way is what a person can understand and choose with clarity; Leah represents help that comes 'not by one's knowledge,' in a form whose goodness is not yet visible. He therefore notes that many of Leah's children's defining episodes - Reuven and Bilhah, Yehudah and Tamar, and the path from Yehudah to Malchus Beis David - initially appeared on the surface as matters a person would not willingly choose to enter. Their greatness was disclosed only after Hashem clarified the hidden intention. This is a powerful complement to R' Tzadok's treatment of Leah's 'hatred.' The concealment is so deep that the outer form can seem to say the opposite of the inner love. Yet the point is not that every troubling appearance is secretly good, nor that one may seek such situations. Beit Yaakov stresses that a person naturally wants to walk securely in the revealed good; the hidden mode is what Hashem may send and later clarify. Thus Leah's cry, and Shimon's 'hearing,' belong to a world in which the inner relationship precedes its visible proof. The more the love is hidden, the more the surface can be misread as rejection; the avodah is to cry from within that concealment until the hidden bond becomes audible.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 1:26: at the creation of man — “נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ” — “let us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness.” Meforshim: Rashi — “b’tzalmeinu” [in Our image] means “in the mold prepared for him”; the “image” and “likeness” denote the higher, God-given faculties that set man apart. R’ Tzadok’s use: the souls of Israel are “a portion of God from above,” bearing all His powers; and “tzelem” and “demus” are “male and female” — the “giving powers and the receiving powers,” corresponding to sight (which acts) and hearing (which receives).

notes.body_html: Bereishis 1:4: the first “seeing” in the Torah, at the making of light — “וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאוֹר כִּי טוֹב, וַיַּבְדֵּל אֱלֹהִים בֵּין הָאוֹר וּבֵין הַחֹשֶׁךְ” — “and God saw the light, that it was good, and God separated between the light and the darkness.” R’ Tzadok’s use: “seeing is mentioned immediately,” at the creation of the light — “for seeing is in the light”; and sight is a “giving” power that can itself “act” (as in the “evil eye” — and, greater still, the “good eye”), yet it grasps only the revealed surface, unlike hearing, which “receives.”

notes.body_html: Bereishis 3:8; Devarim 6:4; Bereishis 3:17: the first “hearing” in the Torah is with man — “וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ אֶת קוֹל ה׳ אֱלֹהִים מִתְהַלֵּךְ בַּגָּן,” “and they heard the voice of Hashem God moving about in the garden” (3:8). Meforshim: the very purpose of hearing is that man “hear the voice of Hashem,” culminating in “שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ,” “Hear O Israel, Hashem is our God” (Devarim 6:4) — Israel the receiver of the Giver’s voice. R’ Tzadok’s use: hearing is the “receiving power”; its corruption began when “the desire ruled over” man, so that he “received the voice of his wife” — “כִּי שָׁמַעְתָּ לְקוֹל אִשְׁתֶּךָ,” “because you listened to the voice of your wife” (3:17) — reversing the order, in which he should receive from God and she from him.
notes.body_plain: Bereishis 3:8; Devarim 6:4; Bereishis 3:17: the first “hearing” in the Torah is with man — “ וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ אֶת קוֹל ה׳ אֱלֹהִים מִתְהַלֵּךְ בַּגָּן ,” “ and they heard the voice of Hashem God moving about in the garden ” (3:8). Meforshim: the very purpose of hearing is that man “hear the voice of Hashem,” culminating in “ שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ,” “ Hear O Israel, Hashem is our God ” (Devarim 6:4) — Israel the receiver of the Giver’s voice. R’ Tzadok’s use: hearing is the “receiving power”; its corruption began when “the desire ruled over” man, so that he “received the voice of his wife” — “ כִּי שָׁמַעְתָּ לְקוֹל אִשְׁתֶּךָ ,” “ because you listened to the voice of your wife ” (3:17) — reversing the order, in which he should receive from God and she from him.

notes.body_html: Berachos 12b: “Rabbah bar bar Chinnana the Elder said in the name of Rav: whoever commits a transgression and is ashamed of it — all his sins are forgiven him, as it says ‘that you may remember and be ashamed — when I have forgiven you for all that you have done, says Hashem God’ (Yechezkel 16:63).”Chassidic parallel - Sefat Emet, Nitzavim 5:2: The Sefat Emet explains 'you are standing today, all of you' as a permanent truth: the collective of Israel always stands before Hashem, and the work of each individual is to nullify himself into that klal. On this basis he writes that even the wicked can return, because the sin is only a contingent separation from the כלל ישראל and the person can return to his root, 'to the inheritance of my fathers I return.' He then reads 've-hasheivosa el levavecha ... ve-shavta' as returning the holy point that exists in every Jew into the heart and body, where the weight of materiality had covered its light. He adds that teshuvah reaches the Kisei HaKavod because the returning person rectifies not only his own crookedness but awakens a return and straightening through the higher worlds. This gives important context to R' Tzadok's 'shame and hiding.' Shame is not proof that the core has been lost. The person hides because the revealed self no longer matches the holy root, but the very pain of that mismatch testifies that the root remains. Hearing the Divine voice from concealment therefore becomes the first movement of reintegration: the sinner does not manufacture a new soul; he returns the ever-present point to the heart. That is why Chazal can speak of forgiveness through genuine shame - the shame is the soul's recognition that its current exterior is foreign to what it truly is.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 68:35: “תְּנוּ עֹז לֵאלֹהִים, עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל גַּאֲוָתוֹ, וְעֻזּוֹ בַּשְּׁחָקִים” — “give strength to God; over Israel is His majesty, and His strength is in the heavens.” Meforshim: the Midrash (and Zohar) read “tnu oz l’Elokim” as though Israel, by their deeds, “sustain their Father in Heaven” and “add strength to the Heavenly retinue [pamalya shel ma’alah]” — for when the righteous do His will, they “give strength” to the manifestation of His kingship. R’ Tzadok’s use: since God “willed” that there be created beings who receive, the very sustaining of Creation “fulfills His will,” so that, “as it were, He receives from the creatures,” having satisfaction from them — the demus below answering the tzelem above.

notes.body_html: Iyov 35:7: Elihu’s words to Iyov — “אִם צָדַקְתָּ מַה תִּתֶּן לוֹ, אוֹ מַה מִיָּדְךָ יִקָּח” — “if you are righteous, what do you give Him? Or what does He take from your hand?” Meforshim: the commentators — a person’s righteousness confers no benefit upon God, who lacks nothing; the whole gain of the mitzvah is the person’s own. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel’s “sustaining of their Father” holds true “only from the side of the Creation” — from the will God set, that there be receivers; but in absolute truth, “if you are righteous, what do you give Him?” — He needs nothing, and the notion of His “receiving from the creatures” is only “as it were.”

notes.body_html: Tehillim 40:7 (and Midrash Shocher Tov): David sings — “זֶבַח וּמִנְחָה לֹא חָפַצְתָּ, אָזְנַיִם כָּרִיתָ לִּי” — “sacrifice and offering You did not desire; ears You have dug open for me.” Meforshim: the plain sense — God “opened my ears” to hear and obey His word, for obedience is more desired than sacrifice; the Midrash (Shocher Tov) reads it of the “ears above,” that “the ears on high are opened only for the need of Israel.” R’ Tzadok’s use: the “ear” is the “vessel of receiving,” which “in truth does not apply Above at all” — yet “for the sake of Israel,” Hashem “wrote of Himself” as one who receives [their cry]; this is the trait of Malchus, which “receives from those who crown Him,” for “without them there is no place for Malchus,” and hence “her feet descend to death.”

"And scales of justice" — scales, in which, when one weighs much, he must place [a counterweight] in the second [pan].” The se’if’s “ears” precisely: the same instrument that receives can be a peles that weighs all alike, or scales in which what is received must be answered from the other side.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §29): “the kabbalists wrote that the trait of day is male and the trait of night female; and therefore in the morning [we say] "emes" and in the evening "emunah"… because she receives the light.” Exactly the se’if: the receiving-power is not a defect introduced by the sin — it is a whole side of the created order, and emunah is its proper name.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 2:1: Sod Yesharim describes Malchus as 'לית לה מגרמה כלום' - it possesses nothing of its own - and yet calls it the completion in which all the preceding sefirot are included. Its kingship appears from Israel's side when, within the darkness and concealment of this world, they freely crown Hashem instead of saying 'my power and the strength of my hand.' He then takes the thought one step further: even the human power to recognize and crown Hashem must itself be 'tithed' back to Him, for the deepest recognition is that the very capacity of bechirah and acknowledgment was illuminated by Hashem. This exactly complements R' Tzadok's paradox of the receiving-power. Malchus is not an independent recipient standing over against the Giver; its whole identity is reception, and nevertheless the created recipient contributes something genuinely desired - the freely offered coronation that can occur only in a world of concealment. Hence the language of 'receiving' Above is relational rather than a statement of Divine need. Hashem lacks nothing, yet He willed a created order in which Israel's response is meaningful. The same middah therefore has two edges: separated from its Source it becomes the fantasy of autonomous reception and 'her feet descend to death'; returned to its Source, its very emptiness becomes the vessel through which kingship is revealed.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §8): “They are not [outwardly] ‘in order,’ yet with all this they cleave to Hashem. And this is the sense of ‘In what way have You loved us,’ etc. — ‘and I loved Yaakov’ (Malachi 1:2) — without any reason at all, only that ‘this one is Mine and My portion.’” (This grounds the se’if’s reading: since ‘I loved Yaakov’ is a bond beyond all reason, the ‘hatred’ of Leah — ‘and Esav I hated’ — is only an outward appearance, belonging to the nations, never touching Israel, whom ‘Hashem heard.’)Chassidic parallel - Noam Elimelekh, Vayeshev 4:5: R' Elimelech of Lizhensk reads Leah's naming of her first four sons as four levels of the tzaddik. Reuven signifies the beloved 'son' who serves Hashem with love; Shimon is the next, more paradoxical level - a righteous person whose rebuke and truthfulness can make him hated by others, and precisely 'because he is hated' Hashem hears all his prayers, as in 'for Hashem has heard that I am hated.' Whatever one makes of that homiletic structure, its use of Shimon's name is directly relevant here: hatred is not evidence of distance from Hashem; it can coexist with, and even become the setting for, an especially intimate Divine hearing. R' Tzadok radicalizes the point by locating the hatred itself only in the outward appearance and by treating Shimon as the faculty of hearing in Knesses Yisrael. The Noam Elimelech helps show the Chassidic background of that move. 'Hearing' belongs exactly where visible approval is absent. Sight can be reassured by what appears before it; hearing must receive a voice from beyond the immediate surface. Thus Leah's 'ki senuah anochi' does not describe the ultimate relation but the condition in which the relation becomes audible. The higher the root, R' Tzadok says, the stronger the opposing shell; the parallel shows how the concealment of love can itself produce the cry and prayer by which the deeper relation is revealed.

R' Tzadok radicalizes the point by locating the hatred itself only in the outward appearance and by treating Shimon as the faculty of hearing in Knesses Yisrael. The Noam Elimelech helps show the Chassidic background of that move. 'Hearing' belongs exactly where visible approval is absent. Sight can be reassured by what appears before it; hearing must receive a voice from beyond the immediate surface. Thus Leah's 'ki senuah anochi' does not describe the ultimate relation but the condition in which the relation becomes audible. The higher the root, R' Tzadok says, the stronger the opposing shell; the parallel shows how the concealment of love can itself produce the cry and prayer by which the deeper relation is revealed.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 42:21: in Egypt, the brothers confess — “וַיֹּאמְרוּ אִישׁ אֶל אָחִיו, אֲבָל אֲשֵׁמִים אֲנַחְנוּ עַל אָחִינוּ, אֲשֶׁר רָאִינוּ צָרַת נַפְשׁוֹ בְּהִתְחַנְנוֹ אֵלֵינוּ וְלֹא שָׁמָעְנוּ” — “and they said, each man to his brother: ’indeed we are guilty concerning our brother, whose anguish we saw when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen.’” Meforshim: Rashi (on Bereishis 37:19) identifies the “each man to his brother” as Shimon and Levi — “brothers in counsel.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Shimon’s whole deficiency is captured in “and we did not listen” — that “he did not use his power of hearing in a place where it was fitting”; never that he would heed the unworthy (that was rather Yosef’s test), for a soul whose strength is the “hearing of a portion of God” cannot listen to what is against His will.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Sod Yesharim, Simchat Torah 46:1; Mei HaShiloach, V'Zot HaBerachah 14: Both Radzin texts make explicit the linkage on which this se'if is built. Mei HaShiloach reads 'Shema Hashem kol Yehudah' as containing Shimon's blessing: Reuven is the 'eyes of the Shechinah,' Shimon the 'ears of the Shechinah,' and Yehudah the heart; Shimon must therefore 'hear the voice of Yehudah,' because Shimon's portion always requires clarification. Sod Yesharim expands the idea at length. Sight, it says, takes in the visible surface, while hearing can reach much deeper. Shimon's danger was precisely that he could 'hear' an exceedingly deep and distant Divine intention whose outer garment still looked contrary to the will of Hashem. Yaakov therefore said 'in their secret, let my soul not enter,' not because the depth contained no truth, but because Yaakov sought a path that would also be beautiful and recognizable on the surface. Moshe's repair was to include Shimon within Yehudah: 'Shema Hashem kol Yehudah.' Once the deep hearing of Shimon is joined to Yehudah's revealed heart and kingship, the inner intent becomes visible also in the garment. This is an exceptionally close complement to R' Tzadok's 'we did not listen.' Shimon's tikkun is not to abandon depth for surface, but to use hearing in the correct place and allow the hidden truth to be tested and clothed through Yehudah.

notes.body_html: R’ Akiva concerning Rashbi: the received tradition that R’ Akiva said of R’ Shimon bar Yochai, “it is enough for you that I and your Creator know your power” — a testimony to Rashbi’s hidden greatness (compare Rashbi’s own words, Sukkah 45b, that he could exempt the whole world from judgment). R’ Tzadok reads it through Rashbi’s name, Shimon: since “we expound names,” and (as he received) the root of his soul was the tribe of Shimon — whose power stays concealed in this world — Rashbi’s supremacy over his colleagues is “not revealed at all in the surface of the revealed Talmud,” known only to his Creator and, by the ruach hakodesh within him, to R’ Akiva.R' Tzadok's broader Rashbi context - Peri Tzadik, Lag BaOmer 1:1: Elsewhere R' Tzadok himself places R' Shimon bar Yochai inside the transmission of Torah shebe'al peh. R' Akiva is the root of Oral Torah, and Rashbi calls his own teachings 'terumah from the terumah of R' Akiva's measures.' R' Tzadok explains that when a master is gathered from the world, his Torah becomes fixed in the hearts of his disciples; this is why Rashbi's passing can be marked as a hillula rather than only as loss. He then cites the Yerushalmi's 'it is enough that I and your Creator know your power' and interprets it literally: no person fully knew Rashbi's power except Hashem and R' Akiva, the root of Torah shebe'al peh. The passage fits this se'if's theme of concealed strength in two ways. First, Rashbi's greatness is not measured by what was publicly ranked during his lifetime; it becomes established in Israel through the inward transmission of Torah. Second, the very medium associated with him - Torah shebe'al peh and its deepest secrets - is knowledge that lives in the mouths and hearts of Israel rather than in a simple visible monument. R' Tzadok's suggestion about the stock name 'Yosef ben Shimon' should therefore be read within that larger pattern: Shimon's power can be hidden in ordinary language, names, and conventions until the inner Torah discloses why those seemingly incidental forms were chosen.

notes.body_html: Yevamos 94b: the sugya of a man told his wife had died, who then married her sister — the status of the children (mamzer / not), and R’ Akiva’s ruling that even “a brother’s wife and a wife’s sister” require a bill of divorce, since each could yet become permitted (by yibum, or after the wife’s death). Background: such fraternal and co-wife cases are, by long learning-convention, set out with the first tribal names — Reuven, Shimon, and Levi. R’ Tzadok adduces Yevamos 94b (citing it as “Reuven and Shimon and Levi”) as one more place where the Talmud’s illustrative persons are drawn from “the first of the tribes” — the very foil to the anomalous, non-Scriptural “Yosef ben Shimon” that is his subject in this se’if.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [סה] אֲבָל נוֹדַע כִּי הַבָּנִים מְבָרְרִים הָאָבוֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי כִּי בַּבָּנִים נִגְלֶה מַעֲמַקֵּי לֵב הָאָבוֹת וְהַנֶּעֱלָמוֹת שֶׁבָּהֶם
notes.body_html: From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): “the sons clarify the fathers” — that in the sons the hidden depths of the fathers’ hearts are revealed — is a foundational teaching of R’ Tzadok’s rebbe, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz, which R’ Tzadok reports here as “I heard” (see §8 above).Izhbitz-Radzin development - Beit Yaakov on Torah, Vayechi 83:1: Beit Yaakov supplies a useful framework for R' Tzadok's statement that clarification comes through an opposite. He describes the tribes as 'gevulei alachson' - diagonal boundaries whose lights are not replicas of one another. A trait that would be a major deficiency for Yosef can, in Yehudah's root, become a virtue: Yosef's holiness is built through restraint and therefore he must be one who 'passes over his measures,' whereas Yehudah's task can require a force that externally resembles the opposite. The point is not moral relativism, but that each holy root reveals a different facet of the Divine will and therefore must be clarified by what tests its particular danger. The same principle helps explain Avraham and Yitzchak in this se'if. If Avraham's Chesed were merely an unbounded temperament, it would collapse into its Yishmaelite counterfeit. The birth of Yitzchak - contraction, pachad, and finally the Akeidah - reveals that Avraham contains the opposite power and can surrender even the object of his greatest love when Hashem commands it. The 'son clarifies the father' because the later generation makes visible what had been latent in the earlier one. Beit Yaakov's tribal examples also preserve R' Tzadok's important qualification: what is a holy opposite in one root is not a license for another person to imitate its outer form. The clarification must arise from the actual Divine task of that soul, not from the appearance alone.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 21:12: when Sarah demands that Yishmael be sent away, God reassures Avraham — “כִּי בְיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע” — “for through Yitzchak shall seed be called for you.” Meforshim: Rashi — “b’Yitzchak” [through Yitzchak] “but not all of Yitzchak,” which excludes Esav; and the Sages (Nedarim 31a) expound that Yitzchak alone is “called your seed,” and not Yishmael. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the dross of Yishmael, who issued from Avraham, is not called his seed” — and this was “clarified through his begetting Yitzchak, who is called his seed,” in whom “the depths of Avraham’s heart were revealed”: that even his revealed trait of Chesed was purely for the sake of Heaven, held together with its very opposite — Yitzchak’s pachad and contraction — as at the Akeidah.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §215): R’ Tzadok teaches that the integration of love (Avraham’s Chesed) and fear (Yitzchak’s tzimtzum and pachad) is the trait of Yaakov — “the form of man upon the Merkavah, the ultimate completion.” “And Avraham was not completed except after the tenth trial, at the Akeidah, when he became included in the trait of Yitzchak (as in the Zohar I:119b), as it says, ‘now I know that you fear [God]’ (Bereishis 22:12).” On this he reads Yeshayah 29:22 — “[the house of] Yaakov, who redeemed Avraham”: “from the side of the trait of Yaakov — the integration [of the opposites], which was itself also latent within Avraham — he was saved [nitzol].” The classical ground R’ Tzadok draws upon: the Gemara (Sanhedrin 19b) expounds the verse to mean that Yaakov redeemed Avraham from the fiery furnace, and the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 63:2) that Avraham was saved in the merit of Yaakov and the tribes destined to issue from him. This is exactly §65’s teaching that “the sons clarify the fathers”: Avraham’s revealed Chesed is shown to have been wholly for Heaven only because it held its own opposite within — proven through Yitzchak’s pachad at the Akeidah, and perfected in the integrating trait of Yaakov, through whose merit the father himself was redeemed.

notes.body_html: Berachos 27b–28a: A student cited to Rabban Gamliel that in R’ Yehoshua’s view the evening prayer is optional. Rabban Gamliel had R’ Yehoshua stand and challenged him publicly, forcing him to remain standing while Rabban Gamliel sat and lectured — until the assembly cried out for the meturgeman (Chutzpis) to stop, saying, “how long will he keep tormenting R’ Yehoshua? — at Rosh Hashanah he tormented him, in the Bechoros affair of R’ Tzadok he tormented him, here too — come, let us depose him”; and they removed Rabban Gamliel from the nesius. Rosh Hashanah 25a: Rabban Gamliel had accepted witnesses on the new moon whom R’ Dosa ben Horkinas and R’ Yehoshua deemed false, and decreed that R’ Yehoshua come to him “with your staff and your money on the day that is Yom Kippur by your reckoning.” R’ Akiva and R’ Dosa persuaded R’ Yehoshua that Rabban Gamliel’s court is authoritative; he came, and Rabban Gamliel rose, kissed him on the head, and said, “come in peace, my master and my student — my master in wisdom, and my student in that you accepted my words.”

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 43b: the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 6:2) teaches that when the condemned man is “about ten cubits from the place of stoning, they say to him: Confess — for so is the way of all who are put to death to confess [she-ken derech kol ha-mumasin misvadin]; and whoever confesses has a portion in the World to Come.” The proof is Achan, whom Yehoshua urged, “My son, give glory to Hashem, God of Israel, and make confession to Him” (Yehoshua 7:19), and whose confession atoned — “on this day of your judgment you are troubled, but you will not be troubled in the World to Come.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Rambam (Hilchos Sanhedrin 13) — even one executed by the court is granted, through his confession, a share in the World to Come; and R’ Yehoshua ben Levi (opening this very amud) — one who “slaughters his [evil] inclination and confesses” is credited “as though he honored the Holy One in two worlds, this world and the next.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why court-imposed punishment is “preferable to those punished by Heaven’s hand” — for the court “makes known to them their sin,” rousing “the stirrings of teshuvah in his heart, to return and confess,” so that the sentence itself becomes “unto life.”

notes.body_html: Eruvin 19a (Reish Lakish): distinct from the teaching that “Avraham raises up” Israel’s sinners from the fire of Gehinnom, Reish Lakish here says that “the wicked do not repent, even at the entrance of Gehinnom [afilu al pischo shel Gehinnom einan chozrin bi-teshuvah]” — expounding “and they shall go forth and look upon the carcasses of the men who rebel against Me” (Yeshayah 66:24): “it does not say ‘who rebelled,’ but ‘who rebel’ — they go on rebelling forever.” Meforshim: Rashi — ha-pordim, they perpetually part from Him; and the Gemara’s own resolution restricts this non-repentance to “the rebels among the nations of the world [poshei umos ha’olam],” never to the sinners of Israel (who do accept the judgment). R’ Tzadok’s use: “only of the nations of the world did they say” they cannot return — “for their sin is in the essence of their soul; such is their very being”; whereas in Israel sin “is not in the essence,” so that even “the wicked and those who commit severe transgressions” can always return.

notes.body_html: Koheles 7:20: “כִּי אָדָם אֵין צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ, אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא” — “for there is no righteous man on earth who does [only] good and never sins.” Meforshim: Rashi and Ibn Ezra — no mortal is so perfectly righteous as to be wholly free of any lapse; and the Sages invoke the verse to teach that even the greatest can be found wanting under exacting measure. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “hair’s-breadth exactitude” that Hashem applies to complete tzaddikim “was not handed to a court at all” — for were the Sanhedrin to judge themselves so precisely, “in themselves too they would find the same,” since “there is no righteous man on earth who never sins”; such judgment “is only through Hashem Himself.”

notes.body_html: “Adorn yourself first” (keshot atzmecha v’achar kach keshot acheirim, Bava Metzia 107b; Bava Basra 60b): the dictum that one must “adorn [correct] yourself, and afterward adorn [correct] others,” derived (Bava Metzia 107b) from “הִתְקוֹשְׁשׁוּ וָקוֹשּׁוּ” (Tzefaniah 2:1) — read as “adorn yourselves [first], then adorn others.” Meforshim: Rashi — a person must first perfect his own conduct before he sets out to reprove his fellow. R’ Tzadok’s use: paired with “there is no righteous man on earth” (Koheles 7:20), the demand of hairsbreadth exactitude belongs to Hashem alone — for a court that would exact it of others “must first adorn itself,” and would then discover the identical lack within its own members; therefore “this matter was not given to the Sanhedrin at all.”

notes.body_html: Zohar, Shemini 36b: R’ Tzadok directs the reader here (an ayein — “see” — reference) in connection with the theme that David’s punishment came about through the great ones of Israel.Chassidic context - Sefat Emet, Lech Lecha 5:5: The Sefas Emes gives a precise framework for the tension here between inward humility and outward honor. He explains the maxim that one who flees honor is pursued by honor: honor is, in truth, the garment of the King - Hashem is the Melech HaKavod - and the servant must therefore flee the temptation to clothe himself in it as a private possession. But when a person returns every honor he receives to Hashem, the honor may actually pursue him, because the more he is honored while refusing to appropriate that honor to himself, the more kavod Shamayim is increased. He reads Avraham's promised public greatness in exactly this way: once Hashem found his heart faithful, Avraham could be made great in the world without that greatness becoming self-reference. This closely complements R' Tzadok's account of Rabban Gamliel. The revealed form of his conduct could be judged as ga'avah and therefore required the removal of kavod in the revealed world; yet that punishment does not establish that his inward motive was a pursuit of honor. On the contrary, once the inner intention is clarified as l'Shem Shamayim, nesius itself can return and become a vehicle of the King's honor. The se'if's measure-for-measure punishment thus concerns the garment through which the act appeared in this world, while the deeper clarification concerns to Whom that garment ultimately belonged.
