notes.body_html: Shabbos 108a: R’ Yehoshua HaGarsi answered a Baytusi who challenged why tefillin may be written on the hides of neveilos u-tereifos (kosher-species animals that died improperly) yet not on the hides of non-kosher animals, with a parable: “[it is comparable] to two men who were sentenced to death by the government [malchus] — one the king himself killed, and one the executioner [ispaklator] killed; which of them is more praiseworthy? Say: the one whom the king killed.” That is: to be put to death by the king’s own hand is the greater dignity. Meforshim: Rashi — the kosher species, even fallen to neveilah, keeps its fitness (its “honor”) because it is of the class “permitted in your mouth,” like the one dispatched by the king himself; the non-kosher animal is like the one killed by the lowly executioner. R’ Tzadok’s use: he reads the mashal straight into Rabban Gamliel’s deposition — to be “put to death” (removed) by the King’s own agents, “the Sages of Israel,” is “the one whom the king killed,” a far greater honor than removal by mere chance or by “the executioner [ispaklator]” — the very word he draws from this Gemara.

notes.body_html: Eichah 3:38: in the heart of Yirmeyah’s lament — “מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת וְהַטּוֹב” — “from the mouth of the Most High does there not go forth [both] evil and good?” Background: the sufferer accepts that all that befalls him, calamity as well as bounty, issues by God’s decree. Meforshim: Rashi — why should a living man complain? the “evil” comes only as the deserved consequence of sin, not as gratuitous evil from Above; and the Sages (Rashi citing the Midrash) read it that “evil” does not descend as evil directly “from the mouth of the Most High” — it comes about of itself, through a person’s own sin, while from Him only good goes forth. R’ Tzadok’s use: since Rabban Gamliel’s punishment issued directly “from the mouth of the Most High,” through His faithful agents acting for Heaven, “there is no evil in it at all” — what wears the face of disgrace is, at its source, unmixed good.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 17:2: in David’s “Tefillah” — “מִלְּפָנֶיךָ מִשְׁפָּטִי יֵצֵא, עֵינֶיךָ תֶּחֱזֶינָה מֵישָׁרִים” — “let my judgment come forth from before You; let Your eyes behold uprightness.” Background: David asks that his case be adjudicated by God directly, not by human eyes that see only the surface. Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — “from before You let my sentence issue,” not from flesh and blood, for You alone “behold uprightness,” seeing the heart’s true intent. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is precisely what David sought — that his judgment come “from before You,” from Hashem who “sees the heart,” so that the punishment is “only for a moment,” reckoned to this world alone; and so too Rabban Gamliel, once his inner intent for Heaven was clarified, was in the end reinstated.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §8): “and it is in cleaving to the Torah, a threefold Torah… for the hidden things, which are the thought in the mind, are "to Hashem our God"; and the revealed things, in deed, are "to us" — and the will that is in the heart stands between.” Exactly the se’if: R’ Gamliel’s true intent belonged to “the hidden things,” which are God’s — so what was answerable here was only the revealed act, and that “only for a moment.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל כֵּן גַּם שָׁם הוּחְזַר, וְהוּא חָזַר לְפַיֵּיס אֶת ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וְהִכִּיר שֶׁלֹּא עָשָׂה כַּהוֹגֶן
notes.body_html: Berachos 28a: After Rabban Gamliel was deposed, he “did not absent himself from the study hall even for a moment,” and when a dispute over an Ammonite convert was decided in R’ Yehoshua’s favor, “Rabban Gamliel said: since this is so, I will go and appease R’ Yehoshua.” He came to R’ Yehoshua’s house, saw its walls “blackened,” and remarked, “from the walls of your house it is apparent that you are a charcoal-maker.” R’ Yehoshua replied, “woe to the generation whose leader you are, for you do not know the hardship of Torah scholars, how they sustain themselves.” Rabban Gamliel said, “I have wronged you — forgive me,” but R’ Yehoshua paid him no heed — until he said, “do it for the honor of my father [Abba],” and R’ Yehoshua was appeased. R’ Akiva then said, “R’ Yehoshua has been appeased; we [deposed him] only for your honor — tomorrow you and I will go early to his door [to restore him].”Chabad parallel - Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25:30: The Alter Rebbe's discussion of hashgachah supplies a useful conceptual background to R' Tzadok's distinction between an event that appears to occur 'by chance' and one visibly carried out by the servants of Hashem. Tanya explains that anger over ordinary worldly injury contains a trace of avodah zarah precisely because 'hakol bidei Shamayim chutz mi-yiras Shamayim': the human agent who caused the loss is not an independent power outside Divine governance. At the same time, the Alter Rebbe explicitly limits this reasoning in matters of avodas Hashem - where there is an obligation to separate another from prohibition - thereby preserving human responsibility and the full force of Torah. That double point fits the present se'if. Rabban Gamliel's removal could have come through what people call mikreh, but to 'those who recognize the truth' the royal decree, political event, and decision of the Sages are all within hashgachah. What changes is not whether Hashem is acting, but the garment through which His judgment becomes visible. Hence R' Tzadok can call deposition through the chachmei Yisrael themselves a greater kavod: the judgment is mediated by servants consciously doing the will of Heaven rather than being hidden behind an apparently accidental worldly chain. The Tanya parallel also keeps the point disciplined - providence does not erase the bechirah or accountability of the actors; it denies only that the worldly agent is an autonomous source of power.

notes.body_html: Bava Metzia 84b–85a: When Rabbi saw that R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon was much sharper than his own son, “Rabbi’s spirit weakened.” R’ Shimon [the father] said, “my son, let it not grieve you — he is a lion son of a lion, and you are a lion son of a fox.” Hence Rebbi’s teaching: “three humble ones: Abba [RaShbaG, Rebbi’s father], the sons of Beseira, and Yehonasan ben Shaul.” The sons of Beseira “seated Hillel at the head and appointed him Nasi” when they saw he was greater; Yehonasan ben Shaul said to David, “you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be second to you” (I Shmuel 23:17). The Gemara concludes that only RaShbaG is certainly [singled out for] humility.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הָעַנְוְותָנוּת, דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא חָשְׁבוּ שָׁם הִלֵּל שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן עָנָיו, וְכֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהֵעִידָה תּוֹרָה עַל עַנְוְותָנוּתוֹ מִכָּל הָאָדָם
notes.body_html: Bamidbar 12:3: “וְהָאִישׁ מֹשֶׁה עָנָיו מְאֹד, מִכֹּל הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר עַל פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה” — “and the man Moshe was exceedingly humble, more than any person on the face of the earth.” Background: the Torah interjects this testimony in the midst of Miriam and Aharon’s speaking about Moshe — he bore their words in silence, never defending himself. Meforshim: Rashi — anav means “lowly and forbearing [shefal v’savlan]”; the Sifrei and Ibn Ezra dwell on his humility despite his unrivalled greatness. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because Moshe was “truly greater than all men,” his humility — like Hillel’s — “is not so great a wonder”; the wonder, and “the essence of humility,” is RaShbaG’s lowering himself before one truly greater than he (Rashbi), whom his generation did not recognize — which is why the Gemara’s list of “the three humble ones” passes over even Moshe and Hillel.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayakhel §5): “but the crown of the Holy One Himself, as it were, one does not merit — only one who makes himself as leftovers, to be as nothing; through this he merits to attain the light of the supernal Keser, which is called "ayin" [nothing].” Exactly the se’if’s “sign of complete humility”: the rung is reached only by one who has made himself nothing — and it is therefore invisible precisely to a generation that measures by something.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם הוּא דָּרַשׁ וְהִתְקִין בִּכְבוֹד הַנָּשִׂיא נֶגֶד הֶחָכָם וְאַב בֵּית דִּין כִּדְאִיתָא [סוֹף הוֹרָיוֹת]
notes.body_html: Horayos 13b: A baraisa taught the honors due the Nasi, Av Beis Din, and Chacham; R’ Yochanan said it was taught in the days of RaShbaG (Nasi), R’ Meir (Chacham), and R’ Nasan (Av Beis Din) — when RaShbaG enacted that the [full standing] honor be shown only to the Nasi. R’ Meir and R’ Nasan, feeling slighted, plotted to ask RaShbaG to expound Uktzin (which he did not know) and thereby depose him. R’ Yaakov ben Karshi overheard and, fearing RaShbaG’s disgrace, sat outside his chamber reviewing the tractate aloud until RaShbaG “gave his attention and learned it.” Next day RaShbaG expounded it, then said, “had I not learned it, you would have shamed me,” and had them removed from the study hall. When R’ Yosi protested, “shall the Torah be outside and we within?”, RaShbaG readmitted them but penalized them that teachings not be cited in their names (R’ Meir → “Acheirim,” R’ Nasan → “Yesh Omrim”). Later they were told in a dream to appease him; R’ Nasan went, R’ Meir did not.

notes.body_html: Berachos 27b: After deposing Rabban Gamliel, [the Sages asked] “whom shall we appoint? R’ Yehoshua? — he is a party to the matter. R’ Akiva? — perhaps [Rabban Gamliel] will punish him [by Heaven], for he has no ancestral merit. Rather, R’ Elazar ben Azariah — wise, wealthy, and tenth in descent from Ezra.” They asked him; he said, “let me consult my household.” His wife warned, “perhaps they will [later] depose you”; he replied, “let a man use a precious cup one day, and let it break tomorrow.” Yerushalmi Berachos 4:1: R’ Akiva “sat distressed,” saying, “not that he is more a master of Torah than I, but he is of greater lineage — fortunate the man whose ancestors have gained merit for him.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְהֲרֵי ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אָמַר ״לִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ יוֹמָא חֲדָא״ כו׳, אַף דְּהָדַר לִתְבַר
notes.body_html: Berachos 28a: when R’ Elazar ben Azariah was offered the office of Nasi after Rabban Gamliel’s removal, his wife warned, “perhaps they will depose you, just as they deposed Rabban Gamliel”; he answered with the folk-saying, “let a person use a precious goblet [kasa d’mokra] one day, and tomorrow let it break” — seize the honor of the hour, though it not endure. Meforshim: Rashi — the “precious cup” is that day’s greatness; better to have served one day than never. R’ Tzadok’s use: on this he says R’ Akiva and R’ Meir “certainly desired” the office “even if they should be punished and it break” — the honor of the moment, done for Heaven, is worth the cost; the Sages held back from appointing them only because “they wished to appoint a Nasi who would endure.”Chassidic context - Tiferet Shlomo, Sh'lach 1: The Tiferes Shlomo reads the Torah's description of the spies as 'ish echad... kol nasi vahem' as a warning built into the very office of leadership. The greatness of a tzaddik, he says, rests in anavah and shiflus; the more truly 'low' he is in humility, the more he can be raised as a rosh. He therefore reads 'lamateh avosav tishlachu kol nasi vahem' homiletically as a charge to the princes to strip themselves of the inward claim of nesius even while carrying its public function. Their later failure began when that office became hisnas'us within the heart. This sharply complements R' Tzadok's description of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. His humility is not proved by surrendering the Nasi's institutional honor - he himself established the order of honor due the Nasi, Chacham and Av Beis Din - but by knowing the truth about himself in relation to one who was genuinely greater, even where the public hierarchy gave him more visible kavod. Humility and nesius are therefore not opposites. The test is whether office is borne as a shelichus or converted into a private measure of self. That is why R' Tzadok can see RaShbaG's enacted honor and his humility as mutually clarifying rather than contradictory: the outward structure remains, while the inward 'nasi' has been stripped of self-importance.

notes.body_html: Eruvin 13b: R’ Acha bar Chanina taught, “it is revealed and known before the One who spoke and the world came into being that in the generation of R’ Meir there was none his equal [she-ein b’doro shel R’ Meir kamoso]; and why did they not fix the halachah according to him? Because his colleagues could not fathom the depth of his opinion” — for he could “declare the impure pure and adduce a justification, and the pure impure and adduce a justification.” (On the same amud: his true name was R’ Nehorai, “because he illumines [meir] the eyes of the Sages in halachah” — see §54.) R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the ground for “R’ Meir was much greater in wisdom than R’ Nasan, for there was none in his generation like him”; yet, as “the initiator” of the move against RaShbaG, R’ Meir deliberately stepped back — “so as not to be like one biased, seeking his own honor” — asking only to be Av Beis Din and not Nasi.

notes.body_html: Sotah 49a: the closing Mishnah of the tractate catalogues what “ceased” with the passing of the great ones — “when R’ Meir died, the composers of parables ceased… when Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, the honor of the Torah ceased… and when Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] died, humility and fear of sin ceased [batlah anavah v’yiras chet].” Meforshim: Rashi and the Bartenura — with Rebbi’s death there was none who so embodied humility; and the Gemara (Sotah 49b) relates that when the tanna taught this, Rav Yosef said, “do not teach that humility ceased — for I am here,” and Rav Nachman, “do not teach that fear of sin ceased — for I am here.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Rebbi, grandson of Rabban Gamliel, “held fast to humility” so completely that humility itself was bound up with him — proof that the family’s inner trait was true humility, which clarifies in retrospect that Rabban Gamliel’s firmness, too, was never for his own honor.

notes.body_html: Horayos 14a: on the last page of the tractate, Rebbi’s son asked why they cite rulings of the Sages “whose water we drink but whose names we do not mention” — namely R’ Meir and R’ Nasan, who had sought to depose Rebbi’s father RaShbaG; and Rebbi taught the ruling as “they said in the name of R’ Meir,” not “R’ Meir said.” Rava observed: “even Rabbi, who is humble [afilu Rabbi da’anavtan hu], [only] taught ‘they said in the name of R’ Meir,’ but did not say ‘R’ Meir said’” — even the humble Rebbi withheld the fuller honor of naming him outright, on account of the affront once aimed at his father’s house. Meforshim: Rashi — the force of the statement is the measure of Rebbi’s humility, that Rava designates him “the humble one.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this proves Rebbi was “even more humble than his father”; hence, when he too “conducted his office of Nasi with authority,” all knew it was for Heaven and none suspected self-seeking.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §28): “[Rebbi] commanded his son (Kesubos 103b), ‘conduct your office of Nasi with authority [nheg nesiuscha b’ramus] and cast fear upon the students.’ And Moshe Rabbeinu, the humblest of all men — Dasan and Aviram said to him, ‘will you make yourself a prince over us?’ (Shemos 2:14); and surely they did not speak mere falsehood, and all the more that such a thing would not be written in the Torah — but they sensed in him, to the outward eye, some measure of ‘exercising authority.’” (Exactly the se’if’s paradox: the very man of whom ‘when Rebbi died, humility ceased’ bids his son rule with authority — because inner humility and an outward bearing of authority, like Moshe’s, are no contradiction.)

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §99): “and regarding all of them it is written "nasi" — except for Yehudah, Shimon and Binyamin.” The se’if’s distinction exactly: the title of office and the inward standing are two different things, and Scripture itself withholds the title precisely where the standing is deepest.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Shmini 7: The Ishbitzer warns that there is such a thing as anavah pesulah. He interprets those who left manna overnight as having regarded themselves as especially humble - perhaps, they thought, they were not worthy that Hashem should provide for them again tomorrow. Yet by singling themselves out as less worthy than Klal Yisrael they had actually left the place Hashem assigned them; what appeared to human eyes as modesty was not the humility Hashem desired. He contrasts this with David's 've'anochi tola'as,' a lowliness that did find favor before Hashem. This is an unusually close complement to R' Tzadok's 'nehog nesi'uscha beramim.' Once genuine humility has been clarified, refusing the responsibility and dignity attached to a Divine office can itself become a distorted humility. Rebbi could be 'anav' and still instruct his son to conduct the nesius with force, because anavah does not mean denying the truth of the role Hashem has given. It means that the role does not become a claim about one's independent self. The Ishbitzer's distinction also explains why outward appearances are insufficient: a deferential posture may conceal self-consciousness, while firm leadership may arise from complete bittul to the task. Thus the son can reveal the father's inward truth precisely by joining two qualities that look contradictory in this world - deep humility and unapologetic exercise of nesius - and showing that both can flow from one l'Shem Shamayim center.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 11a: The Gemara relates that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dictated letters intercalating the year, signing them with characteristic humility (concluding, “and it seemed proper to me and to my colleagues”). Comparing his manner to that of his son Rebbi, the Gemara exclaims, “come and see the difference between the mighty former ones [Rabban Gamliel] and the humble latter ones [Rebbi]” — Rebbi being still more self-effacing.

notes.body_html: Berachos 7b (“shema garim”): amid the Gemara’s expositions of names as portents (Reuven, Ruth, Yehudah), it asks, “from where that the name has an effect [shema garim]? R’ Eliezer said: the verse states, ‘go, see the works of Hashem, who has set desolations [שַׁמּוֹת] in the earth’ (Tehillim 46:9) — do not read שַׁמּוֹת [shamos, desolations] but שֵׁמוֹת [sheimos, names]” — a person’s name is among “the works of Hashem in the earth.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Maharsha — the name (given, as the Arizal teaches, with a trace of ruach hakodesh) draws down and shapes the bearer’s nature and path; and R’ Meir “would scrutinize names” (Yoma 83b) — distrusting the innkeeper “Kidor” from “ki dor tahpuchos heimah” (Devarim 32:20), and proven right. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “the name is the essence of the soul and the vitality,” the Sages’ stock pair “Yosef ben Shimon” is chosen not for its frequency in the market but for its root meaning — the tribal names Yosef and Shimon fitted, at their source, to model “the son who clarifies the father”; hence “not every Yosef and Shimon in the world is like the tribes,” yet the name still “has an effect,” bearing “some connection to the root of his name.”R' Tzadok - close parallel (Pri Tzadik, Korach 8:4): In Pri Tzadik R' Tzadok returns explicitly to Chazal's stock expression 'Yosef ben Shimon' and gives essentially the same root-level reading developed here. All Israel, he explains, can be called by Yosef's name - 'she'eiris Yosef' - because 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim,' and the Zohar associates bris with the title tzaddik. He then makes the striking point that this remains true even of Shimon, although the majority of the twenty-four thousand who died at Baal Peor came from Shimon and their sin appears to be the very opposite of Yosef's defining shemiras habris. That is why 'Yosef ben Shimon' is so expressive: at the level of the revealed episode, Shimon and Yosef appear opposed; at the root, Shimon too is included in Yosef's name of tzaddik. This cross-reference strengthens the present se'if's claim that the defect is not part of Shimon's essential shoresh. It also guards against a superficial reading. R' Tzadok is not erasing the severity of Peor - Pri Tzadik speaks precisely while acknowledging the twenty-four thousand - but distinguishing the historical manifestation from the enduring Jewish root. The phrase 'ben Shimon' is therefore not a legal fiction that makes the past disappear; it is a compressed statement that the child/clarification can disclose what the father's outward history concealed: the covenantal point that was never the essence of the fall.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 104a (“bra mezakeh abba”): explaining why the Mishnah omits the wicked Amon from the kings with no share in the World to Come (out of honor for his righteous son Yoshiyahu), yet lists Menasheh despite his righteous father Chizkiyahu, the Gemara rules: “the son confers merit upon the father [bra mezakeh abba], but the father does not confer merit upon the son, as it is written, ‘and none delivers from My hand’ (Devarim 32:39) — Avraham does not deliver Yishmael, and Yitzchak does not deliver Esav, from the judgment.” Meforshim: Rashi — a father is credited for having raised a worthy son, but cannot shield an unworthy one from his own judgment. R’ Tzadok’s use: the punishment of the boel aramis is that he has “no son who offers a meal-offering” — no son to “clarify his root and grant him merit,” for “a son grants merit to a father”; his concealed Jewish root, which would otherwise surface in such a son, cannot be revealed in this world’s outward order — though from the side of the hidden Binah it remains entirely intact.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל כֵּן ״לְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים מַרְפֵּא״ וּמַמְתִּיק לְכָל הַדִּינִים עַל פִּי לְשׁוֹנָם לְבַד כִּי כָּל שִׂיחָתָם תּוֹרָה
notes.body_html: Mishlei 12:18: “יֵשׁ בּוֹטֶה כְּמַדְקְרוֹת חָרֶב, וּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים מַרְפֵּא” — “there is one whose rash speech is like the piercings of a sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Ralbag — reckless words wound like a blade, whereas the measured speech of the wise soothes and heals; the marpei (healing) is set against the madkros charev (sword-thrusts) of careless talk. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “words of Torah have an efficacious power in all the worlds,” which conduct themselves “according to the Torah that issues from the mouth of the true Sages of Israel,” their very expression “heals and sweetens all the judgments” — so that when the Sages framed even the boel aramis by way of the wholesome example “Yosef ben Shimon,” speaking “according to the absolute truth,” they thereby “sweetened the most severe sins of Israel in their root.”Izhbitz-Radzin clarification - Mei HaShiloach Anthology, Siddur 1 (citing Tiferet Yosef, Naso): A short Izhbitz teaching on 'neshamah shenasata bi tehorah hi' gives an especially helpful map for R' Tzadok's distinction between root and revealed judgment. It says that a person contains nefesh, ruach and neshamah; no sin or blemish reaches the neshamah, whereas ruach alludes to the human power of bechirah, through which one can choose good and reject evil. The two statements belong together. The untouched purity of the neshamah is not a reason to deny culpability in the sphere of choice; rather it identifies a deeper point from which return remains possible after choice has gone wrong. That is exactly the balance required by this se'if. R' Tzadok can maintain that the hidden root of a Jew is not defined by the ugliest outward act, while also insisting that the din of this world follows the deed as it emerged through bechirah and that the root may remain unrevealed here. The Izhbitz formulation prevents the doctrine of hidden holiness from becoming an excuse before the act: ruach is specifically the arena in which man must choose. Only afterward can the enduring neshamah explain why even a severe fall does not become the final definition of the Jewish soul. In this sense, the future clarification is a revelation of identity, not a retroactive permission to have violated the revealed will of Hashem.

Exactly the se’if: Shimon’s separation is folded into Yehudah, in whom it is complete — for the measure is exactly where a thing serves the mind and where it dissolves it, which is the whole difference between Israel and Amalek.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 34 (Shimon and Levi at Shechem): after Shechem son of Chamor defiled Dinah, “the two sons of Yaakov, Shimon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, each took his sword and came upon the city unawares, and slew every male” (34:25), “and Chamor and Shechem his son they slew by the sword, and took Dinah from Shechem’s house” (34:26); to Yaakov’s rebuke they answered, “should he treat our sister like a harlot?” (34:31). Meforshim: Rashi — they are called “Dinah’s brothers” because they endangered themselves for her; the Ramban weighs at length the justice of the deed; and Yaakov, on his deathbed, still censures their zeal — “Shimon and Levi are brothers, instruments of violence… cursed be their wrath” (Bereishis 49:5–7). R’ Tzadok’s use: Shimon is “the principal zealot [mekane] in the matter of Dinah,” for his very soul-root is “the utmost separation from the peoples” — he could not bear that a daughter of Israel be joined to Shechem the Canaanite; and Levi “joined [nilveh] him,” though Levi’s separateness is “revealed in this world” (Kohanim and Levi’im set apart even from Israel), whereas Shimon’s — the hidden holiness of all Israel’s utter separateness — stays concealed here.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Tzav §1): “"do not bring me to a trial" — and through this [prideful] thought he came to that deed, as they said, "whoever is haughty is as though he came upon all the forbidden relations"; and afterward his heart was broken within him, in the utmost lowliness.” Exactly the se’if: the deficiency in question is bound to self-exaltation, and the separation that answers it is therefore a lowering — the very posture Shimon’s root supplies.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, V'Zot HaBerachah 14: The Ishbitzer makes the Shimon-Yehudah relationship explicit. Reading 'Shema Hashem kol Yehudah' as containing Moshe's otherwise unspoken blessing to Shimon, he describes the twelve tribes as limbs of the Shechinah: Reuven is the eyes, Shimon the ears, and Yehudah the heart, possessing a lev naki u-mevorar. The blessing therefore means that Shimon - the power of hearing - must listen to the voice of Yehudah, because Shimon's portion continually requires birur. This is almost a direct gloss on the architecture of the present se'if. R' Tzadok explains Shimon's deepest root as the capacity for pure receiving, while Yehudah represents the openly recognizable Jewish rejection of avodah zarah and the heart that can give the hidden reception a revealed form. The Ishbitzer shows why those powers must be joined. Hearing reaches what sight does not yet display, but precisely for that reason it can receive a depth whose correct application has not yet been clarified in the visible world. Yehudah's heart becomes the measure by which that hearing is clothed and tested. Thus Shimon's tikkun is not to become less receptive; it is to have his exceptional receptivity pass through a clean, clarified lev. The concealed holiness of Shimon can then emerge as the opposite of assimilation: a faculty that hears only the Divine voice and rejects every alien sovereignty.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Korach §1): citing the Arizal, R’ Tzadok explains that there are rungs called igulim (circles) and rungs called yosher (straight-line): the world of tohu before creation was igulim, the world of tikkun began with yosher, “and in the Future the aspect of igulim will be revealed as well. And this is the secret of what they said at the end of Taanis — ‘the Holy One will in the Future make a circle-dance [machol] for the tzaddikim’ — for ‘machol’ denotes a circle… and in the aspect of igulim there are no rungs at all, for all are equal, like a circle that has no beginning and no end [ein bo rosh v’sof].” He continues that this was precisely Korach’s error: since at Matan Torah there was a flash of the future tikkun (all hearing “Anochi” directly, “and Hashem in their midst” — He seated among them, they around Him in the circle, with no ranks), Korach claimed “all the congregation are holy… and why then do you exalt yourselves?” — treating the Future’s revealed equality as if it were already fully present, whereas in truth it awaits the Future, and Shabbos is but a taste of it (one-sixtieth of the World to Come).

notes.body_html: Mei HaShiloach (the Izhbitzer) — parallel (Korach, on “u-madua tisnas’u al kehal Hashem”): R’ Tzadok’s own teacher frames the same idea: “Korach’s claim was that there is no elevation among Israel, of one over his fellow, for ‘Hashem is in their midst’ — that Hashem dwells within all of them equally [shaveh b’shaveh], as is explained in the Gemara (Taanis 31a) that in the Future the Holy One will make a machol for the tzaddikim — and a machol is [danced] in a circle, in which no one is closer [to the center] than his fellow. notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: כִּי אָז לֹא יִלְמְדוּ עוֹד אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְלֹא יְקַבְּלוּ אֶחָד מֵחֲבֵירוֹ כְּלָל, רַק כּוּלָּם יְקַבְּלוּ בְּשָׁוֶה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַד, וְלֹא יִהְיֶה מְצִיאוּת לְכֹחַ הַהַשְׁפָּעָה לְהַזּוּלַת
notes.body_html: Yirmiyah 31:33 (in some editions 31:34): the prooftext for the circle’s equality — “וְלֹא יְלַמְּדוּ עוֹד אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְאִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו לֵאמֹר דְּעוּ אֶת ה’, כִּי כוּלָּם יֵדְעוּ אוֹתִי לְמִקְּטַנָּם וְעַד גְּדוֹלָם” — “and no longer will each man teach his fellow, nor each his brother, saying, ‘Know Hashem,’ for they shall all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — in the Messianic era the knowledge of Hashem will be so direct and universal that no one will need a teacher. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the very “rung of circles” — for then “none will receive from another at all, but all will receive equally from Hashem alone,” with “no existence for the power of bestowal upon another,” and hence no ranks and no elevation of one soul over its fellow.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev §6): “only that the letter mem has also an open mem, which can be spoiled — as afterward, that though the yetzer hara was uprooted, it later returned to its place; and the letter samech indicates as it will be in the Future.” Exactly the se’if: in this world even an uprooting is reversible — the closed circle of the samech, with no opening and no gradation, belongs to the Future alone.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Beit Yaakov on Torah, Vayigash 24:5: Beit Yaakov develops precisely the image R' Tzadok uses here for the Future: 'the Holy One will make a machol for the tzaddikim.' A machol, he explains, is a circle, and in a circle there is no first and last and therefore no one stands intrinsically closer than his fellow. He connects this to Krias Shema, in which a person gives over his entire self to Hashem and recognizes that he possesses no independent power; when wisdom is known to have been received from Hashem rather than owned by the recipient, it cannot become a basis for self-exaltation. This complements the se'if's contrast between the ranked order of olam hazeh and the future revelation of igulim. Here, hierarchy is needed because Divine light is received through differentiated vessels - teacher and student, greater and lesser, giver and receiver. The future circle does not deny the distinct histories or avodah of the tzaddikim; it reveals the deeper point in which every one of them is directly turned toward the same Center. That is why R' Tzadok can connect this state specifically with Shimon's faculty of pure hearing. When reception is no longer distorted into a claim of superiority, every soul can hear from Hashem without one person's light becoming a barrier to another. The equality of the circle is therefore not flattening but the disclosure that the Source of every differentiated gift was one all along.

notes.body_html: Shoftim 1:2–3: “after the death of Yehoshua,” when Israel asked who should go up first against the Canaanite, “Hashem said: Yehudah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand” (1:2); “and Yehudah said to Shimon his brother: Go up with me in my lot, and let us fight the Canaanite, and I too will go with you in your lot; and Shimon went with him” (1:3). Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — Shimon’s territory lay within Yehudah’s portion, so the two conquered together; and (the Midrash) Yehudah, whom Shimon accompanied, later repaid him. R’ Tzadok’s use: the revealed victory over the nations comes by Yehudah’s way — “repudiation of idolatry” — so “Yehudah is the first, fit for this”; but the command to leave no survivor (utter non-connection) is essentially Shimon’s power, and since Shimon’s rung is hidden, the command could not fall on him explicitly — so Yehudah “included him,” saying “I too will go with you,” the revealed carrying the hidden.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §13): “but when it is not so — then even though he is fenced-in from envy, desire and honor, this is as though he were not fenced-in, and as though he possessed envy, desire and honor, which drive a person [from the world].” Exactly the se’if: the nations’ claim rests on the outward fence alone, and an outward fence without its root is reckoned as no fence — which is why the revealed victory must come from Yehudah, with Shimon in his lot.

notes.body_html: Devarim 20:16: of the seven Canaanite nations the Torah commands, “רַק מֵעָרֵי הָעַמִּים הָאֵלֶּה… לֹא תְחַיֶּה כָּל נְשָׁמָה” — “only from the cities of these peoples… you shall let no soul live.” Meforshim: Rashi — they must be utterly destroyed, with no treaty and no survivor, “so that they not teach you to do like all their abominations” (Devarim 20:18). R’ Tzadok’s use: “that they leave no root or branch, for they have no connection or joining with them” — this utter separation is “the power of Shimon,” whose soul-root is the total separateness of Israel from the peoples; it surfaced in the conquest, though (being unrevealed) it was folded into Yehudah’s explicit command rather than commanded to Shimon by name.

notes.body_html: Yevamos 76b: Rav Pappa said, “shall we arise and derive [halachah] from Shlomo?!” Shlomo did not [truly] marry the foreign women [for the sake of marriage], but only “clung to them in love,” as it is written, “of the nations concerning which Hashem said — you shall not intermarry with them — Shlomo clung to them in love” (I Melachim 11:2). The apparent difficulty from “vayischaten” [“and he intermarried,” I Melachim 3:1] is resolved: out of the great love he bore them, Scripture regards it as though he had intermarried in Hashem [i.e., only in love, not in true marriage].Further Chassidic context - Bnei Yissaschar, Tamuz and Av 1:9:2: The Bnei Yissaschar builds an extended teaching on the very verse R' Tzadok invokes: 'Yehudah said to Shimon his brother: ascend with me in my lot... and I too will go with you in your lot' (Shoftim 1:3). In his scheme of the months, Nisan belongs to Yehudah and Av to Shimon. Nisan already bears the revealed character of redemption, while Av is, in the present order, the month in which that good is hidden and waits to be reversed. He therefore reads Yehudah's invitation as a prophetic joining of the two lots: in the earlier redemptions Shimon's future good is carried within Yehudah's revealed geulah, while in the ultimate redemption even the month of Shimon will be transformed into joy and Yehudah will, as it were, enter Shimon's lot. This does not duplicate R' Tzadok's particular explanation of the conquest; it adds a striking Chassidic afterlife to the same textual pairing. In R' Tzadok, Yehudah goes first because the revealed rejection of avodah zarah must lead, yet the complete uprooting of the nations' root is identified with Shimon's deeper hidden power. Bnei Yissaschar similarly treats their partnership as a union of revealed redemption with a good that is still concealed. The verse thus becomes a pattern: Yehudah gives Shimon's hidden strength a historical entrance, and Shimon's eventual clarification reveals a deeper redemption within Yehudah's first ascent.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §4): “He derives from the creation of the world, regarding the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, that ‘first there is darkness’ [berisha chashucha] — one must accept the yoke of Heaven even from within the darkness, the folly, and the absence of [good] deeds; and then, in the end, he will fulfill it in ‘wealth and the light of day’ — the clear apprehension through which the deed is [afterward] drawn forth.” (Exactly the se’if’s pattern — ‘first darkness, then light’: the trials that hold a person back before a high rung are the built-in ‘darkness’ of creation, from within which the yoke must be accepted before the light can come.)

notes.body_html: Shabbos 77b: R’ Zeira, finding R’ Yehuda in a cheerful mood and ready to answer questions about the natural world, asked him, “why do the goats walk at the head of the flock and the ewes follow?” He answered, “it is as in the creation of the world, which at first was dark and afterward light [b’reisha choshocha v’hadar nehora]” — the (dark) goats precede the (white) ewes, just as in creation the darkness of “and there was evening” preceded the light of “and there was morning.” Meforshim: Rashi — such is the order of the world, darkness first and light following. R’ Tzadok’s use: so too “before entering some rung there are trials that seek to hold one back,” for the order of ascent mirrors the order of creation — “first darkness, then light,” and “the gloom of dawn that precedes the shining light is the most intense darkness”; hence the deed of Shittim came just before entering the Land, and the foreign-wives stumble at the return to the Land in Bavel — each at once followed by the light.

notes.body_html: Rambam, Hilchos Gerushin 2:20: “One whom the law requires to divorce his wife, and who refuses — a Jewish court, in every place and time, beats him until he says ‘I want to,’ and he writes the get, and it is valid.” Why is it not void as coerced? “For we call [an act] ‘coerced’ only [when] one is pressed to do a thing he is not obligated in by the Torah — but one whose evil inclination has overpowered him to nullify a mitzvah or commit a transgression, and who is beaten until he does what he is obligated to do — this is not coerced by [others]; rather he coerced himself by his own evil intent” — for at his core his will is to be a Jew and fulfill the mitzvos.Chassidic background - Kedushat Levi, Likutim 113: R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev interprets Chazal's 'beresha chashokha vehadar nehora' - first darkness and then light - as a basic order of avodas Hashem. Yirah is the gate and beginning; after a person has labored to place yiras Shamayim upon his face, ahavah can follow, and from that love a still more inward yirah can later be born. Darkness here is therefore not a sanctification of failure but the constricted first stage through which a larger illumination becomes receivable. That distinction fits R' Tzadok's rule in this se'if that before a higher rung there is a nisayon that appears as its opposite. Shittim before entry into Eretz Yisrael, or the dangerous admixture surrounding a later elevation, is the spiritual analogue of the created order in which evening precedes morning. The trial exposes whether the coming light can be carried without being captured by its counterfeit. Kedushat Levi is especially useful here because he formulates the sequence prospectively as avodah - fear, self-discipline and purification precede love. R' Tzadok's retrospective observation that darkness often precedes a new revelation should therefore not be read as permission to manufacture a fall. The Chassidic parallel instead describes the darkness as the narrow gate of preparation: a place where the opposite power is confronted and bounded so that the subsequent light can emerge as a true acquisition rather than an untested inspiration.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Shemos §5): "“the reapers of the field” — the reapers who cut away all the thorns and briars that surround the supernal rose." Exactly the se’if: “your people are all tzaddikim” in truth, and the sins that seem to disfigure them are only the thorns encircling the rose — cut away, never part of it.

notes.body_html: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:6: On “for the sun has gazed upon me,” a parable: a townswoman had a Kushite maidservant who said, “tomorrow my master will divorce his wife and marry me,” “for he [once] saw her hands blackened.” Her companion answered, “fool! if for his beloved wife, whose hands were blackened for an hour, [you imagine] he would divorce her — you, blackened from your mother’s womb, all the more so!” So the nations taunt Israel, “this nation exchanged its glory” (Tehillim 106:20); Israel reply, “if we, enslaved but briefly, were [so] penalized, you all the more” — and further, “we are like a prince whose face darkened in the desert sun, [but] with a little water his body whitens and returns to its beauty; whereas you are blackened from your mother’s womb,” for even in the womb [the gentile fetus] worshipped idols with its mother.

notes.body_html: Avodah Zarah 65a: Rava brought a gift to Bar Sheishach on his festival, knowing he was no idolater. He found him “sitting up to his neck in rosewater, with harlots standing before him.” Bar Sheishach said, “have you the like of this in your World to Come?” Rava replied, “ours is finer than this — for upon you [gentiles] there is the dread of the government, while upon us there will be no dread of any government.” As Bar Sheishach was summoned away by the king, he cursed, “may the eye that wishes to see your harm burst”; Rava answered “Amen” — and Bar Sheishach’s eye burst.

notes.body_html: Yechezkel 23:20: in the prophet’s parable of the two sisters Oholah (Shomron) and Oholivah (Yerushalayim), who lusted after Egypt and Assyria, it is said of the paramours — “אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׂר חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם וְזִרְמַת סוּסִים זִרְמָתָם” — “whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys, and whose issue is like the issue of horses.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — the verse marks the coarse, animal grossness of the gentile nations (here Egypt), likened to “the flesh of donkeys.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the source for “this is holy flesh [besar kodesh], and that is the flesh of donkeys” — that the very bodies of the Children of Israel differ in essence from the bodies of the nations “from birth, from womb and conception”; and since the title “tzaddik” pertains to the holiness of the body, it is rooted in this intrinsic difference — a holiness “not yet revealed in actuality,” while the wicked are still “blackened.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁהֵם שְׁזוּפִים וּשְׁחוֹרִים עַל זֶה אָמַר ״הֲלוֹא כִּבְנֵי כּוּשִׁיִּים אַתֶּם לִי״ וְגוֹמֵר
notes.body_html: Amos 9:7: “הֲלוֹא כִבְנֵי כֻשִׁיִּים אַתֶּם לִי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נְאֻם ה’” — “are you not like the children of the Kushites to Me, O Children of Israel? says Hashem” — the verse continuing, “did I not bring up Israel from the land of Egypt…?” Meforshim (plain sense): Rashi — when Israel sin, they make themselves, as it were, “like the Kushites” (dark) before Me; yet the very next words affirm that God redeemed them from Egypt and His bond to them endures. R’ Tzadok’s use: as long as the wicked of Israel remain “sunburnt and blackened,” the title “tzaddik” — the holiness of the body — does not yet rest upon them in this world; and he cites the received reading (see the following note) that the verse’s “Kushite” blackness is the blemish of the bris.Chassidic parallel - Likutei Moharan 14:3:6: R' Nachman states the root-point of this se'if with unusual directness: even the poshei Yisrael, so long as the name Yisrael is still said of them, remain Israel - 'af al pi shechata, Yisrael hu.' Precisely because they are still called 'sinners of Israel,' he says, they retain an achizah and shoresh in the supernal thought; an illumination from that root can reach the sinner and awaken teshuvah. This closely complements R' Tzadok's image of the thorn surrounding the rose. The sin is real - the person is called a poshe'a - but it does not become the ontological root from which the name Yisrael flows. The enduring root is what makes return possible rather than what makes repentance unnecessary. R' Tzadok pushes the same distinction into his discussion of the body and the bris: the outward blackening can be severe enough that the title tzaddik is not manifest in this world, yet the blemish remains a covering rather than the ultimate substance of Knesses Yisrael. Likutei Moharan helps state the logic of that claim without minimizing judgment: illumination comes from a root above the fall and summons the person back to it. The permanent Jewish name is therefore not a declaration that the deed was harmless; it is the theological reason that the deed need never be the final word about who the sinner is.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §1): “The essence of holiness is the holiness of the covenant [kedushas ha-bris], as they said in Vayikra Rabbah (24): ‘every place you find a fence against immorality [geder ervah], you find holiness’; as R’ Yehudah ben Pazi said, ‘anyone who fences himself from immorality is called holy.’” (This is the se’if’s reading of the Kedoshim haftarah: the holiness for which all Israel are called ‘holy’ is precisely the holiness of the bris — ‘wherever you find a fence against immorality, you find holiness.’)

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 2:3: “קֹדֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל לַה’, רֵאשִׁית תְּבוּאָתֹה, כָּל אֹכְלָיו יֶאְשָׁמוּ, רָעָה תָּבֹא אֲלֵיהֶם” — “Israel is holy to Hashem, the first of His produce; all who consume them will bear guilt, evil will befall them.” Meforshim: Rashi — Israel is God’s own consecrated portion, like terumah or the first-fruits, so that the nations who “consume” (harm) them are held guilty. R’ Tzadok’s use: the prooftext that “in truth all Israel are holy” — their essential holiness is inviolable, and any nation that presumes upon them is punished.

notes.body_html: Amos 9:9: the prophet’s closing vision — “כִּי הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה וַהֲנִעוֹתִי בְכָל הַגּוֹיִם אֶת בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל, כַּאֲשֶׁר יִנּוֹעַ בַּכְּבָרָה, וְלֹא יִפּוֹל צְרוֹר אָרֶץ” — “for behold, I command, and I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations, as [grain] is shaken in a sieve, yet not a pebble shall fall to the ground.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — like a sieve that retains the kernels while only dust and chaff fall through, Israel is sifted among the nations, yet no worthy one is lost. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the assurance that in all the scattering “no spark is lost” — the ingathering gathers even the scattered sparks (of “wasted seed”) from the four corners, so that “not even one pebble falls to the ground, and no outcast is banished from Him.”

notes.body_html: Devarim 11:12: of Eretz Yisrael — “אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר ה’ אֱלֹהֶיךָ דֹּרֵשׁ אֹתָהּ, תָּמִיד עֵינֵי ה’ אֱלֹהֶיךָ בָּהּ” — “a land which Hashem your God seeks out; the eyes of Hashem your God are always upon it.” Meforshim: Rashi — God’s providence rests upon the Land continually; the Sages (Kesubos 110b and the doresh midrash) that Eretz Yisrael is under His direct, unmediated care. R’ Tzadok’s use: the phrase “the land Hashem seeks out” alludes to the “supernal Land,” the true and proper recipient of the shefa (flow); hence the flow belongs there, and its temporary descent outside the Land — absorbed by the nations — “was not fixed to remain so.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְכֵיוָן דְּ״עַל פִּי ה׳ יַחֲנוּ וְעַל פִּי ה׳ יִסָּעוּ״ כְּסוֹתֵר עַל מְנָת לִבְנוֹת בִּמְקוֹמוֹ הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק בַּמֶּה מַדְלִיקִין] גַּבֵּי מִשְׁכָּן
notes.body_html: Bamidbar 9:23: of the cloud upon the Mishkan in the wilderness — “עַל פִּי ה’ יַחֲנוּ וְעַל פִּי ה’ יִסָּעוּ” — “by the word of Hashem they would encamp, and by the word of Hashem they would journey.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Ramban — every encampment and every journey was dictated by God through the cloud, never by the people’s own initiative. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel’s exilic “journeys” are, like the Mishkan’s, “one who dismantles in order to rebuild in [another] place” (Shabbos 31b) — a purposeful relocation by Hashem’s word, not a banishment, so that the holiness travels with them.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְכֵן בִּכְלַל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לָאָרֶץ שֶׁהֵם דּוּגְמַת הַמִּשְׁכָּן, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ ״שׁוֹכֵן אִתָּם בְּתוֹךְ טוּמְאוֹתָם״, וּשְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּקֶרֶב הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
notes.body_html: Vayikra 16:16: of the Yom Kippur purgation of the Sanctuary — “וְכֵן יַעֲשֶׂה לְאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד הַשֹּׁכֵן אִתָּם בְּתוֹךְ טֻמְאֹתָם” — “so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them amid their impurity.” Meforshim: Rashi — even when Israel are impure, the Shechinah remains among them. R’ Tzadok’s use: since Hashem “dwells with them amid their impurity,” His Shechinah is exiled with Israel and rests “within the hearts of the Children of Israel”; therefore each place of exile is sanctified, and “there became their place.”Chassidic context - Be'er Mayim Chaim, Bereishis 1:2:7: The Be'er Mayim Chaim explains Chazal's statement that Israel were exiled among the nations 'so that converts be added to them' in the kabbalistic sense of holy nitzotzos. The sparks themselves are in exile. When Israel enter a foreign place, the holy vitality there is drawn to them by spiritual affinity - 'matza min es mino vene'or,' like a small flame absorbed into a greater fire - and when Israel leave, they carry that vitality out. He reads 'es asher shalat ha'adam be'adam l'ra lo' in the Arizal's sense: the temporary dominion of the side of kelipah is ultimately 'for its own harm,' because the holiness it swallowed will be forced to come out with Israel. This gives a very concrete Chassidic background to R' Tzadok's assertion that exile itself becomes part of the birur and that no holy spark can be finally lost. The holiness of Israel is not dissolved by geographic dispersion; rather, precisely because the Shechinah remains with them 'betoch tum'osam,' their presence can draw out what is secretly akin to holiness in the place of exile. The point is not that exile is good in its revealed pain, but that Divine providence refuses to allow dispersion to be spiritually sterile. What looked like Israel being swallowed among the nations becomes, at the end of the process, 'chayil bala vayeki'enu' - the captor is compelled to release the holy life that had been hidden within it.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [עח] וְזֶהוּ שְׁלֵימוּת הַתִּיקּוּן דְּבַיּוֹם הַהוּא ״אָקִים אֶת סוּכַּת דָּוִד הַנּוֹפֶלֶת״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״וְנִגַּשׁ [חוֹרֵשׁ בַּקּוֹצֵר]״ ״וְדוֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים [בְּמוֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע]״, וְדָרְשׁוּ רַז״ל עַל יְהוּדָה וְיוֹסֵף
notes.body_html: Amos 9:11: the closing consolation of Amos — “בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אָקִים אֶת סֻכַּת דָּוִיד הַנֹּפֶלֶת… וּבְנִיתִיהָ כִּימֵי עוֹלָם” — “on that day I will raise up the fallen sukkah of David, and wall up its breaches, and raise up its ruins, and build it as in days of old.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — the Messianic restoration of the House of David; the Gemara (Sanhedrin 96b–97a) speaks of the coming of “ben David” and this “fallen sukkah.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is “the perfection of the rectification” — the tikkun completed when the Davidic line (Yehudah, joined to Yosef’s guarded bris) is fully raised up.

notes.body_html: Amos 9:13: “הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים… וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ בַּקֹּצֵר וְדֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים בְּמֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע” — “behold, days are coming… when the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes the sower of seed.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — the plain sense of overflowing abundance (each labor running straight into the next); and the Sages expounded the pair “treader of grapes” and “sower of seed” upon Yehudah and Yosef. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the sower of seed [moshech hazera]” alludes to the guardian of the bris — Yosef, who “draws his seed to its proper place and lets nothing flow to the outer forces”; while Yehudah’s beginning (Er, “a treader of grapes”) appeared its very opposite, until the rectification makes the two meet.

notes.body_html: Niddah 31a: R’ Abahu expounded: what is [the meaning of] “who has counted the dust of Yaakov, and the number of the rova of Israel” (Bamidbar 23:10)? It teaches that the Holy One sits and counts the revi’iyos of Israel, [awaiting] when the drop from which a tzaddik will be formed shall come. And over this matter the eye of Bilaam the wicked was blinded. He said, “shall He who is pure and holy, and whose ministers are pure and holy, gaze at this?!” — immediately his eye was blinded, as it is written (Bamidbar 24:3), “the utterance of the man whose eye is blocked [shesum ha’ayin].”

notes.body_html: Iyov 24:15: “וְעֵין נֹאֵף שָׁמְרָה נֶשֶׁף לֵאמֹר לֹא תְשׁוּרֵנִי עָיִן” — “and the eye of the adulterer watches for twilight, saying, ‘no eye shall behold me’.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Ralbag — the adulterer waits for dusk so that no eye should see him; the verse locates the sin in the eye. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the essence of adultery is in the eye,” for “the eye sees and the heart covets”; this is why guarding the eyes (Bamidbar 15:39) is the fence of chastity, and why Bilaam, who fancied himself “pure of eyes,” was struck blind.

notes.body_html: Yoma 74b: expounding “טוֹב מַרְאֵה עֵינַיִם מֵהֲלָךְ נָפֶשׁ” — “better is the seeing of the eyes than the wandering of desire” (Koheles 6:9) — Reish Lakish taught, “the sight of a woman is better [more affecting] than the very act.” Meforshim: Rashi — the eye’s beholding stirs desire even more than the deed itself. R’ Tzadok’s use: a further proof that “the essence of coveting is from the eye”; hence the eye is precisely where the yetzer does its work, and where the nations “stretch out the hooves” — displaying a pure-eyed exterior exactly where their root is worst, while Israel’s apparent evil is only the outward crust over a good root.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Tiferet Yosef, Hoshana Rabba 2: Tiferet Yosef develops the Davidic power of 'Sukkas David hanofeles' in language that closely matches R' Tzadok's treatment of Yehudah and David here. He explains 'chasdei David hane'emanim' as the illumination by which Hashem can later show that actions which appeared to be lacking light were, at their root, full of Divine light and holiness. David's distinctive strength is his radical self-surrender to Hashem; because he does not claim even the spiritual benefit of his own avodah, he can descend to places whose outer garment looks barren and then raise the actions of Israel that seem to possess no light. This is why Mashiach can be called bar nafli - the son of falling - and yet be the one who raises the fallen sukkah. The parallel fits R' Tzadok's use of Er, Yehudah, the serpent's counsel and the Davidic line. The early appearance can be the inverse of the final form; the 'fall' belongs to the garment in which the building first enters history, while the completed Malchus discloses what Divine purpose was being carried through that history. Yet Tiferet Yosef's emphasis on bittul is essential: the hidden light is not something a person may declare about his own questionable conduct in advance. It is Hashem who later illuminates the concealed root. The Davidic power is therefore not license to trust an apparent fall, but the capacity - after surrender and clarification - to reveal that even a fallen garment can be raised into the enduring house of David.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §6): “From them flow the two inclinations of jealousy and desire, which are two opposites: for one who is a ‘man of desire’ [baal taavah] is [by nature] good to [his fellow] creatures. And among the nations this appears to the outward eye — one whose eye is good to others and who has love for them; and this is the matter of the mitzvah of ‘sending portions’ [mishloach manos] — to declare that this [generosity] too is in truth only in Israel alone. For the love and ‘good eye’ of the nations toward their fellows is, likewise, only for some ulterior motive, for their own benefit.” (Exactly the se’if’s principle: ‘a man of desire is good-eyed’ — but only in Israel’s root do the traits interconnect wholly for the good, whereas in the nations the very same ‘good eye’ is self-serving, the reverse.)

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 40:26: “שְׂאוּ מָרוֹם עֵינֵיכֶם וּרְאוּ מִי בָרָא אֵלֶּה, הַמּוֹצִיא בְמִסְפָּר צְבָאָם” — “lift up your eyes on high and see who created these — He who brings out their host by number.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — raise your eyes to the heavens and recognize, from the ordered march of the stars, the Creator who marshals them each by name; a summons to awe of God through beholding His handiwork. R’ Tzadok’s use: the eye of the Jew “has no true pleasure except through” this looking-upward — and thereby he attains yirah (fear), the very letters of re’iyah (seeing), so that the faculty of desire itself is turned into the faculty of fear, “which draws after it love and pleasure,” whose object is the Holy One Himself.

notes.body_html: Bereishis 20:11: when Avimelech asks Avraham why he had called Sarah his sister, Avraham answers — “כִּי אָמַרְתִּי רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה, וַהֲרָגוּנִי עַל דְּבַר אִשְׁתִּי” — “for I said, surely there is no fear of God in this place, and they will slay me over the matter of my wife.” Meforshim: Rashi — where there is no fear of God, nothing restrains a place from desire and bloodshed; yiras Elokim is the fence that holds a society back from such sin. R’ Tzadok’s use: from here it is “known” that “even a ‘bad fear’ and the fear of punishment nullifies evil desires” — and all the more the fear of Heaven of Israel, which is “the ultimate of their pleasure” and “draws after it love.”Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 1: Tanya offers a parallel - though not identical - map for the structure R' Tzadok describes here. The Alter Rebbe teaches that every Jew, tzaddik or rasha, possesses two souls. The animal soul of Israel comes from kelipas nogah, which contains an admixture of good; even natural traits such as rachmanus and gemilus chasadim can therefore arise from it. He also traces the negative middos to different elements within that animal vitality: anger and pride to fire, appetite to water, frivolity and self-display to air, and lethargy and sadness to earth. The significance for this se'if is twofold. First, middos that appear separate on the surface are branches of one underlying life, which helps explain R' Tzadok's insistence that 'all the evils are connected' and, more deeply, that the good traits of Israel are interconnected at their root. Second, Tanya distinguishes the Jewish animal soul, whose kelipas nogah itself contains good, from the spiritual source he assigns to the nations. R' Tzadok uses a different terminology - body, nefesh, ruach and the uniquely holy neshamah - so the systems should not be mechanically identified. But both refuse to judge the spiritual root from a single visible middah. Bilaam can display an outward restraint while carrying ayin ra'ah, nefesh rechavah and ruach gevohah together within; conversely, the mixed outer life of a Jew can contain a good root that the revealed appearance has not yet disclosed.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [פ] וְדַרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּ״אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳״ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״טוֹב רֳאִי״
notes.body_html: 1 Shmuel 16:12: at the anointing of David, “וַיִּשְׁלַח וַיְבִיאֵהוּ וְהוּא אַדְמוֹנִי עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם וְטוֹב רֹאִי” — “and he sent and brought him; and he was ruddy, with fair eyes and goodly to look upon.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak note his beauty as a mark of fitness for kingship; and the Midrash contrasts David’s “ruddy… yet with fair eyes” (who would shed blood only by the ruling of the Sanhedrin) with Esav’s mere ruddiness. R’ Tzadok’s use: David’s rung is “a woman who fears Hashem” (Mishlei 31:30), the receiving Malchus — and “of fair eyes / goodly to look upon” marks that his “desire” was never for a passing pleasure but for the mate fit for him since the six days of Creation, the wellspring of the eternal Davidic throne.Chassidic context - Agra DeKala, Matos 47; cf. Be'er Mayim Chaim, Tazria 13:2:2: Agra DeKala takes Chazal's statement that Bas Sheva was destined for David 'from the six days of Creation' and explains it through Malchus itself. David, he says, was not seeking an ordinary human pleasure; he perceived that Bas Sheva belonged to the enduring inheritance of Malchus, the mother of Shlomo and the doorway through which the Davidic kingship would be built. The later opening of the Temple gates in Shlomo's day became a retrospective clarification: only through invoking David did the gates open, revealing publicly that David was a merkavah for Malchus and that this bond had a primordial root. That formulation is a close complement to R' Tzadok's contrast between a passing hana'as sha'ah and a desire attached to what endures forever. The Be'er Mayim Chaim adds the necessary boundary. He too cites 're'uyah hayesah Bas Sheva l'David misheshes yemei Bereishis,' but immediately stresses the language 'ela she'achalah pagah' - the matter was premature - and warns emphatically that no person may say, 'I will sin in order to reach higher teshuvah,' for 'echtah ve'ashuv' blocks repentance. This pairing is especially important in the present context. A hidden destined root can be revealed after the fact in David's unique history; it never authorizes a person prospectively to override the revealed will of Torah. The eternal quality R' Tzadok identifies is known through the completed Davidic building, not through a private claim made at the moment of desire.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §54): “only that all is in nature; and behold, the rung of Yitzchak is the Name Elokim — meaning that the natural governance too is watched over by Hashem, and He directs it.” Exactly the se’if: David’s “desire” was for the mate fitted to him since Creation — a pairing set within the natural order itself, which is precisely why it is not called iniquity.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §59): “how many strings were in the harp? Seven — like all the matters of this world: seven days in a week, seven years in a shemitah, seven shemitos in a yovel, corresponding to the seven days of building; for the world was lacking Shabbos — and in the days of Mashiach [there will be eight].” Exactly the se’if: David’s longing is not for the pleasure of an hour but for the eighth string — the rung that this world’s sevenfold order does not yet contain.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §52): “"head [from Ephraim]" — this is the rung of Yosef, the binding and unifying of the whole congregation, for they are all holy… but Yehudah is the completeness of the deed.” Exactly the se’if: David’s “desire” belongs to the completeness of the deed, not to a passing pleasure — which is why what would be iniquity in another is not called iniquity in him.

notes.body_html: Yalkut HaMachiri, Tehillim 118 (on Tehillim 51:7): Yishai separated from his wife for three years. Then, desiring a fair maidservant, he told her, “prepare yourself tonight, that you may come to me with a bill of freedom.” The maid told her mistress [Yishai’s wife], “save yourself, and me, and our master from Gehinnom,” and revealed it; the mistress said, “prepare yourself, and so will I.” That night the maid extinguished the lamp, and when Yishai’s wife came to the door, the mistress entered and the maid went out; she was with him all night and conceived David. Because of his love for that maidservant, David came out “ruddy,” and his brothers wished to kill him and his mother — until Yishai said, “leave him to be our servant and shepherd.” When Hashem sent Shmuel to “Yishai the Bethlehemite,” Yishai said, “there yet remains the youngest, tending the flock”; when Shmuel came, the oil bubbled up and Hashem said, “arise, anoint him, for this is he.” And David’s mother “rejoiced within and grieved without,” until, when “he took the cup of salvations,” all rejoiced.

notes.body_html: Bamidbar 30:6: in the laws of vows — when a father annuls his daughter’s vow on the day he hears it — “וַה’ יִסְלַח לָהּ כִּי הֵנִיא אָבִיהָ אֹתָהּ” — “and Hashem will forgive her, for her father restrained her.” Meforshim: Rashi (from the Sifrei; and the Gemara, Kiddushin 81b) — the verse speaks of one who intended a forbidden thing but was, unknown to her, already permitted, and still requires atonement — “if this one needs forgiveness, all the more so one who [truly] sinned.” R’ Tzadok’s use: even had Yishai merely “chanced upon his own wife,” thinking her the maid, Scripture would still call it a sin needing forgiveness — proof that his act was no sin at all, but the amah ha’Ivriah case, where he could have designated her as wife, sensing she was not his true mate.

notes.body_html: Devarim 17:14: of the future request for a king — “כִּי תָבֹא אֶל הָאָרֶץ… וְאָמַרְתָּ אָשִׂימָה עָלַי מֶלֶךְ כְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר סְבִיבֹתָי” — “when you come to the land… and you say, ‘let me set a king over me, like all the nations that surround me’.” Meforshim: the Ramban and the Sifrei debate whether this is a mitzvah or a concession to the people’s request; and the phrase “like all the nations” flags that mundane kingship is, in essence, a gentile institution. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the matter of kingship pertains only to the nations, for the Children of Israel have no king but the Holy One”; hence the following verse’s “som tasim” — Israel’s king is only “what they themselves set up and accept upon themselves.”

notes.body_html: Tzefaniah 3:9: of the Future — “כִּי אָז אֶהְפֹּךְ אֶל עַמִּים שָׂפָה בְרוּרָה, לִקְרֹא כֻלָּם בְּשֵׁם ה’ לְעׇבְדוֹ שְׁכֶם אֶחָד” — “for then I will transform the peoples to a pure tongue, that they all call in the name of Hashem, to serve Him with one accord.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — in the Messianic era the nations’ speech and worship will be purified, all serving God together. notes.body_html: Mishlei 12:4: “אֵשֶׁת חַיִל עֲטֶרֶת בַּעְלָהּ, וּכְרָקָב בְּעַצְמוֹתָיו מְבִישָׁה” — “a woman of valor is the crown of her husband, but one who shames is like rot in his bones.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Ralbag — a worthy wife is her husband’s crown and glory; the Sages read the verse also of the Torah and of the God-fearing soul. R’ Tzadok’s use: the kings of Israel — “to whom He apportioned of His honor to those who fear Him, who have nothing of their own” — are the very “woman who fears Hashem,” the Malchus that “crowns her husband,” receiving all from Above and keeping nothing for itself; hence David is “king of Israel,” who absorbs the flow from Israel and bestows nothing upon the nations. Izhbitz-Radzin context - Sod Yesharim, Eighth Day of Pesach 2:1: R. Gershon Henoch of Radzin develops precisely the paradox of Malchus on which R' Tzadok is building. Malchus, he writes, is the final middah and 'leis lah migarmah klum' - it has nothing from itself - yet the essential act of Jewish kingship is that Israel crown Hashem through their own bechirah while living inside the concealment of this world. The person experiences his good choice as his own acquired 'kav,' and only after it has truly entered his possession is he taught to return even that acquisition to Hashem, recognizing that the very capacity to recognize and choose was itself illuminated by Him. Thus bittul does not abolish bechirah; it is its culmination. The same passage applies this to worldly possession: one who recognizes that even after something reaches his hand it has not passed from the Reshus of Hashem becomes a trustworthy vessel for blessing. This is a particularly exact complement to the present description of malchei Yisrael. Their kingship is not an autonomous transfer of Divine kavod to 'flesh and blood,' as though a second center of power had been created. It is the middah that receives everything and returns everything to its Source, 'eishes chayil ateres ba'alah.' David's Malchus can therefore be supremely powerful while remaining 'leis lei migarmei klum': the more completely the king receives the life of Israel and owns none of it independently, the more fully the kingship itself becomes a revelation of Malchus Shamayim. Sod Yesharim thus supplies the Izhbitz grammar for R' Tzadok's contrast between gentile sovereignty, which appears as independent possession, and Jewish Malchus, whose deepest acquisition is the knowledge that even its acquired power never left Hashem's domain.

notes.body_html: Devarim 16:19: in the charge to judges — “לֹא תִקַּח שֹׁחַד, כִּי הַשֹּׁחַד יְעַוֵּר עֵינֵי חֲכָמִים וִיסַלֵּף דִּבְרֵי צַדִּיקִם” — “you shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous.” Meforshim: Rashi — once a judge accepts a bribe he can no longer see the case straight, for his heart inclines toward the giver; the verse teaches that any self-interest blinds even the wisest. R’ Tzadok’s use: “every error comes about through some self-interest [negi’ah] in the heart,” which is “like the bribe that blinds the eyes of the wise” — so that even a great man like Yishai, but for the flicker of “intent for his own pleasure,” would have attained the truth; the faintest personal stake bends the mind’s sight.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §14): “the yetzer hara does not entice a person to commit a transgression, but to perform a mitzvah — for it beautifies the transgression to him as though it were a mitzvah that he must pursue.” Exactly the se’if: desire is not an alien intruder but the very engine of pursuit — which is why without it “one does not beget at all,” and why the Torah itself is acquired only through it.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְאִם לֹא בְּתַאֲוָה כָּל כָּךְ יִהְיֶה עָצֵל וְסָכָל, וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּתַאֲוָה כְּלָל לֹא יוֹלִיד כְּלָל
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §35): “As they said in Yoma (69b), that when they captured the yetzer of forbidden relations, ‘no egg was found’ [lo ishtakach beitza] — [all birth ceased]. And the yetzer of forbidden relations is the sinking into idle imagination, like sleep; and this is what will not be entirely nullified even in the Future, as the Zohar writes — for were it not [for some residue of desire], ‘the craving for Torah would not be found’ either.” (This is the se’if’s naturalist principle carried to its root: ‘without desire, there is no birth’ — so that even the Future retains a measure of desire, redirected as the ‘craving for Torah.’) Chassidic context - Be'er Mayim Chaim, Tazria 13:2:2: The Be'er Mayim Chaim gives a remarkably close account of why the force of a middah is not itself the enemy. Discussing the Rambam's therapeutic uprooting of anger and pride, he distinguishes what he calls a lower teshuvah from a higher teshuvah. For the higher return it is not sufficient merely to stop using a powerful desire in the old direction; the person must take the very middah and its heat and turn it into avodas Hashem. He explains David's 'vechatasi negdi tamid' in this sense: David remembers the intensity and burning with which the inclination once drew him, so that the same force can now become an intense longing for Torah, mitzvos and closeness to Hashem. The defect is not the existence of energy, yearning or fire, but its object and its corrupted form. This directly illuminates R' Tzadok's definition of yetzer as 'chashkus halev' - a strong movement of desire that can be good or evil - and his insistence that the root-power will not simply disappear in the Future. What must disappear is the zuhama; the power itself is whitened and redirected. The Be'er Mayim Chaim also supplies an essential boundary for reading the se'if: he immediately warns that no one may deliberately sin in order to attain the superior intensity of teshuvah, for 'echtah ve'ashuv' is itself a corruption of avodah. The transformation is retrospective and therapeutic. Prospectively, the task is to govern the desire according to Torah; after a fall, teshuvah can reveal that the same human force that gave energy to the sin can be reclaimed as the very energy of holiness.

notes.body_html: From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): the teaching R’ Tzadok “heard” — that Yosef was “clean of desire and never came to any emission,” the paradigm of the guarded tzaddik — is his rebbe’s, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz (see §8 above). Navi context - Be'er Moshe on I Melachim 11:26: On the very verse cited here concerning Yerovam ben Nevat, the Be'er Moshe (ad loc., p. 198 of the uploaded Melachim volume) brings Sanhedrin 101b: 'Why did Yerovam merit kingship? Because he rebuked Shlomo; and why was he punished? Because he rebuked him publicly.' He uses this as a paradigm of 'mishpetei Hashem emes tzadku yachdav': one and the same historical act can contain a point deserving reward and another point deserving punishment, because Divine judgment weighs intention, substance and mode with the precision of a hair's breadth. The rebuke of Shlomo was, in itself, a good act and earned Yerovam kingship; the public manner, which amounted to raising a hand against Malchus Beis David, carried its own punishment. This is especially helpful beside R' Tzadok's treatment of Yerovam. The se'if is not presenting him as a flat villain: he could be extraordinarily clean in one sphere, find favor with Achiyah HaShiloni, and still be undone by jealousy and the form in which his opposition to Yehudah emerged. Be'er Moshe's reading of the exact Navi passage gives the same non-binary structure in legal-moral terms: genuine virtue in an act does not cancel its defect, and a defect does not require denying the genuine virtue that was also present. That makes Yerovam an apt illustration of R' Tzadok's broader thesis that future birur does not rewrite responsibility; it separates intertwined strands until the true good can be acknowledged without disguising the point that required judgment.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §63): “for the mon was by miracle, and it is deducted from one’s merits — unlike in Egypt, where it was natural food, which is [truly]”free“; and this is "now our soul [is dry]."” Exactly the se’if: what is at issue is the misuse of the permitted — for even a wholly permitted sustenance is reckoned against a person, and it is precisely there that the unwritten prohibition lies.

notes.body_html: Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 1: וכן למוציא זרע לבטלה, שחייב מיתה בידי שמים, כמו שכתוב בתורה גבי ער ואונן, ודינו כחייבי כריתות לענין זה The Baal HaTanya reaches the identical pairing on which this se’if turns — the iniquity of wasting seed, established from Er and Onan rather than from any explicit prohibition — and likewise treats the fasts prescribed for it in the mussar works as a means “to be saved from sufferings,” not as the mitzvah of teshuvah itself. Direct Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 7: The Tanya contains an unusually exact parallel to the distinction R' Tzadok makes in this se'if. The Alter Rebbe explains that vitality invested in permitted physical matters derives from kelipas nogah and is therefore capable of being raised when the person returns to avodas Hashem. He then turns explicitly to the vitality in drops of seed emitted wastefully and states that, although it descends into the side of impurity, it can be raised through proper teshuvah. He adds the striking textual point: 'therefore the sin of wasting seed is not mentioned in the Torah among the forbidden unions, even though it is more severe than them' in the quantity of impurity it generates. The reason he gives is structural: in forbidden unions the vitality becomes bound in a form of kelipah from which ordinary teshuvah cannot simply lift it, whereas in wasted seed the vitality is clothed and held differently and therefore remains capable of ascent. R' Tzadok's formulation is not identical to Tanya's kabbalistic mechanics, but the convergence is extraordinary. Both notice the same absence from the Torah's explicit list of arayos, both refuse to infer leniency from that absence, and both understand the absence as pointing to a different relation between the fallen spark and its possible return. Tanya thereby gives an important control on R' Tzadok's provocative language: the point is certainly not that the act is permitted - the Alter Rebbe calls it severe - but that severity and metaphysical irretrievability are not synonyms. The Torah's silence can therefore coexist with grave culpability while still intimating that the spark is not, in ultimate truth, an eternal nidach.

notes.body_html: Sukkah 5b: discussing the faces of the Keruvim, the Gemara asks — “what is [the face of] a cherub [keruv]? R’ Abahu said: like [that of] a child [ke-ravya], for in Babylonia they call a child ‘ravya’.” Meforshim: Rashi — the cherubs bore the faces of children; and the Gemara resolves the verse “the face of the keruv… the face of a man” (Yechezkel 10:14) as the small face of a child versus the large face of an adult. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “keruv” denotes a child, the “Keruvim and the ever-turning flaming sword to guard the way to the Tree of Life” (Bereishis 3:24) allude to the “sin of youth [chatas ne’urim]” — for “the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (Bereishis 8:21), and in childhood no one, save Eliyahu (an angel from his very origin), is wholly clean of desire.
