notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (תַּעֲנִית ד.) דְּ״אוֹרַיְיתָא מַרְתְּחָא לֵיהּ״, דְּהִנֵּה ״כֹּה דְבָרַי כָּאֵשׁ״, וְהֵם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹקִים חַיִּים וְיֵשׁ בָּזֶה חַיִּים וְתוֹסֶפֶת חִיּוּת
notes.body_html: Taanis 4a: “Rava said: If a young Torah scholar [tzurva mei-rabbanan] grows hot-tempered, it is the Torah within him that makes him seethe [Oraisa hi de-ka marsecha lei], as it says (Yirmeyah 23:29), ‘is not My word like fire?’” Chabad clarification - Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25:30: The Alter Rebbe draws almost the exact distinction needed for R' Tzadok's discussion of anger. He returns to Chazal's statement that anger is 'like serving avodah zarah' and explains that this applies to ordinary worldly matters: 'hakol bidei Shamayim chutz miyiras Shamayim,' so rage at the human agent treats that agent as though he possessed autonomous power outside Divine providence. But he then explicitly limits the rule: in 'mili diShmaya,' where one must separate another from prohibition, this reasoning does not apply, and he cites the very Torah expression 'vayiktzof Moshe.' Thus the Tanya does not flatten every manifestation of anger into one category. There is an anger born of wounded selfhood and denial of hashgachah, and there can be a forceful response whose entire content is responsibility to the revealed will of Hashem. This sharpens the present se'if's use of 'Oraisa ka-martecha lei.' The fire of Torah can make the scholar seethe, but that does not sanctify personal irritability; it means that the same faculty of gevurah can be requisitioned by Torah when the situation truly calls for it. R' Tzadok's reading of Moshe then becomes even more precise: Moshe's anger was not wrong merely because anger is always evil. Its defect lay in the fact that at Mei Merivah the force did not match the particular Divine revelation of that moment. The prospective test is therefore exacting: holy anger is not whatever the righteous person feels intensely, but anger subordinated to the command and measure of Heaven.

notes.body_html: Bamidbar 20:10: at the waters of Merivah — “וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם שִׁמְעוּ נָא הַמֹּרִים, הֲמִן הַסֶּלַע הַזֶּה נוֹצִיא לָכֶם מָיִם” — “and he said to them, ‘listen now, O rebels; shall we bring forth water for you from this rock?’” Meforshim: Rashi — “ha-morim” means fools / rebels (some render it “those who would instruct their teachers”); the commentators dispute what precisely Moshe’s sin was — Rashi holds it was striking the rock instead of speaking to it, while the Rambam (Shemonah Perakim, ch. 4) holds it was the anger betrayed in “shimu na ha-morim.” R’ Tzadok’s use: he follows the anger-reading — “shimu na ha-morim” and the striking of the rock “were part of anger and wrath, not according to Hashem’s revealed will”; and so even Moshe, buried opposite Pe’or as the utter opposite of desire, “died through his [own] sin” (Shabbos 55b) — the flash of that anger — proof that no one born clean of desire escapes some deficiency of anger.

The Gemara challenges: it was taught that “four died [only] through the counsel of the serpent [b’etyo shel nachash], without sin of their own — Binyamin son of Yaakov, Amram father of Moshe, Yishai father of David, and Kilav son of David” — proving that there is death without sin and suffering without iniquity, and refuting Rav Ami.

notes.body_html: Mishlei 3:16: of Wisdom (the Torah) — “אֹרֶךְ יָמִים בִּימִינָהּ, בִּשְׂמֹאולָהּ עֹשֶׁר וְכָבוֹד” — “length of days is in her right hand; in her left, riches and honor.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Gemara (Shabbos 63a) — to those who engage the Torah for its own sake [lishmah] she grants “length of days” (her “right”), and even to those who do not, “riches and honor” (her “left”). R’ Tzadok’s use: “all the promises of the Torah are [couched as] length of days” — for the teshuvah of Yesod (the bris) redeems what would be death into “a lengthening of his days and years”; yet “a long thing still has an end, only that it is long” — unlike Yaakov, whose inheritance is “without bounds [bli meitzarim],” and who therefore “did not die at all.”

notes.body_html: From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): R’ Tzadok’s “I have received” — the interpretation of the language of the Tikkunei Zohar cited here — is a teaching of his rebbe, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz (see §8 above). Direct Izhbitz source - Mei HaShiloach I, Bereshit 6: The source from R' Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz is exceptionally close to R' Tzadok's language here. Commenting on the trees and rivers of Gan Eden, Mei HaShiloach identifies 'Etz HaChaim' with 'teshuvah amitis shemerape'os es hakodem' - true teshuvah that heals what came before. He returns to the point a second time: the river Peras corresponds to baalei teshuvah because 'teshuvah merape'es es hakodem,' and Peras reaches back to the first source; complete return therefore means arriving again at one's primordial shoresh. This sheds light on why R' Tzadok can put the Tree of Life, the bris and the repair of the past into one conceptual chain. Ordinary moral improvement moves forward from the present. Etz HaChaim-teshuvah reaches to the source from which the damaged history emerged and heals the prior deficiency at that root. At the same time, R' Tzadok is carefully distinguishing the measure in which that truth can be disclosed in this world: the full revelation of life without death is guarded, while teshuvah can already convert what would have produced death into arichus yamim. Mei HaShiloach therefore supplies the inner meaning of the 'Tree of Life' without requiring an overstatement about present experience. The baal teshuvah reaches the original river, while this-worldly revelation may still show mortality and temporal limits. This is also a fitting expansion of R' Tzadok's explicit 'kibalti' from his rebbe in the footnote: the Ishbitz teaching is not merely a biographical source but a direct conceptual gloss on his claim that true teshuvah is a healing of the earlier root.

Commenting on the trees and rivers of Gan Eden, Mei HaShiloach identifies 'Etz HaChaim' with 'teshuvah amitis shemerape'os es hakodem' - true teshuvah that heals what came before. He returns to the point a second time: the river Peras corresponds to baalei teshuvah because 'teshuvah merape'es es hakodem,' and Peras reaches back to the first source; complete return therefore means arriving again at one's primordial shoresh. This sheds light on why R' Tzadok can put the Tree of Life, the bris and the repair of the past into one conceptual chain. Ordinary moral improvement moves forward from the present. Etz HaChaim-teshuvah reaches to the source from which the damaged history emerged and heals the prior deficiency at that root. At the same time, R' Tzadok is carefully distinguishing the measure in which that truth can be disclosed in this world: the full revelation of life without death is guarded, while teshuvah can already convert what would have produced death into arichus yamim. Mei HaShiloach therefore supplies the inner meaning of the 'Tree of Life' without requiring an overstatement about present experience. The baal teshuvah reaches the original river, while this-worldly revelation may still show mortality and temporal limits. This is also a fitting expansion of R' Tzadok's explicit 'kibalti' from his rebbe in the footnote: the Ishbitz teaching is not merely a biographical source but a direct conceptual gloss on his claim that true teshuvah is a healing of the earlier root.

notes.body_html: Kesubos 104a: it is related that at Rebbi’s passing “he raised his ten fingers toward Heaven and said: Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that I toiled with my ten fingers in the Torah, and I derived no benefit from this world even with my small finger; may it be Your will that there be peace in my repose” — whereupon a Divine Voice proclaimed, “he enters in peace” (Yeshayah 57:2). Meforshim: Rashi — despite all his wealth and honor, Rebbi took no personal pleasure from this world; and the earlier commentators note the precision of “even with my little finger” (compare Pesachim 112b, “not all the fingers are alike”). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the mark of the rung of holiness, which stands above mere piety — Rebbi did not merely restrain pleasure but sanctified it, so that even within his enjoyment “he derived no benefit from this world”; and he was the one who clarified, in this world, the hidden holiness that belongs to all Israel. Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 7: Tanya's treatment of kelipas nogah helps define the kind of kedushah R' Tzadok attributes to Rebbi. The Alter Rebbe distinguishes a permitted physical act performed merely to satisfy the body's appetite from the same physical vitality used 'lehar'chiv da'ato laHashem uleSoraso' or for the mitzvah of Oneg Shabbos and Yom Tov. In the latter case the vitality of the food and wine is itself clarified and rises to Hashem 'ke'olah u'chekorban.' Even an ordinary word of humor can be elevated when its purpose is to open the mind and gladden the heart for Torah and avodah. This is more than abstinence. The physical thing, precisely because it belongs to the mixed and permitted realm, can become a carrier of holiness. That distinction closely complements R' Tzadok's assertion that kedushah is higher than chassidus. Rebbi's statement that he benefited from this world 'not even with the small finger' cannot mean that his wealthy table or bodily life literally did not exist; R' Tzadok reads it to mean that the enjoyment was not appropriated as an independent worldly end. In Tanya's terms, the vitality itself can be taken up into avodah. Thus the fence of the bris and the sanctification of permissible enjoyment are two sides of the same Yesod: first the power is guarded from prohibited dispersion, and then the permitted physical life is joined to its Divine purpose. Rebbi's holiness is therefore not a flight from embodiment but the clarification of embodiment until even pleasure no longer stands opposite avodas Hashem.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 98b: In the discussion of the Mashiach’s identity: “Rav said: if he is from among the living, it is one such as Rabbeinu HaKadosh [Rebbi]; if from among the dead, it is one such as Daniel, the treasured man.” Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 2:5: R' Tzadok's description of the Nasi as the 'head' who contains the full stature of his generation has a direct parallel in Tanya. The Alter Rebbe writes that although Jewish souls occupy innumerable levels, in every generation there are 'rashei alfei Yisrael' whose souls are literally the aspect of 'head and brain' in relation to the souls of the multitude, just as later generations can stand to earlier ones as heel to head. The metaphor is organic rather than merely administrative: one national body can contain radically different limbs while the head serves as the integrating consciousness of the whole. This makes R' Tzadok's inference from Rebbi's personal kedushah to the latent holiness of the generation much easier to follow. If the Nasi were only an unusually pious individual, his achievement would testify only about himself. If his neshamah is the rosh of the generational komah, a revelation concentrated in him can disclose what exists in potential throughout the body even before every limb has actualized it. The same structure explains the transition from Rebbi to Mashiach in this se'if. Rebbi represents 'tachlis hagilui bekoach': the head already carries the form of the whole and his Mishnah holds the later Oral Torah in seed. Mashiach is the stage at which that latent form spreads through the whole body 'bepo'al.' Tanya thus gives a close Chassidic analogue for the collective anthropology behind R' Tzadok's language, without implying that the moral state of every individual was already equal to Rebbi's; head and heel are not identical, but they belong to one living stature.

notes.body_html: Erchin 17a: On the verse “this is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face — Yaakov, selah” (Tehillim 24:6), R’ Yehudah Nesi’ah and the Rabbanan disagreed: one said “the generation [is] according to the leader [parnas],” and one said “the leader according to his generation.” The Gemara challenges [that this cannot concern their relative worthiness] — for there was Tzidkiyah, who was worthy though his generation was not, and Yehoyakim, who was not worthy though his generation was; “rather,” it concludes, “we speak with regard to tukfa (severity) and nichusa (mildness).”

notes.body_html: Sotah 49b (the closing Mishnah of the tractate; also as a baraisa, Avodah Zarah 20b): R’ Pinchas ben Yair’s ladder of ascent — a graded sequence of traits, from care and alacrity up through kedushah (holiness), “and holiness leads to [the higher rungs, culminating in] ruach hakodesh, and ruach hakodesh to the resurrection of the dead, and the resurrection of the dead comes through Eliyahu.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Maharsha trace the progressive self-refinement that opens onto the highest attainments. R’ Tzadok’s use: in his girsa (which he holds to be the primary one) kedushah is “the last of the [human] rungs” — the summit of a person’s own effort, which then brings him to ruach hakodesh, the coming of Eliyahu, and the resurrection; and Rebbi, “the holy one,” embodied this rung.

notes.body_html: Niddah 73a (the closing words of the entire Talmud): “the school of Eliyahu taught: whoever studies halachos every day is assured that he is destined for the World to Come, as it is stated, ‘his ways [halichos] are eternal’ (Chavakuk 3:6) — read not halichos [ways] but halachos.” Meforshim: Rashi — “halachos” denotes the fixed traditions (the Mishnah and baraisos); one who reviews them daily attains eternal life. R’ Tzadok’s use: “halachos” means the Mishnah (called “halachos”/“hilcheta” throughout Shas) — the Oral Torah, in which the Written Torah is grasped by Israel’s souls — and through it one merits “eternal life”; fittingly the Talmud seals itself with this very promise. Chassidic context - Tiferet Shlomo, Birkat HaTorah 8: The Tiferes Shlomo comments on the exact closing ma'amar of Shas, 'kol hashoneh halachos bechol yom muvtach lo shehu ben Olam Haba,' and reads 'hashoneh' dynamically. A person should 'change' the halachah each day by reaching a deeper and newer apprehension even in the very halachah he studied yesterday. He then joins the derashah 'al tikrei halichos ela halachos' back to its literal wording: through living halachah the student changes the 'halichos olam,' drawing new good flow into the world's conduct. 'Ben Olam Haba' consequently does not refer only to a reward postponed until death; Torah draws something of Olam Haba into the present day, renewing the world through fresh apprehension. This is a strong complement to R' Tzadok's use of the same passage. R' Tzadok stresses Mishnah as the form in which Torah Shebe'al Peh makes the Written Torah graspable to Jewish hearts and thereby opens chayei olam. Tiferes Shlomo adds the experiential mechanism: Oral Torah is not a static archive. The learner revisits fixed halachah and brings latent meaning into new actual apprehension, so that 'halachos' are literally 'halichos' - movement. That sits especially well with the se'if's description of the light hidden after the sin and recovered through toil in Torah Shebe'al Peh. The text is fixed, yet its stored light can be newly disclosed each day. The assurance of Olam Haba therefore belongs precisely to repeated study: what is eternal is not inert repetition but the unending capacity of Torah to yield new life from the same Divine source.

notes.body_html: Nedarim 22b: Rav Adda b’Rabbi Chanina taught, “had Israel not sinned, there would have been given to them only the Five Books of the Torah and the Book of Yehoshua alone — for it [Yehoshua] is the apportionment of Eretz Yisrael.” Meforshim: the Ran and the commentators — before the sin, the light of the Written Torah alone would have disclosed everything; only the Torah (the way of life) and the settling of the Land (Yehoshua) would have been required. R’ Tzadok’s use: at Sinai the Written Torah by itself would have sufficed — “the Torah is from the side of time and the soul, given in the wilderness, while the fixing of place is set out in the Book of Yehoshua” — but the sin concealed that light (like the primordial light stored away in the Torah), and its recovery is the whole work of the Oral Torah.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [פט] וְהִתְחִיל הִתְעוֹרְרוּת גִּילּוּי אוֹר זֶה בִּימֵי רַבִּי בְּחִבּוּר הַמִּשְׁנָה
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §64): “a rung that one is able to walk to, and no further; and as it says [Berachos 17a],”the righteous sit" — meaning and do not walk to a rung [beyond]." Exactly the se’if: the Mishnah is the one text in which every Jewish soul has its own fixed portion — each standing where his rung sets him, which is why its merit gathers all of them in together. Chassidic context - Arvei Nachal, Vayeshev 1:5: The Arvei Nachal supplies a strikingly direct explanation for R' Tzadok's claim that the roots of Jewish souls and the Oral Torah belong together. He writes that every Jew has a particular achizah and deveikus of his neshamah in Torah; one soul's portion cannot be supplied by another, even by someone greater. This is why, at times, a lesser talmid chacham can say a Torah insight that a greater sage cannot: 'bekartelisa de'anya tishkach marganisa' - a pearl can be found in the poor man's basket - because that point is his own portion. The nitzotzos a person releases through Torah chiddush are therefore joined specifically to his soul. He connects this idea to the same promise, 'kol hashoneh halachos bechol yom muvtach lo shehu ben Olam Haba.' This makes a particularly organic addition to the present se'if. When R' Tzadok says the Mishnah includes the root of the souls and that later generations unfold Oral Torah according to their own souls, he is not merely saying that everyone studies a common book. The common corpus contains differentiated points waiting for the corresponding souls to draw them into actuality. The Mishnah can consequently be a gathering-place without erasing individuality: precisely because every soul has a non-interchangeable Torah point, the totality of those points forms one Torah Shebe'al Peh. The ingathering effected by Mishnah study is thus both communal and personal - no Jewish spark is superfluous, because no other soul can reveal exactly the same facet of the Divine Torah.

notes.body_html: Taanis 9a: R’ Yochanan, pondering a verse in Mishlei, wondered aloud, “is there anything written in the Writings [Kesuvim] that is not alluded to in the Torah?” — whereupon the young son of Reish Lakish showed him the allusion (in “their heart failed them… what is this that God has done to us,” Bereishis 42:28); the principle emerging is that everything in the later Scriptures is already hinted at in the Chumash. Meforshim: Rashi — R’ Yochanan sought, and was shown, that nothing in Nach lacks a root in the Five Books. R’ Tzadok’s use: he extends this — “there is nothing that is not hinted at in the Written Torah, only that it is there by allusion and concealment”; hence all the souls of the later generations (whose root is the Oral Torah, the expansion of the Written) lay “stored and concealed” within the wilderness generation, who received the Written Torah, “for from them they came forth.”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [צ] וְיָדוּעַ דְּעַל יְדֵי עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע, דְּגַם תּוֹרָה שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמּוּשֶּׂגֶת עַתָּה הוּא מִסִּטְרָא דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בַּתִּיקּוּנִים], נִמְסְרוּ הַרְבֵּה דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לַחִיצוֹנִים שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהוֹצִיא מֵהֶם
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §46): “In the Zohar (I 27a) they said that the Oral Torah is from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil — ‘valid and invalid,’ etc.; that is, the Tree of Knowledge is the human intellect, which has variations this way and that; but the Tree of Life is ‘in the midst of the garden,’ at the central point, which does not incline to the extremes — and that is the Written Torah.” (Precisely the se’if’s teaching: the Torah as it is grasped now, in this world, is ‘from the side of the Tree of Knowledge’ — its light dispersed toward the extremes, some of it needing to be ‘extracted’ back from the outer forces.) Chassidic parallel - Sefat Emet, Bo 18:2: The Sefas Emes reads the Egyptian exile itself as a preparation for Torah and explicitly distinguishes a written and an oral dimension within that process. The Divine 'signs' placed in Pharaoh correspond to what is given from Above, while 'lema'an tesaper' points to the human articulation and expansion of Torah Shebe'al Peh. He then states the governing principle: 'kol galus hu lehotzi nitzotzos kedoshos shenis'arvu bahem' - every exile exists to draw out holy sparks that became mixed among the nations. During exile those sparks are concealed and the wicked mistake the borrowed vitality for their own power; at redemption Israel remove the hidden illuminations for whose sake they were sent there, and it becomes clear that 'Ani Hashem' was the truth throughout. This is exceptionally close to R' Tzadok's image of Torah-words being handed to the chitzonim and later reclaimed. The frightening passages and even the words placed in the mouths of Lavan, Pharaoh, Bilaam and Balak become Torah not because their speakers were independent teachers of holiness, but because a Divine spark can be clothed in an alien voice and later gathered into the Torah of Israel. Sefas Emes also clarifies why extraction and redemption are one motion: once the good hidden in the foreign garment has been taken out, the apparent autonomous power of that garment collapses. R' Tzadok extends the same dynamic from the written record of the early exiles to the continuing development of Torah Shebe'al Peh; Sefas Emes gives the Chassidic language of nitzotz and geulah that makes that continuity explicit.

And here it said "in sichah" and not "in dibbur" — for we have said that words of Torah are called dibbur, unlike sichah [conversation].” Exactly the se’if’s distinction: what was handed to the outer forces went out as sichah, and the labor is to draw it back into dibbur.

notes.body_html: Avodah Zarah 2b (R’ Yochanan): expounding “Hashem came from Sinai, and shone forth from Seir upon them, appeared from Mount Paran” (Devarim 33:2; cf. Chavakuk 3:3), the Gemara asks what God “sought in Seir and in Paran,” and answers — “this teaches that the Holy One took the Torah round to every nation and tongue [Edom in Seir, Yishmael in Paran, and the rest], but they did not accept it, until He came to Israel, and they accepted it.” Meforshim: Rashi — each nation, offered the Torah, refused when a commandment clashed with its ancestral trait (Esav balked at “you shall not murder,” Yishmael at “you shall not steal”). R’ Tzadok’s use: the Holy One offered the Torah to every nation because “it too had some aspect of connection to it” — there are, within the nations, letters of Torah, “the spark that enlivens them”; but their root being in evil they refused, and those Torah-letters “were taken from them and given to Israel,” “the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov” — so that “a gentile who engages in the Torah is liable to death.”

notes.body_html: Avodah Zarah 2b: In the Future the Holy One will bring a Torah scroll, place it in His bosom, and say, “let whoever occupied himself with it come and take his reward.” The nations gather in confusion; He asks the kingdom of Rome first, “with what did you occupy yourselves?” They answer, “Master of the world — we established many marketplaces, built many bathhouses, amassed much silver and gold — and we did it all only for Israel, that they might occupy themselves with the Torah.” He replies, “fools of the world — all that you did, you did for your own needs: you set up marketplaces to place harlots in them, bathhouses to indulge yourselves; and the silver and gold are Mine, as it says, ‘Mine is the silver and Mine the gold’ (Chaggai 2:8). Is there any among you who declares this? — and ‘this’ is nothing but the Torah.” They depart crestfallen; the kingdom of Persia enters after them — and so with every kingdom.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [צא] אֲבָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא מַה שֶּׁחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹצְאִים מִלִּבָּם, דָּבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּיַד בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §26): “In truth they said (Midrash Rabbah, Eichah [2:9]): ‘there is Torah among the nations of the world — do not believe,’ for it is ‘the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov’ alone. And in the manner they said (Tanchuma, Ki Sisa 34), that ‘in the Future the nations will say, we are Israel,’ etc. — [the Torah is] ‘My mystery.’ And this is [the meaning of] the resting of the Shechinah: that they will not attain the wisdom of the Oral Torah.” (Exactly the se’if’s distinction: the Oral Torah is ‘the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov’ alone — ‘whoever says there is Torah among the nations, do not believe’ — for it is drawn from Israel’s own heart and is in Israel’s hand alone.) Chabad context - Likkutei Torah, Pinchas 4:11: Likkutei Torah gives a precise reason that Torah Shebe'al Peh cannot be reduced to human wisdom. 'Malchus peh Torah Shebe'al Peh karinan lah': the mouth/Malchus is called Oral Torah, and although Malchus 'leis lah migarmah klum,' it is the revelation of the innermost Divine will. Torah and mitzvos, the Alter Rebbe explains, are the pnimiyus ratzono, and that inner will descends all the way into the most physical details of the six orders of Mishnah in order to lift the lower world into its Source. Thus the human mouth and the concrete halachic case are not alternatives to revelation; they are the vessels through which the inner will becomes articulated below. This complements R' Tzadok's distinction between chochmah among the nations and Torah found in the heart of Israel. A philosopher can reach a true intellectual proposition and it remains chochmah. Torah Shebe'al Peh is a different category because its claim is not simply that the conclusion is clever or correct, but that the inward Divine ratzon is being disclosed through the covenantal mouth of Knesses Yisrael. This is also why its apparently mundane discussions do not make it less 'mistorin': the very descent into physical particulars is the form in which pnimiyus ratzon reaches the earthly realm. Likkutei Torah therefore supplies a Chabad parallel to R' Tzadok's Binah/Malchus language: the Oral Torah has no independent 'self' that could be duplicated by foreign philosophy, yet precisely as the receptive mouth of Israel it becomes the place where the hidden Divine will is spoken.

notes.body_html: Menachos 29b: R’ Yehudah Nesi’ah asked R’ Ami about the verse “trust in Hashem forever, for in Kah [the letters yod and heh] Hashem is the Rock of worlds” (Yeshayah 26:4) — why “b’Kah” rather than “Yah”? [The answer, expounded by R’ Yehudah bar R’ Il’ai:] these are the two worlds the Holy One created — one with a heh and one with a yod — derived from “these are the generations of the heavens and the earth b’hibar’am” (Bereishis 2:4): read not b’hibar’am but b’heh bera’am, “He created them with a heh” — hence this world was created with heh and Olam Haba with yod. And why was this world created with a heh? Because it resembles a portico [akhsadra], open below, so that whoever wishes to leave may leave. And why is its [left] leg suspended [not joined to the roof]? Because if one repents, he is brought back in [through the small upper opening]. And let him re-enter by the way he left? — that would not avail, as Reish Lakish taught: “if [one comes] to the scoffers, He scoffs at him; but to the humble He gives grace” (Mishlei 3:34) — one who comes to purify himself is assisted; one who comes to defile himself, an opening is made for him. And why does the heh have a crown [taga]? The Holy One says: if he returns, I bind a crown for him. Direct Chabad parallel - Likkutei Torah, Metzora 13: The Alter Rebbe formulates the symbolism of teshuvah in the very letters R' Tzadok is expounding: 'teshuvah' is 'tashuv hei legabei yud,' the return of the heh to the yud, and the 'hei ila'ah' is Binah. Sin produces a separation from the yud, the bittul of supernal Chochmah, and from that separation the chitzonim are able to draw nurture; teshuvah restores the upper heh to its relation with the yud. The immediate context in Likkutei Torah describes an awakening of ratzo and inner fire from mochin de'Imma followed by its reintegration into bittul - a return that is therefore not emotional escape but a repaired joining of Binah to its Source. This is almost the exact kabbalistic vocabulary of the present se'if. R' Tzadok reads Menachos' suspended heh as the architecture of the baal teshuvah: after exiting, he does not simply retrace the lower route but is assisted through the upper opening and crowned, corresponding to the hei ila'ah of Binah, 'libo yavin vashav.' Likkutei Torah gives the inner-letter mechanism for that ascent. The crown is not merely an honor added after repentance; the entire movement is a restoration of a severed higher relation. It also supports R' Tzadok's linking of teshuvah and Torah Shebe'al Peh: if the upper heh is Binah, then the return of the heart and the renewed expansion of Divine understanding are aspects of one repair. The greater the reintegration of Binah, the more the hidden light can flow from heart to articulated Torah rather than feeding what stands outside holiness.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [צג] וְיָדוּעַ דִּכְמוֹ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הָיָה רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים, כֵּן הָיָה דָּוִד רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל בַּעֲלֵי רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Noach §4): "“[one who] fears God” — the term “fear” is expounded of prayer and mercy; and so it is expounded, “who among you fears Hashem” — of one who regularly comes to the synagogue." Exactly the se’if: David is master of all possessors of ruach ha-kodesh — and the faculty at issue is the one that expresses itself in prayer, from which the whole spread of Torah afterward began. Izhbitz-Radzin context - Tiferet Yosef, Hoshana Rabba 2: Tiferet Yosef develops the distinction between seeing and hearing in a way that directly illuminates R' Tzadok's Davidic model of ruach hakodesh. Sight, he explains, takes in an external surface at once; hearing cannot receive two voices simultaneously, but it can penetrate to the depth of a matter. He reads 'hatu oznechem ulechu elai, shim'u u'sechi nafshechem... chasdei David hane'emanim' as a summons to incline the inner depth of the heart to Hashem and to follow the Divine light from its first ratzon down to the final action. When a person's inward ear is so directed, he can perceive that Hashem is continually occupied with forging an eternal covenant with Israel. He identifies this capacity with 'chasdei David': David's avodah can receive illumination even into actions whose outer garment appeared to lack light, because his inner life is surrendered to Hashem. This closely complements R' Tzadok's claim that after Moshe, master of prophecy, David becomes master of baalei ruach hakodesh and inaugurates a Torah that wells from awakened Binah in the heart. The shift is not from revelation to merely private creativity. It is from the visual clarity of prophecy to a deeper inward hearing that must be drawn through the heart and then articulated by sages. Tiferet Yosef thus helps explain why teshuvah and the growth of Torah Shebe'al Peh advance together from David onward: both require the heart to penetrate beneath the surface garment and receive the hidden Divine intention that can then become speech, teaching and renewed life.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וּמִמֶּנּוּ הַתְחָלַת הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַרְבָּצַת הַתּוֹרָה וְהַחָכְמָה בִּישִׁיבוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת וְתַלְמִידִים רַבִּים שֶׁלֹּא עַל יְדֵי נְבוּאָה, וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, שֶׁמִּמֶּנָּה בָּא לַהֲקָמַת עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §74): “"the face of Moshe was as the face of the sun" — whose light is from his own essence, and therefore it is never lacking — and so Moshe, even though Israel sinned with the Calf, [was told] "and I shall make you a great nation"; "the face of Yehoshua as the face of the moon" — his light from another.” Exactly the se’if’s pairing: Moshe is master of the prophets because his light is his own — and David stands in the corresponding place for the possessors of ruach ha-kodesh.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְעַל כֵּן נִתְגַּלָּה אָז כְּלָלוּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּחִבּוּר הַמִּשְׁנָה, דְּכוֹלֶלֶת בְּכֹחַ גַּם כָּל מַה שֶּׁיִּתְחַדֵּשׁ מֵחַכְמֵי הַדּוֹרוֹת אַחַר כָּךְ
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §3): “that they were revealing to me certain things from the root of my soul; and among the things they told me was that the generation of Mashiach will be those very souls of the generation of the wilderness.” Exactly the se’if: the line runs from the master of prophecy through the master of ruach ha-kodesh to the later sages — one continuous root reappearing, and not a succession of unrelated generations.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [צד] וְעַל כֵּן נִרְאֶה לִי דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלוּלוֹת בְּחִבּוּר הַמִּשְׁנָה, וְכֵן כְּלוּלִים בָּהּ גַּם כָּל הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁיִּקָּלְטוּ עַל יְדֵי הַגָּלֻיּוֹת בֵּין אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא קִיבּוּץ הַגָּלֻיּוֹת
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Sukkos §34): “the spreading of blessing in all matters — that even a coin becomes blessed, which is a thing outside the way of nature; and it is from the aspect of Aharon, as it says, "the beard of Aharon," which descends according to his measures like the dew of Chermon — "for there Hashem commanded the blessing: life forever."” Exactly the se’if: the ingathering and the length of days are one blessing, commanded where Israel are gathered together — “life forever,” at the place of joining.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: דְּאָז יִהְיוּ כָּל הָעַמִּים ״מִשְׂרְפוֹת סִיד״, וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים יֹאחֲזוּ בִּכְנַף אִישׁ יְהוּדִי וְיִהְיוּ גֵּרִים גְּרוּרִים כַּמְבוֹאָר בַּכְּתוּבִים וּבְדִבְרֵי רַז״ל
notes.body_html: Yeshayah 33:12: “וְהָיוּ עַמִּים מִשְׂרְפוֹת שִׂיד, קוֹצִים כְּסוּחִים בָּאֵשׁ יִצַּתּוּ” — “and the peoples shall be as the burnings of lime, as thorns cut down that are kindled in the fire.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — the nations who oppressed Israel will be consumed like lime in a kiln, like severed thorns cast to the flame. R’ Tzadok’s use: in the ingathering, once the holy sparks are reclaimed from the nations, “all the peoples will be ‘burnings of lime’” — drained of the vitality the indwelling spark had lent them — while “those who remain grasp the corner of a Jew’s garment” and become attached converts.

notes.body_html: Zechariah 8:23: “כֹּה אָמַר ה’ צְבָאוֹת… אֲשֶׁר יַחֲזִיקוּ עֲשָׂרָה אֲנָשִׁים מִכֹּל לְשֹׁנוֹת הַגּוֹיִם, וְהֶחֱזִיקוּ בִּכְנַף אִישׁ יְהוּדִי לֵאמֹר: נֵלְכָה עִמָּכֶם, כִּי שָׁמַעְנוּ אֱלֹהִים עִמָּכֶם” — “in those days ten men of all the languages of the nations shall take hold of the corner of the garment of a Jewish man, saying: let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — in the Messianic age the nations will cling to Israel, recognizing that the Divine Presence rests upon them. R’ Tzadok’s use: “those who remain of the nations will grasp the corner of a Jewish man’s garment and become ‘attached converts [geirim gerurim].’”

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְאָז יִתְגַּלּוּ כָּל מַדְרֵיגוֹת הַתְּשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲלוֹתֶיהָ בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת גָּלוּי בְּפֹעַל, וּמִמַּדְרֵגַת הַאֲרָכַת שָׁנִים ״נִזְכֶּה וְנִחְיֶה״ וְגוֹ׳ לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ וּלְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁהוּא ״עוֹלָם שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ אָרוֹךְ״ וְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם בִּמְהֵרָה בְּיָמֵינוּ אָמֵן
notes.body_html: Hoshea 6:2: “יְחַיֵּנוּ מִיֹּמָיִם, בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי יְקִמֵנוּ, וְנִחְיֶה לְפָנָיו” — “He will revive us after two days; on the third day He will raise us up, and we shall live before Him.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — a prophecy of Israel’s future revival and resurrection. R’ Tzadok’s use: from the rung of a mere “lengthening of years,” Israel will ascend to “and we shall live” — the full life of the days of Mashiach and the World to Come.

notes.body_html: “A world that is wholly long” (Kiddushin 39b; Chullin 142a): expounding the reward of “that your days may be lengthened” (Devarim 5:16; 22:7), the Gemara teaches — “‘that it may be well with you’ — in the world that is wholly good; ‘and that your days may be lengthened’ — in the world that is wholly long [olam she-kulo aroch].” Meforshim: Rashi — the Torah’s promise of “length of days” points, at its depth, to the eternal World to Come. R’ Tzadok’s use: from the “lengthening of years” granted in this world, Israel will merit “the life of Olam Haba — the world that is wholly long,” eternal life; and on this note he seals the entire siman, “that the study of Mishnayos is a segulah for length of days.”
